parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Fight or Flight is a R-rated action comedy with clear genre conventions. The violence is sustained but stylized in the way of contemporary action comedies rather than realistic or gory. Strong language throughout. The values are straightforward: one competent person protects another person in danger at personal risk. There is no political messaging, no gender ideology, and no progressive subtext. Teenagers 15 and up who enjoy action comedies in the John Wick or Nobody vein will find this entertaining and ideologically unambiguous. Not appropriate for younger children due to violence and language.

tropeAudit.name: Individual competence deployed to protect another person in danger
tropeAudit.explanation: Cole is a mercenary recruited to identify a specific passenger on a commercial flight. When assassins start killing everyone who might be that passenger, Cole shifts from identifier to protector. The decision point is immediate and unambiguous: he can look out for himself, or he can use his skills to protect Suri. He chooses protection. The film does not make this choice complicated or tortured. He decides to fight. This is the classical action film framework: one person, already capable, uses that capability in service of someone who needs it.

tropeAudit.name: Resourcefulness and improvisation under extreme constraint
tropeAudit.explanation: A commercial airplane is one of the most confined action settings available. No backup is coming. No weapons beyond whatever can be scavenged or improvised. Cole cannot call for reinforcements, cannot escape the situation, and cannot stop fighting because the next wave is always already there. The film's resourcefulness sequences, where Cole uses the plane itself as a fighting environment, are the clearest expression of the traditional action film value: competence plus improvisation plus refusal to quit equals survival. No moral ambiguity required.

tropeAudit.name: Moral clarity: the antagonists are clearly and simply wrong
tropeAudit.explanation: Fight or Flight does not attempt to humanize the assassins or complicate Cole's decision to fight them. They are trying to kill people. He stops them. The film's moral universe is clean in the way that genre films used to be before Hollywood decided moral clarity was naive. Cole does not have a crisis about whether violence is justified. The situation is clear. So is the response.

tropeAudit.name: Protection of a civilian at personal risk as its own reward
tropeAudit.explanation: Cole is not paid to protect Suri. He is not motivated by loyalty, love, or personal history. He protects her because she is in danger and he is the person present who can do something about it. That unadorned sense of obligation, the idea that capability creates responsibility, is a traditional value that contemporary films increasingly feel the need to complicate or undermine. Fight or Flight just plays it straight.

tropeAudit.name: Female lead as capable professional rather than passive protected object
tropeAudit.explanation: Suri is not purely a damsel. She has agency, makes decisions, and contributes to her own survival. This is moderate woke scoring: a female character with agency in a man-protection film has become standard enough that it barely registers as ideological, but it is present. Severity 1 because it does not undercut the film's traditional structure. Centrality Low because Cole's competence remains the film's primary engine.

tropeAudit.name: Diverse ensemble in action context (Indian female lead, Chilean villain)
tropeAudit.explanation: Charithra Chandran as Suri and Marko Zaror as the primary antagonist give the film a more internationally diverse cast than similar genre entries. The casting is not ideologically forced and does not draw attention to itself as diversity programming. Low severity, low centrality.

summary.overall:
Fight or Flight is a film that knows exactly what it is and delivers that thing with efficiency and occasional flair. It is a contained action comedy set on a commercial airplane, built around one premise: one competent man protects one person against a plane full of trained killers. That premise runs 98 minutes and does not waste any of them.

Josh Hartnett's return to genre leading-man territory has been one of the better Hollywood second acts of the decade. His performance in Oppenheimer showed that the weariness he has acquired from a complicated career could be an asset. In Fight or Flight, that same quality works differently: Cole is a professional who has seen too much and does not particularly want to be here, but here he is, and the job needs doing. Hartnett plays reluctant competence better than almost anyone working today.

The confined setting is the film's best asset. Action films in airports or on planes have to solve the same problem: how do you create variety and momentum when the geography is a metal tube? Madigan and his stunt choreographers solve it by treating different sections of the plane as distinct environments, each with its own tactical logic, each offering different improvisational possibilities. The fight sequences work because the space is used rather than ignored.

Marko Zaror, the Chilean martial artist who has appeared in everything from Machete Kills to Netflix action films, is the most physically impressive element of the film. His sequences with Hartnett are the closest Fight or Flight gets to genuine action choreography rather than action editing: two people who know what they are doing moving through space with purpose. The rest of the film's action is serviceable. These sequences are special.

The VVWS score of +11 TRAD reflects a film with essentially no ideological content. Fight or Flight is not making an argument. It is executing a genre. In 2025, when even action comedies feel compelled to have a thesis, that restraint is its own kind of statement. The values implied by the plot, competence, protection of the vulnerable, refusal to walk away when violence is the only option, are traditional by structure rather than by deliberate choice. They are traditional because the genre is traditional. That is good enough.

Not a masterpiece. A well-made action comedy that delivers on its promises and does not try to be something it is not.
summary.adultInsight: Fight or Flight sits in an interesting position in Josh Hartnett's career narrative. He walked away from leading-man Hollywood in his early 30s and returned in his 40s, and something about that trajectory shows in how he plays Cole: a man who has lost the vanity about heroism that younger actors bring to these roles. Cole is not trying to look good. He is trying to keep someone alive. That quality, earned rather than performed, gives the film a texture it would not have with a different lead.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R for action violence and language. Fight or Flight is an entertainment-oriented action comedy with clear genre conventions. The violence is sustained and stylized rather than realistic. No sexual content. The values are unambiguous: one person protecting another at personal risk. Teenagers 15 and up who enjoy action films will find this appropriate and ideologically clean. Not appropriate for younger children due to violence and language.

fidelity_casting.assessment: Fight or Flight is an original screenplay. No source fidelity concerns apply. Josh Hartnett was cast against the trend of younger, more conventionally heroic action leads, which gives the film a distinct quality. No race-swapping or forced diversity insertions are applicable to original material.

comparison_films.comparison: Liam Neeson action thriller set on a commercial airplane. Similar spatial constraints, similar one-man-vs-the-plane premise. Fight or Flight is lighter in tone and less interested in conspiracy mechanics. Non-Stop is more paranoid. Both use the airplane geography well.

author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: The Piano Lesson does not qualify as a woke trap. The margin is positive (+5 TRAD), automatically disqualifying it under VVWS v1.1 criteria. The film's values orientation, centered on family legacy, ancestral obligation, and a man's drive to own land, is evident from its premise and marketing as an August Wilson adaptation. seoTitle: Is The Piano Lesson (2024) Woke? Netflix Review | VirtueVigil
seoDescription: VirtueVigil's full VVWS v1.1 review of The Piano Lesson (2024). Samuel L. Jackson, John David Washington, Danielle Deadwyler. Netflix. Is it woke? Verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN (+5 margin).
seoKeywords: is The Piano Lesson appropriate for families

director.name: Malcolm Washington
director.ideology: MIXED, LEANING TRADITIONAL. Malcolm Washington is August Wilson's grandson making his feature directorial debut adapting his grandfather's work. The ideological framing of the film is largely August Wilson's, not Hollywood's. Wilson's plays are rooted in Black American experience but they are not progressive in the contemporary sense. His worldview is about family obligation, ancestral debt, masculine purpose, spiritual continuity, and the cost of forgetting where you came from. Malcolm Washington is faithful to that worldview, which makes this a more traditionally grounded film than its Netflix pedigree might suggest.
director.profile: Malcolm Washington previously directed music videos and shorts. This is his first feature, and it is a serious debut. He handles the ensemble with assurance, keeps the film's theatrical origins present without making it feel like a filmed stage play, and stages the supernatural finale with real conviction. What he brings beyond craft is something harder to teach: he clearly understands what the play is actually about, and he makes sure the film communicates it.

writers.names: Virgil Williams and Malcolm Washington (screenplay), August Wilson (source play)
writers.profile: The source play is one of the centerpieces of August Wilson's Pittsburgh Cycle, ten plays covering Black American life decade by decade through the 20th century. The Piano Lesson is set in Pittsburgh in 1936 and is, at its core, a debate about how to honor the past while building a future. Williams and Malcolm Washington's adaptation preserves the play's essential architecture and its central conflict. The screenplay expands the physical world of the play, a single house, into a broader environment without losing the chamber-drama intensity that makes the source material work.

lead_producer.name: Todd Black / Jason Blumenthal / Steve Tisch

composer.name: Branford Marsalis
composer.profile: Marsalis brings blues, gospel, and jazz idioms to a score that feels organically connected to Pittsburgh in 1936 without being a museum exhibit of period sound. The music does something important in the supernatural sequences: it does not signal 'horror.' It signals 'presence.' The ancestors in this film are not villains. They are participants. Marsalis's score treats them that way.

cinematographer.name: Tobias Lindholm
cinematographer.profile: Actually the cinematography is by Tobias A. Schliessler, whose work here emphasizes the warmth and claustrophobia of the family home. The house is photographed as a living space full of accumulated history. The piano at the center of the room is treated as a physical presence that commands the camera. The supernatural sequences shift style without becoming incoherent. The transition is handled skillfully.

casting_director.name: Francine Maisler
casting_director.profile: Samuel L. Jackson as Uncle Doaker is quietly extraordinary. Doaker is a witness and a keeper of history. He knows the price that was paid for the piano and he is not going to let anyone forget it. Jackson plays him with stillness and weight. John David Washington as Boy Willie is the film's engine: ambitious, loud, funny, infuriating, and ultimately more complicated than he first appears. Danielle Deadwyler as Berniece carries the piano's emotional meaning throughout. The ensemble is uniformly strong, which matters for a play that requires every character to hold their own against the material.

The thematic content, family legacy, ancestral obligation, the responsibility to honor those who sacrificed before us, is the kind of material that can generate meaningful family conversation. Teenagers who study American history or literature will benefit from understanding August Wilson's work. The supernatural finale may disturb younger viewers, but it is not graphically violent. fidelityCasting.assessment: STRONG
fidelityCasting.explanation: The Piano Lesson is an August Wilson play about a Black American family in 1936 Pittsburgh, and every principal cast member is Black. This is both historically appropriate and artistically correct. No ideological casting manipulation. Samuel L. Jackson's age relative to the character is a slight stretch from the play's original conception but serves the film well, as his gravitas matches what Doaker represents in the family's moral architecture.

summary.overall:
August Wilson is underrated in contemporary culture. Not by academics or theater people, who treat him with the respect he deserves. But by the broader culture that increasingly equates Black American storytelling with contemporary progressive politics. Wilson's work does not fit that mold. His plays are about property, ancestry, obligation, masculine purpose, and the cost of forgetting where you came from. Those are not progressive themes. They are ancient themes. Which makes The Piano Lesson, adapted for Netflix by Malcolm Washington and arriving in 2024, a useful corrective.

The setup: Boy Willie Charles (John David Washington) arrives from Mississippi at the Pittsburgh home of his sister Berniece (Danielle Deadwyler) and Uncle Doaker (Samuel L. Jackson) with a plan. He wants to sell the family piano, an heirloom carved by his enslaved great-great-grandfather with portraits of the family, and use the money to buy the land in Mississippi where their family was once enslaved. Own the land. Build something. Stop living on someone else's property.

Berniece refuses. The piano is the family's history. It was stolen from a white family at the cost of two of their relatives' lives. You do not sell the blood of your ancestors.

This is the central argument of the play, and it is not one with a clear winner. Wilson is not making a simple case for one side. Boy Willie is not wrong. Berniece is not wrong. They are both right about different things, and the tension between them, the obligation to the past versus the obligation to the future, is something every family that has ever argued about what to do with an inheritance will recognize.

The film earns TRADITIONAL LEAN because its fundamental values are traditional ones. Ancestral obligation is not a progressive concept. The idea that you owe something to the dead who paid a price so you could live is not a progressive concept. Boy Willie's hunger to own land, to plant his feet in a place that belongs to him, is one of the oldest masculine drives in human civilization. The film honors all of this without irony.

Malcolm Washington directs with real authority for a debut feature. He keeps the chamber-drama energy of the play alive while expanding the physical world. Samuel L. Jackson does the quiet work here: Doaker is the keeper of the family's history, and Jackson plays him with the kind of gravity that comes from actually understanding what you're carrying. John David Washington as Boy Willie is the film's engine, funny and infuriating and ultimately more than the loudmouth he appears to be. Danielle Deadwyler is very good. The ensemble is uniformly strong.

The supernatural finale, where Berniece finally plays the piano to call on the ancestors to cast out the ghost that has been terrorizing the house, is handled with conviction. Branford Marsalis's score does not signal horror. It signals presence. The ancestors in this film are not demons. They are invested. The film believes in them. That spiritual dimension, the idea that the dead have a legitimate claim on the living, is not a modern progressive position. It is very old.

The woke trope score reflects the film's framing of slavery and racial oppression as the primary identity lens for the characters. That framing is present and authentic, but it is not the film's only or even primary interest. Wilson uses history to talk about human beings, not the other way around. The net margin is +5 TRAD, which is correct.

This is a serious film made with care about material that deserves care. It is not perfect. The pacing sags slightly in the middle and the first-time direction occasionally leans on the source material rather than fully translating it. But as an introduction to August Wilson for audiences who have not read the plays, it is exactly what it needs to be.
summary.adultInsight: Wilson's Pittsburgh Cycle asks a version of the same question in every play: what do Black Americans owe to the history that made them, and what does that history owe to them in return? The Piano Lesson gives the most direct answer of any play in the cycle: the debt runs both ways. The piano is not just a symbol of suffering. It is a symbol of survival. The ancestors carved their faces into it so they would not be forgotten. Berniece has been too afraid to play it. When she finally plays it at the end, she is not just driving out a ghost. She is paying the debt she has been avoiding. Adult viewers who think about the nature of inherited obligation, financial, spiritual, historical, will find the film richer than its Netflix drama packaging suggests.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for thematic content and brief language. Appropriate for teens 13+ and families. One of the more thematically rich films VirtueVigil has reviewed at this rating level. The material about ancestry, legacy, and obligation is appropriate for teenage viewers and can generate meaningful family conversation.

tropeAudit.name: Ancestral legacy and family honor as binding moral obligation
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's central argument is that you cannot sell your ancestors. The piano was carved by Boy Willie and Berniece's great-great-grandfather to preserve the family's faces for eternity. Their relatives died so it could be recovered. Selling it would be a transaction with the dead, and the dead did not agree to it. This is a profoundly traditional moral position: the living are stewards of what was built and preserved by those who came before them. They do not own it outright. They hold it in trust.

tropeAudit.name: Man's drive to own land and build a future through honest work
tropeAudit.explanation: Boy Willie's goal is not abstract. He wants to buy specific land in Mississippi. He wants to put his name on a deed. He wants to plant something in soil that belongs to him. This drive, the masculine hunger for property and permanence, is treated by the film as legitimate and admirable, not as materialism to be overcome. Wilson understood that the right to own land was not just economic for Black Americans in 1936. It was existential. The film honors that without the progressive framework that would turn it into a statement about reparations.

tropeAudit.name: Family bonds and communal loyalty honored above personal gain
tropeAudit.explanation: Every major character in the film places family obligation above individual interest at some point. Doaker has stayed in Pittsburgh to watch over the family. Wining Boy, the wastrel uncle, returns to help. Even Boy Willie, whose plan would theoretically benefit himself most, frames his desire in terms of what their father would have wanted, what the family's future requires. The communal bond is the film's assumed moral baseline.

tropeAudit.name: Spiritual and ancestral dimension treated as real and authoritative
tropeAudit.explanation: The ghost of Sutter is not a metaphor in this film. It is a presence. The family acknowledges it, argues about it, and eventually confronts it. More importantly, when Berniece plays the piano to call on the ancestors, they respond. The spiritual world is depicted as a reality that the living must negotiate with. This is a traditional and very old worldview. It is not the Christianity of the church-going Avery, but it is a framework that takes the claims of the dead seriously and treats spiritual reality as something that demands a response.

tropeAudit.name: Slavery and racial oppression as the primary identity framework
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's characters understand themselves primarily in relation to their history as enslaved people and their descendants. The piano's value is defined by the slavery that produced its carvings. Boy Willie's land hunger is defined by the history of dispossession. This is authentic to Wilson's source material and to the historical reality of 1936 Pittsburgh. VVWS scores it as a woke trope because it employs the identity-as-oppression-history framework, not because the historical content is inaccurate.

tropeAudit.name: Systemic racism as explanatory lens for family conflict and individual choice
tropeAudit.explanation: The conflict over the piano cannot be fully separated from its racial history. The piano was owned by a white family whose ancestors owned Boy Willie and Berniece's ancestors as property. The transaction, whatever choice the family makes about the piano, takes place in a world shaped by that history. Wilson does not let the characters or the audience forget this context. VVWS scores the framing as a mild woke element; Wilson's treatment of it is more historically grounded than ideologically programmed.

director.name: Sofia Coppola
director.ideology: STRONGLY WOKE. Coppola has never pretended otherwise. Her films are consistently about women trapped by powerful men, by wealth, by social expectation. She is a gifted filmmaker making films that proceed from a feminist worldview, and Priscilla is probably the most direct expression of that worldview in her career. Give her credit for consistency. She is not hiding the ball.
director.profile: Coppola is a legitimately talented director. Her visual sense is excellent. Her control of tone, pacing, and period atmosphere is nearly unmatched in contemporary American cinema. The problem for VirtueVigil readers is not her craft. It is what she does with it. In Priscilla, all of that craft is in service of a portrait of marriage as captivity. The film is beautiful and uncomfortable simultaneously, which is probably what Coppola intended.

writers.names: Sofia Coppola (screenplay), Priscilla Presley and Sandra Harmon (source memoir)
writers.profile: The film is adapted from Priscilla Presley's 1985 memoir 'Elvis and Me.' Coppola's screenplay is faithful to the memoir's emotional arc, which positions Priscilla as a young woman who fell in love with a force of nature and gradually realized she had been absorbed into his world rather than building one of her own. Coppola strips out most of the adulatory mythology around Elvis and keeps almost entirely to Priscilla's subjective experience. The result is a one-sided portrait, but the source material is inherently one-sided.

composer.name: Phoenix
composer.profile: Coppola's longtime collaborators Phoenix provide a score that leans heavily on period atmosphere without being merely nostalgic. The music reflects Priscilla's inner world more than Elvis's public persona, which fits the film's approach exactly. Some reviewers found it distracting. Others found it the film's most original element. Both responses are legitimate.

cinematographer.name: Philippe Le Sourd
cinematographer.profile: Le Sourd shoots the film in a warm, slightly overexposed style that makes Graceland look simultaneously gorgeous and suffocating. The interiors feel like a cage you would want to live in, which is the point. His work here is among the best cinematography of 2023.

casting_director.name: Francine Maisler
casting_director.profile: Cailee Spaeny won the Venice Film Festival Best Actress prize for this performance, and the award is deserved. She is onscreen for almost every minute of the film's runtime and carries it entirely through physical presence and small choices rather than big speeches. Jacob Elordi is used deliberately as a symbol more than a fully developed person, which reflects Coppola's thesis. He is beautiful and remote and never quite reachable. That's intentional. Whether it is fair to the historical Elvis is a separate question.

parentalGuidance.mpaaDescriptors: Sexual content, brief language, mature thematic content involving a controlling relationship
contentWarnings: Sexual content and implied intimacy, not graphic but present
Depiction of an adult man pursuing a relationship with a 14-year-old girl
Emotional manipulation and psychological control depicted as the central dynamic
Prescription drug use and sleeping pill dependency
Brief language
parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Priscilla is not appropriate for younger children and carries real complexity for teenagers. The film's depiction of an older man pursuing a very young girl is handled without gratuitousness but also without apology. Parents with older teenagers (16+) who watch it should be prepared to discuss what healthy versus controlling relationships look like. The film treats the controlling dynamic as obviously problematic, which can be a useful entry point for that conversation. The values framing of the film itself is feminist and not traditional, so parents should bring their own context.

fidelityCasting.assessment: STRONG
fidelityCasting.explanation: Priscilla Presley is white and Cailee Spaeny is white. Elvis Presley is white and Jacob Elordi is white. The historical figures are cast with fidelity to their actual backgrounds. Elordi's physical resemblance to Elvis (particularly the height and bone structure) is striking. No race-swapping or ideological substitution in the main cast.

summary.overall:
Sofia Coppola is one of the most consistent directors working in American cinema. Consistent in craft. Consistent in worldview. And in Priscilla, consistent in producing a film that is both genuinely beautiful and ideologically predictable.

The film adapts Priscilla Presley's memoir to tell the story from her point of view: a 14-year-old American girl stationed in Germany meets Elvis Presley, falls under his spell, is brought back to Graceland, and spends the next decade learning that being chosen by the most famous man in the world means being reshaped entirely to his specifications. She dyes her hair black. She keeps the hours he keeps. She waits. He tours. He is unfaithful. She endures. Eventually she leaves.

Coppola's thesis is not subtle. Elvis is filmed from a slight distance throughout. We never really get inside his head. He exists as a force of nature that Priscilla orbits. That framing is deliberate. The film is not interested in Elvis's perspective or complexity. It is interested in what it feels like to be the person who loves someone who cannot stop being Elvis long enough to actually be present.

Calilee Spaeny is extraordinary in the lead. She won the Venice Best Actress prize and it is not a sentimental award. She conveys years of patient endurance in small gestures: the way she watches Elvis perform for others in the room, the way she adjusts herself to his preferences reflexively, the way she registers something breaking before we consciously see it break. It is a performance that works through accumulation. By the end you feel the weight she has been carrying.

Jacob Elordi is used differently. He is not asked to give a full performance in the way Baz Luhrmann asked Austin Butler to give one. He is asked to be a symbol, warm and remote and never quite reachable. The result is that Elvis in this film is not so much a person as an atmosphere. Some viewers found this approach unsatisfying. The argument for it is that the film is Priscilla's experience, and Priscilla's experience of Elvis was partly that he remained unknowable.

Philippe Le Sourd's cinematography makes Graceland look like a beautiful prison. The interiors are gorgeous and suffocating in equal measure. Phoenix's score reflects Priscilla's interior world rather than Elvis's mythology. All of Coppola's craft is pointed in the same direction.

From a VirtueVigil perspective, the problems are clear. The film scores WOKE because its entire structure frames marriage to a powerful man as captivity and self-discovery as departure. The traditional understanding of marriage, as a binding covenant between two people who navigate its difficulties together, is not available in this film's emotional vocabulary. Elvis is consistently coded as the jailer. Priscilla's decision to leave is coded as maturity and self-actualization. The traditional reading, that she might have worked to save the marriage or that her choices in staying also carried moral weight, is simply absent.

None of this makes the film poorly crafted. It doesn't. But craft in service of a bad thesis is still a bad thesis. Priscilla is a beautifully made feminist portrait of marriage as captivity. VirtueVigil readers will recognize what they are watching from the first act.
summary.adultInsight: The film raises a question it deliberately declines to answer: is Elvis Presley's behavior in this film unusual for powerful men of his era, or is it the normal operation of male authority in traditional society? Coppola seems to suggest the latter. Priscilla's parents hand her over to Elvis with something between pride and relief. The women at Graceland accept the rules without complaint. The system is presented as systemic, not individual. Adult viewers who think seriously about traditional gender structures will find this argument more interesting than the film's critics on either side typically acknowledge. Coppola is not making a simple villain movie. She is making an argument about what the whole arrangement looked like from inside it.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R for sexual content and mature thematic content. Not appropriate for children. Appropriate for parents and teenagers 16+ with discussion context about relationship dynamics, control, and the difference between devotion and submission.

tropeAudit.name: Powerful man controls and isolates young woman as the film's central thesis
tropeAudit.explanation: This is not a subplot. It is the entire film. From the moment Elvis invites Priscilla to Graceland, through a decade of waiting and adjusting and being reshaped to his specifications, the film's thesis is that this relationship was fundamentally about one powerful person controlling a young woman's life. The depiction is authentic to the memoir and central to every scene. The controlling dynamic is not one element among others. It is the subject.

tropeAudit.name: Marriage framed as patriarchal trap requiring feminist liberation to escape
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's emotional arc is a classic feminist liberation narrative: woman discovers selfhood by leaving a powerful man. When Priscilla tells Elvis she is leaving, the film's emotional temperature changes. The muted palette brightens slightly. The score opens up. Coppola frames the departure as a kind of birth. The implication is that the marriage was the problem to be solved and independence the solution. This framing is deeply embedded in the film's structure.

tropeAudit.name: Age-gap relationship framed as inherently predatory and exploitative
tropeAudit.explanation: Elvis is 24 when he meets 14-year-old Priscilla. The film does not editorialized with voiceover about this, but the visual and emotional framing leaves no ambiguity about the power imbalance. The parents' willingness to allow the relationship is presented as complicit rather than naive. The historical facts make this trope authentic rather than invented, but Coppola's framing emphasizes the exploitation angle throughout.

tropeAudit.name: Leaving a marriage depicted as the primary act of female self-realization
tropeAudit.explanation: The film ends with Priscilla driving away from Graceland. The departure is the film's emotional payoff. No effort is made in the final act to show the cost to her child or to explore what reconciliation might have looked like. Departure equals maturity. The traditional counter-narrative, that the difficult work of staying and repairing might also constitute self-actualization, is not available in this film's framework.

tropeAudit.name: Period-accurate 1960s domestic life depicted without condescension
tropeAudit.explanation: Coppola is a scrupulous period filmmaker. The costuming, production design, and social rituals of Graceland in the 1960s are rendered authentically and without the snide distance that lesser directors might bring to depicting a traditional domestic arrangement. The world is shown as it was, with some sympathy for why it made sense to people who lived inside it. This is a small traditional credit in an otherwise hostile film.

tropeAudit.name: Long-term devotion in an imperfect marriage acknowledged as real
tropeAudit.explanation: Priscilla genuinely loves Elvis. The film does not reduce her commitment to naivety or delusion. Her love is treated as real even as the film critiques the conditions under which it operates. A few scenes show the two of them in genuine warmth. This small acknowledgment of authentic love within a flawed marriage earns a minimal traditional credit, though the film's overall architecture ultimately subordinates this to the liberation narrative.

seoTitle: Is Maestro (2023) Woke? Bradley Cooper Netflix Review | VirtueVigil
seoDescription: VirtueVigil's VVWS v1.1 review of Maestro (2023). Bradley Cooper, Carey Mulligan, Netflix. Leonard Bernstein biopic. Trope audit, parental guidance. Verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN (+3 margin).

externalScores.oscarCategories: Best Picture, Best Actor (Cooper), Best Actress (Mulligan), Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Makeup and Hairstyling

director.name: Bradley Cooper
director.ideology: MIXED. Cooper is a difficult figure to categorize ideologically. He is not a performative progressive. His public profile is more about craft than politics. A Star Is Born showed real sensitivity to addiction and male vulnerability without going woke in the ideological sense. Maestro is similarly complicated: it takes a bisexual man as its subject and treats his homosexual relationships sympathetically, but it also centers the marriage and gives Felicia Mulligan the film's moral weight. Cooper is a craftsman who made a complicated film about a complicated man. The film's score is TRADITIONAL LEAN because Cooper allowed the marriage to be the center, not the affairs.
director.profile: Cooper's second directorial feature follows A Star Is Born (2018). He wrote, directed, produced, and starred in both. Maestro was seven years in development. The level of commitment to the project is evident in every frame. Whether you agree with every choice, the film is not a careless one. The controversy over Cooper's prosthetic nose and the decision not to cast a Jewish actor as Bernstein is worth noting: Steven Spielberg and the Bernstein family approved the casting, which puts the debate in a different light.

writers.profile: Singer co-wrote Spotlight and First Man. His work tends toward careful, research-intensive biopics with strong dramatic structure. Here the screenplay is divided between two time periods (early/courtship in black and white, later years in color) and two emotional registers: the intoxicating early romance and the complicated later marriage. The structure works better in the first half than the second. The late-film confrontation between Bernstein and Felicia about his affairs is the script's best scene. It is written with real honesty about the kind of love that survives things it shouldn't have to survive.

lead_producer.name: Bradley Cooper / Martin Scorsese / Steven Spielberg

composer.name: Leonard Bernstein (archival) / N/A original score
composer.profile: The film uses Bernstein's own music throughout, which is both obvious and the right call. Cooper's conducting sequences, particularly the Ely Cathedral sequence where Bernstein conducts Mahler's Second Symphony, are among the most visually and musically striking in recent biopic filmmaking. Cooper trained for six years with Yannick Nezet-Seguin and conducted the actual orchestra himself. The scene works.

cinematographer.name: Matthew Libatique
cinematographer.profile: Libatique shot A Star Is Born and Black Swan. His work here is remarkable: the shift from black-and-white for the early years to color for the later period is not a gimmick. The black-and-white sections feel like memory idealized. The color sections feel like life lived imperfectly. The Ely Cathedral conducting sequence is a single extended shot and it is extraordinary. The film earned its cinematography Oscar nomination.

casting_director.name: Francine Maisler
casting_director.profile: Carey Mulligan as Felicia is the performance of her career. The film belongs to her in its second half. Her confrontation scene with Cooper over his affairs is devastating not because it is loud but because it is quiet. She has loved this man for decades. She knows who he is. The grief in the scene is not surprise. It is exhaustion. Cooper disappears into Bernstein reasonably well. The prosthetic makeup is occasionally distracting in close-ups but Cooper's physicality and movement as Bernstein are convincing in the conducting sequences.

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Maestro is not appropriate for children and requires maturity in teenage viewers. The film deals with marital infidelity, bisexuality, and a decades-long complicated marriage. Parents who choose to watch with older teenagers should be prepared to discuss what the film shows about commitment, sacrifice, and the complexity of loving a deeply flawed person over a lifetime. The film's emotional center, Felicia's devotion and Bernstein's grief at her death, is genuinely moving and provides real discussion material. The values framework of the film is not traditionally religious but treats marriage with more seriousness than most contemporary Hollywood productions.

fidelityCasting.assessment: MIXED
fidelityCasting.explanation: The casting of Bradley Cooper, who is not Jewish, as Leonard Bernstein drew significant commentary. The Bernstein family and Steven Spielberg, who is Jewish, approved the casting and publicly defended it. Bernstein's actual daughter Jamie said she was moved by Cooper's portrayal. The prosthetic nose was the point of most criticism. Whether casting a non-Jewish actor as a Jewish historical figure constitutes a fidelity problem depends on your view of the practice. Carey Mulligan as Chilean-Costa Rican Felicia Montealegre is a similar question. The film does not engage in ideological race-swapping. These are casting choices in the longstanding Hollywood tradition of casting name actors regardless of specific ethnic match.

summary.overall:
The critics who said Maestro was a vanity project were not entirely wrong. Bradley Cooper spent seven years making a film in which he transforms himself into Leonard Bernstein, wears a prosthetic nose, trains to conduct a real orchestra, and plays opposite Carey Mulligan in what turns out to be the film's best performance. There is an element of self-conscious ambition here that occasionally tips toward the grandiose.

But the critics who dismissed it for that reason missed what the film actually does.

Maestro is fundamentally a film about a marriage. Specifically, it is about the marriage between Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegre, a Chilean-Costa Rican actress who loved one of the most brilliant and most exhausting men in 20th-century American music for over thirty years. He was bisexual. He had male lovers throughout their marriage. She knew. She stayed. The film asks why, and it answers with more honesty than most Hollywood productions would risk.

The film is structured in two halves. The black-and-white first half follows the early years: the electric romance, the courtship, the sense that two extraordinary people have found each other. Mulligan and Cooper have real chemistry here. The period is rendered beautifully by cinematographer Matthew Libatique. The music, Bernstein's own, is used throughout to indicate emotional states that dialogue refuses to make explicit.

The color second half is harder. Bernstein is older, his affairs more open, his energy more self-destructive. Felicia has cancer. The marriage is under strain in ways that go beyond infidelity. The film's best scene is a confrontation between them where Mulligan sits across from Cooper and tells him, quietly and without drama, what it has cost her to love him for this long. It is not an accusatory scene. It is more like a reckoning. She is not surprised by him. She is tired. And she still loves him.

That scene is why Maestro scores TRADITIONAL LEAN rather than WOKE. The film treats the marriage as real and serious and worth the cost. Felicia's sacrifice is not presented as weakness or complicity. It is presented as love, complicated and freely chosen. When Bernstein delivers the eulogy at Felicia's funeral, the grief in the scene is the grief of a man who knows he did not deserve the love he was given and accepted it anyway. That is not a progressive moral. That is closer to Dostoevsky.

The woke tropes score reflects the film's sympathetic treatment of Bernstein's bisexuality. His same-sex relationships are not framed as aberrations or as the villain of the piece. They are part of who he is. The film does not ask you to condemn him for them. VirtueVigil scores that as a woke element because the VVWS framework measures trope presence, not artistic intent. A more complete traditional reading of the marriage, one that treated the infidelity as genuinely morally costly rather than as a character trait to be accommodated, would have scored higher.

But the film is what it is. And what it is, is more serious about marriage than most films that get praised for celebrating marriage. Felicia Montealegre deserved better. The film knows that. It says so without saying so. Maestro earns TRADITIONAL LEAN.
summary.adultInsight: The Bernstein family's involvement in and approval of the film is unusual for a Hollywood biopic. Most estates are protective. The Bernsteins were apparently willing to let the full picture be shown. What the full picture shows is a man who loved his wife, loved his family, loved music, and loved men, sometimes simultaneously and sometimes in ways that hurt people he cared about. The film does not resolve this into a simple moral lesson. Adult viewers who have watched long marriages navigate complicated terrain will recognize something true in the film's refusal to assign a verdict. Some things are not resolvable. They are endured. And the endurance, done with love, becomes its own kind of answer.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R for sexual content, brief drug use, and language. Appropriate for adults and mature teenagers 16+ with discussion context. The film provides real material for conversations about commitment, sacrifice, and what marriage actually requires over a lifetime.

tropeAudit.name: Marriage as long-term commitment, the film's emotional and moral center
tropeAudit.explanation: The film is structured around the marriage of Leonard Bernstein and Felicia Montealegre. Everything else, the affairs, the career, the music, the public persona, is orbiting that central relationship. The film's emotional climax is not a conducting triumph or a public scandal. It is Bernstein's grief at Felicia's death. Cooper stages the eulogy scene with real weight. The marriage is treated as the most significant thing in Bernstein's life, more significant than his genius. That is a traditional framing, whatever complications surround it.

tropeAudit.name: Wife's sacrifice and decades-long loyalty treated with deep respect
tropeAudit.explanation: Felicia Montealegre is the moral center of the film, and Carey Mulligan plays her as a woman of immense dignity and inner strength. Her choice to stay in the marriage despite knowing about Bernstein's affairs is treated not as weakness or naivety but as a form of love that costs something and is chosen anyway. The confrontation scene where she articulates what this has cost her is one of the most honest depictions of marital sacrifice in recent American cinema. The film respects her.

tropeAudit.name: Family as anchor for a brilliant but chaotic man
tropeAudit.explanation: The film shows the Bernstein household as a genuine family: children, domestic life, shared routines. When Bernstein eventually leaves Felicia for a male lover and the family unit fractures, the film does not celebrate the departure. The cost to the children and to Felicia is shown plainly. Bernstein returns after Felicia's cancer diagnosis. Whether that return is redemption or guilt or love or all three is left for the viewer. But the family is shown throughout as something real and worth returning to.

tropeAudit.name: Bisexual protagonist's same-sex affairs depicted sympathetically as authentic to his identity
tropeAudit.explanation: The film does not frame Bernstein's bisexuality as a moral failing to be condemned. His male lovers are depicted as real relationships with their own emotional weight. The David Oppenheim relationship in particular is shown with warmth in the early part of the film. The film is not making the case that Bernstein's affairs were fine. It is showing them as authentic to who he was. That distinction matters for VirtueVigil scoring: VVWS records sympathetic LGBTQ depictions as woke tropes regardless of narrative context.

tropeAudit.name: Male infidelity with same-sex partners treated as character complexity rather than moral failing
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's treatment of Bernstein's affairs with men positions them as inseparable from his artistic genius and emotional complexity. The implicit argument is that you cannot have the Bernstein who conducted West Side Story and Chichester Psalms without also having the Bernstein who could not commit to one person. This is a romantic-artist framing that treats transgression as the cost of genius rather than as a moral question. Cooper does not fully interrogate this framing.

title: Heads of State
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
rating: PG-13 (Action Violence, Language, Brief Suggestive Content)
studio: Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer / The Safran Company / Potboiler / Big Indie Pictures

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Heads of State does not qualify as a woke trap. The margin is positive (+8 TRAD), disqualifying it automatically. More to the point, the film's political satire of the American president as a buffoonish action movie star is visible in every piece of marketing. Nobody watching the trailer was surprised. The political commentary is front-loaded rather than concealed. Audiences knew what they were getting.

seoTitle: Is Heads of State Woke? Idris Elba John Cena Film Review | VirtueVigil
seoDescription: VirtueVigil's full VVWS v1.1 review of Heads of State (2025). Idris Elba vs. John Cena. Prime Video action comedy. Trope audit, parental guidance. Verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN (+8 margin).
seoKeywords: Heads of State woke or not

director.name: Ilya Naishuller
director.ideology: MIXED. Naishuller is a Russian-born filmmaker best known for Hardcore Henry (2015) and Nobody (2021). His politics are not prominently ideological. His films are primarily exercises in kinetic action filmmaking. With Heads of State, he inherited a script with clear political commentary baked in, and he delivered what he was hired to deliver: well-staged action sequences and a brisk pace. The political satirizing of the American president doesn't appear to be his agenda so much as the screenplay's, and he applies his craft to it without appearing to relish it.
director.profile: Naishuller made Hardcore Henry as an experiment in first-person action filmmaking. Nobody, his previous collaboration with producer Peter Safran, was a lean, effective action film that punched above its modest budget. His instincts are for momentum and physical clarity. Heads of State is his most expensive and commercially visible project. The action sequences in Trieste particularly are well-directed, and the film moves. His weakness is that he directs tone in broad strokes, and the political comedy in the first act needed more precision than he brought to it.

writers.names: Josh Appelbaum, Andre Nemec, Harrison Query
writers.profile: Appelbaum and Nemec are journeymen television writers whose credits include Alias and Mission: Impossible Ghost Protocol. Harrison Query wrote the original story. The screenplay's central conceit, an action movie star elected president, is pointed at a specific political target and the film doesn't pretend otherwise. The script's strengths are in the action mechanics and the interplay between the two leads. Its weakness is in the political satire, which is too blunt to land as satire and too mild to function as serious commentary. The result is something that agitates viewers who recognize the target while not being sharp enough to actually say anything about him.

composer.name: Steven Price
composer.profile: Price has scored major action and adventure films including Gravity and Suicide Squad. His work here is solid and functional, supporting the action sequences without competing with them. The score does its job and doesn't leave a strong impression, which is what this kind of film needs from its composer.

cinematographer.name: Ben Davis
cinematographer.profile: Davis is one of the more accomplished cinematographers working in mainstream British cinema, with credits including Guardians of the Galaxy, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing Missouri, and Wrath of Man. He brings visual quality to what could have been a flat streaming product. The European locations, Spain, Belarus, Warsaw, Croatia, Trieste, are photographed with geography and texture. The film looks better than its genre requires.

casting_director.name: Lucy Bevan / Laray Mayfield
casting_director.profile: The casting of Idris Elba and John Cena as the central pair is the film's entire premise, and it works better than it has any right to. Elba brings genuine gravitas to a role that could have been a sketch character. Cena plays the buffoon with more charm than the script deserves. Priyanka Chopra Jonas as MI6 officer Bisset is given more to do than the female-action-hero role usually offers, though the script ultimately relies on her as the competent adult in the room. Jack Quaid as the CIA station agent is a bright spot in a supporting cast that doesn't get much depth.

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Heads of State is a PG-13 action comedy designed for broad audiences. The violence is action-movie standard, choreographed and consequences-minimized. Parents should be aware that the film satirizes the American president as a dumb action movie star, which reads as clearly political to adults and may spark conversation with older teens. The espionage thriller elements, Russian arms dealer as villain, NATO as the thing worth protecting, are pro-Western in their overall orientation. Fine for teens 13 and up who enjoy action comedies.

fidelityCasting.assessment: NEUTRAL
fidelityCasting.explanation: Heads of State is an original story, not an adaptation, so fidelity casting is evaluated against internal logic and the roles as written. Elba as the British PM is not a race-swapped historical figure but a fictional character created for the film. Cena as an American president who was formerly an action movie star is clearly designed to suggest a specific real-world figure, though the film keeps that suggestion implicit. Priyanka Chopra Jonas as a senior MI6 agent is the most notable casting choice from a demographics perspective: the character is of South Asian heritage in a role that could have been written for anyone. No historical figures are subject to casting substitution here.

summary.overall:
Heads of State wants to be two things at once: a politically sharp satire and a big dumb action comedy. It's better at the second than the first, which means audiences willing to meet it on its own terms will have a decent time.

The premise: the US President is Will Derringer, a former action movie star elected on the strength of his screen persona. The UK Prime Minister is Sam Clarke, a serious military veteran who finds Derringer embarrassing. Air Force One gets shot down over Belarus. The two world leaders have to survive, trust each other, and stop a Russian arms dealer named Viktor Gradov from using stolen intelligence to blow up NATO.

Nobody is confused about what 'Will Derringer: action movie star turned president' is a reference to. The film knows it, the marketing knew it, and the casting of John Cena as a man who's famous for physical dominance and limited sophistication makes the allusion explicit. It's a sharp enough conceit on paper. The execution is less precise.

The problem with political satire is it needs to either commit or back off. Heads of State does neither cleanly. Derringer starts the film as a genuine buffoon. By the third act he's competent, physically brave, and has earned Clarke's respect. The film's arc is a redemption story for a character the screenplay introduced as a joke. You can't do both. Either the dumb action star president is the joke, or he's the hero. Trying to make him both produces a film that feels politically uncertain rather than boldly satirical.

What saves it is the chemistry between Elba and Cena, and the action sequences. Elba plays Clarke with the kind of weight that makes you forget you're watching a genre exercise. His scenes with Cena in the middle of the film, stranded in Eastern Europe, arguing about leadership and trust while being hunted, are the film's best work. Cena is more charming here than he's been in anything else: he plays dumb well, but he also lands the moments where Derringer's genuine decency comes through.

The film's values alignment is genuinely interesting from a VirtueVigil perspective. The NATO alliance is portrayed as something worth protecting. Russia is unambiguously the source of the threat. A Russian arms dealer is the villain, assisted by American political traitors. The film doesn't spend energy on moral equivalence between the West and its adversaries. The Western alliance defends itself and wins. That's a traditional framework.

The complications come from the political satire, which targets American populism rather than progressivism, and from Priyanka Chopra Jonas as the MI6 operative who is consistently the most competent adult in the room. Neither of these undercuts the film's overall orientation enough to push it below TRADITIONAL LEAN, but they're worth noting.

Ilya Naishuller stages action with clarity and energy. The Trieste summit sequence in the third act earns the film's runtime. If you're going to Prime Video for a well-made action comedy that doesn't ask you to feel bad about Western civilization, Heads of State delivers that.
summary.adultInsight: The 'action movie star becomes president' premise is more interesting as a cultural observation than the film fully develops. The real question it raises but doesn't pursue: what does it mean that a democracy chose its leader based on a cinematic persona? The film treats Derringer's election as a joke without examining what it says about the electorate that put him there. That's the thread a sharper screenplay would have pulled. What we get instead is a story about whether Derringer can rise to the occasion, which is a more comfortable question. Adult viewers who want to think about democratic legitimacy and celebrity politics will find the film gesturing at something it ultimately declines to explore.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for action violence throughout, brief strong language, and some suggestive material. The violence is action-movie standard with minimal consequences. The political satire is legible to adults and older teens. Parents of politically engaged teenagers might use the film's premise as a conversation starter about celebrity and democratic politics, or might find its specific target too pointed for family viewing. Fine for most 13-year-olds.

tropeAudit.name: Male friendship forged under pressure
tropeAudit.explanation: The Clarke-Derringer relationship is the film's emotional spine. Two men who despise each other are forced to depend on each other for survival, and the film earns their eventual friendship through the specific shared experiences of Eastern European chaos, bad hotels, and firefights. This is the classic buddy action template and it works here because Elba and Cena have genuine chemistry. Traditional male friendship, built through shared ordeal rather than sentiment, is what the film is actually about underneath the political scaffolding.

tropeAudit.name: Defense of the Western alliance as unambiguous good
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's entire plot is about preventing the destruction of NATO. NATO solidarity is not presented as a complicated geopolitical question. It's the thing worth protecting. Russia is the source of the threat. The arms dealer wants to use stolen intelligence to dissolve the alliance because a fractured West is easier to exploit. The film doesn't entertain moral equivalence. Defending the Western alliance is simply the right thing to do, and the climax vindicates that. This is a strongly traditional geopolitical framework.

tropeAudit.name: Unambiguous foreign adversary as villain
tropeAudit.explanation: Viktor Gradov is a Russian arms dealer. He is simply the enemy. The film doesn't ask audiences to understand his perspective, sympathize with his grievances, or consider whether Western policy created him. He wants to destroy the intelligence infrastructure of the Anglo-American alliance for profit, and he needs to be stopped. This is a traditional good-versus-evil structure applied to contemporary geopolitics.

tropeAudit.name: Competence and personal courage validated through action
tropeAudit.explanation: Both Clarke and Derringer have to get their hands dirty. Clarke's military background gives him physical skills that prove essential. Derringer's action-movie training, played initially for laughs, turns out to be genuinely useful. The film validates competence regardless of its origin. Men who can act under pressure, who don't freeze when it counts, are the film's heroes. Institutional authority matters less than what a person is capable of when the situation demands it.

tropeAudit.name: American president depicted as buffoon and populist joke
tropeAudit.explanation: Will Derringer is an action movie star who got elected president of the United States. The implication is pointed at a specific political figure and the film knows it. The film spends its first act making Derringer the comic relief: he's boorish, unsophisticated, and embarrassing next to the serious British PM. The arc redeems him, but the initial framing is anti-populist satire aimed at a clear target. Audiences who voted for a president the film is satirizing will notice.

tropeAudit.name: Female spy as primary competent adult
tropeAudit.explanation: Priyanka Chopra Jonas's Bisset consistently outperforms and outsmarts the two male leads. She survives situations that kill trained agents. She knows things neither Clarke nor Derringer knows. She makes the critical decisions in the climax. This is the standard female-as-the-real-competent-one template that modern action films deploy so frequently it's become its own genre convention. It's not severe, and Bisset is a likable character. But the structural positioning of the woman as the adult who makes things work while the men bumble is a recognizable trope.

tropeAudit.name: Female American official as the ultimate traitor
tropeAudit.explanation: The big twist is that the American Vice President, Elizabeth Kirk (Carla Gugino), is the real villain who has been working with Gradov to bring down NATO. An American woman in a position of institutional power is the ultimate traitor. This lands awkwardly in a film that also uses Bisset as its most competent female character. The female villain is a separate trope from female empowerment, but both are present here, and together they reflect a screenplay that was making political decisions about gender rather than building characters from the ground up.

seoTitle: Is Fountain of Youth Woke? John Krasinski Natalie Portman Apple TV+ Review | VirtueVigil
seoDescription: VirtueVigil's full VVWS v1.1 review of Fountain of Youth (2025). John Krasinski, Natalie Portman, Guy Ritchie. Apple TV+ adventure. Trope audit, parental guidance. Verdict: TRADITIONAL (+10 margin).
seoKeywords: Fountain of Youth woke or not

director.name: Guy Ritchie
director.ideology: TRADITIONAL LEANING. Ritchie is one of the few working directors in mainstream cinema whose sensibility runs counter to progressive orthodoxy. His films celebrate masculine competence, witty banter between self-reliant men, the pleasure of craft and scheme, and the idea that the smartest and most capable people usually win. He's not political in the heavy-handed sense. His worldview is more Kipling than Karl Marx: men doing interesting things in a world that rewards skill and punishes pretension. Fountain of Youth is probably the most family-accessible film he's made, and his instincts show in what the film celebrates and what it ultimately refuses to endorse.
director.profile: Ritchie's filmography includes Snatch, Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, the Robert Downey Jr. Sherlock Holmes films, The Man from U.N.C.L.E., Aladdin, and The Gentlemen. He's at his best when the material is witty, kinetic, and built around capable characters scheming their way through impossible situations. Fountain of Youth is Ritchie applying his sensibility to an Indiana Jones-style adventure film. The critics who disliked it were largely measuring it against its $180 million budget and Apple's promotional ambitions. Measured against what the film is actually trying to do, it's more successful than that.

writers.profile: Vanderbilt wrote Zodiac, The Amazing Spider-Man films, and White House Down. He's a reliable commercial screenwriter who can build plot and lay clues. His screenplay for Fountain of Youth is criticized for feeling generic, and the criticism has some merit: the adventure-film structure hits its beats predictably. The film's moral architecture, the Fountain as a trap for the selfish and a gift to no one, is more interesting than the mechanics around it. Vanderbilt put the right moral at the center. The path to it feels well-worn.

lead_producer.name: David Ellison / Guy Ritchie / Tripp Vinson
lead_producer.company: Skydance Media / Toff Guy Films / Vinson Films

composer.name: Christopher Benstead
composer.profile: Benstead has worked with Ritchie on multiple projects and his score here is one of the film's better elements. It's energetic, period-aware, and tonally consistent with Ritchie's taste for propulsive, stylized music. The adventure sequences benefit from his work.

cinematographer.name: Ed Wild
cinematographer.profile: Wild shoots the film's multiple international locations with visual coherence and energy. London, Vienna, Egypt, and Thailand all feel like distinct environments rather than interchangeable backlots. The pyramid sequence is particularly well-lit, using actual darkness and torchlight rather than the studio-bright artificiality that kills so many adventure climaxes.

casting_director.name: Lucy Bevan
casting_director.profile: Krasinski and Portman as siblings is a slightly odd pairing on paper but works in practice: they share a sibling shorthand in their scenes that feels earned rather than performed. Krasinski is the natural choice for a charming, competent everyman adventurer. Portman brings real intelligence to Charlotte, the smarter sibling who is also the moral center of the film. Domhnall Gleeson as the villain is good until the third act, where the script doesn't give him enough to do. Eiza Gonzalez as Esme is underused given how much the film hints at her backstory. Stanley Tucci appears briefly and is, as always, a pleasure.

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Fountain of Youth is one of the more family-friendly films VirtueVigil has reviewed with a TRADITIONAL verdict. The action is standard PG-13 adventure-film fare. The film's central moral, that eternal life isn't worth the cost to the people you love, is the kind of lesson parents can discuss openly with children. Charlotte's commitment to her son Thomas as her primary motivation throughout is a strong depiction of maternal instinct. Appropriate for children 10 and up with parents; teens can watch independently.

fidelityCasting.assessment: STRONG
fidelityCasting.explanation: Fountain of Youth is an original story, so fidelity casting is assessed against the characters as written. Luke and Charlotte Purdue are siblings, and Krasinski and Portman play that relationship convincingly. No historical figures are race-swapped or substituted. Arian Moayed as the Interpol inspector is a Middle Eastern actor playing a character with no specified ethnicity; the casting is appropriate. No ideological manipulation of the character roster is evident.

summary.overall:
The critics were unfair to Fountain of Youth. A 35% on Rotten Tomatoes for a Guy Ritchie adventure film starring John Krasinski and Natalie Portman on a $180 million budget tells you more about critical expectations than it does about the film.

The expectations trap here is obvious: Apple spent $180 million and wanted a franchise starter. Critics wanted Indiana Jones or The Mummy, not a mid-tier adventure with prettier photography. The comparison is always punishing. Fountain of Youth is not Raiders of the Lost Ark. It's not trying to be. What it is, evaluated on its own terms, is a competent, occasionally charming adventure film with a genuinely strong moral at its center.

The premise: Luke Purdue (Krasinski) is a treasure hunter who has continued his late father's quest to find the mythological Fountain of Youth. His estranged sister Charlotte (Portman) is a museum curator with a failing marriage and a son she's fighting to protect. Luke needs her expertise. She needs his lawyer. They head across multiple continents, collecting paintings and avoiding assassins and uncovering ancient secrets, while a terminally ill corporate raider named Owen Carver (Gleeson) finances the whole expedition with the specific intention of claiming immortality for himself.

The film's moral is delivered cleanly and without apology. When Luke finally reaches the Fountain and a drop of his blood touches the water, he has a vision: he can live forever, but the energy will drain from those he loves most. He refuses. He chooses his sister over eternal life. The Fountain, in Vanderbilt's conception, isn't an evil object. It's a mirror. It shows you what you're willing to sacrifice, and if what you'd sacrifice is the people you love, the Fountain provides exactly that at the cost of everything that makes life worth living. Carver, who loves no one, drains himself to nothing.

This is a traditional moral. It's been the moral of countless adventure films, fairy tales, and religious parables. Don't sacrifice the people you love for power or immortality. Accept death as the price of love. Choose family.

Ritchie executes this with his characteristic energy and style. The set pieces are well-staged. The sibling dynamic between Krasinski and Portman is the film's best element: they argue like actual siblings, which means they're mean in specific ways and then move on. The film looks expensive and it should: the pyramid interior in the final act is genuinely impressive, and the London, Vienna, and Cairo locations are photographed with care.

The weaknesses are real. The screenplay is predictable in its structure. The supporting characters, particularly Gleeson's Carver and Gonzalez's Esme, are underdeveloped. The film takes about twenty minutes too long to get to the pyramid. And the ending is very clearly sequel-fishing, which Hollywood adventure films do now as a reflex.

From a values standpoint: Fountain of Youth is a solid TRADITIONAL. The family bond between Luke and Charlotte is the film's emotional engine. Charlotte's maternal drive, protecting her son Thomas at every decision point, is her defining characteristic and the film treats it with respect. The villain is simply greedy and dies for it. The Fountain is guarded by a secret society that has kept it from the world because immortality for anyone means death for someone else. The film believes in human mortality as a condition worth accepting rather than a problem requiring a technological solution. That's a traditional position.

VirtueVigil readers who want a family-friendly adventure film with a clean moral and Guy Ritchie's visual energy: this is worth the Apple TV+ subscription.
summary.adultInsight: The Fountain of Youth myth has theological depth that Vanderbilt's screenplay acknowledges without fully exploring. The film's vision of immortality, that it is zero-sum, that whatever energy you add to yourself must be drained from someone else, is closer to the logic of dark magic than to Western religious traditions about eternal life. Christianity doesn't promise immortality at someone else's expense. It promises resurrection as a gift. The film's Fountain is a dark-side counterfeit of that promise: you can have eternal life, but only by taking it from the people you love. The refusal of that bargain is Luke's moral act, and it aligns with the Christian understanding that eternal life offered at the cost of love is not actually eternal life. It's just a longer version of the same emptiness. Adult viewers with religious backgrounds may find more to think about here than the film's critics noticed.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for action violence, brief language, and thematic elements. One of the more family-accessible films VirtueVigil has reviewed at the TRADITIONAL level. The moral is appropriate for children and can generate meaningful conversation about sacrifice, love, and what makes life worth living. Appropriate for families with children 10 and up.

tropeAudit.name: Sibling bond and family reunion as emotional core
tropeAudit.explanation: Luke and Charlotte's estrangement and reconciliation through shared danger is the film's emotional architecture. The adventure is the mechanism. The relationship is the point. Ritchie keeps returning to their sibling dynamic: they fight like people who know each other's vulnerabilities, they protect each other instinctively, and by the end they've rebuilt something that was broken. The family bond is treated as worth the risk and worth the work. That's traditional.

tropeAudit.name: Human adventure and the celebration of exploration
tropeAudit.explanation: The film celebrates curiosity, adventure, and the human drive to discover what's hidden. Luke and his father before him dedicated their lives to following historical clues into dangerous territory because the pursuit itself had meaning. This is a traditional framing of exploration: it's a calling, a form of honor paid to the world's mysteries, not a colonial extraction project. The film trusts that adventure is inherently good and that people who pursue it are doing something worth doing.

tropeAudit.name: Rejection of immortality in favor of love and mortality
tropeAudit.explanation: This is the film's moral center. Luke reaches the Fountain. He can live forever. The cost is the people he loves. He refuses. He chooses Charlotte and Thomas over eternal life. The film presents mortality as a condition that love makes bearable and immortality without love as a form of death worse than dying. This is not a progressive moral position. It's a deeply traditional one, present in every major religious and philosophical tradition that has grappled with the Fountain of Youth myth. Carver drinks and loses everything because he loves no one. Luke refuses and is healed because he loves his family. The moral is as clear as any fairy tale.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal instinct and protection of child
tropeAudit.explanation: Charlotte's primary motivation throughout is protecting her son Thomas. Every decision she makes tracks back to him. When she storms off from the team in Vienna, it's because Thomas is at risk. When she returns, it's because Thomas himself persuades her that the adventure is worth it. Her maternal drive is presented without irony or complication. It's simply what mothers do: they protect their children at cost to themselves. The film treats this as natural and good.

tropeAudit.name: Sister consistently smarter and more morally sound than brother
tropeAudit.explanation: Charlotte is the one who sees through Owen Carver's deception, figures out the code hidden in the Wicked Bible, and insists on involving the authorities when the situation becomes dangerous. Luke is charming and physically capable but morally impulsive and repeatedly wrong about people. The script gives Charlotte most of the intellectual wins while giving Luke most of the action. This is a minor version of the female-is-actually-the-smart-one template. Not severe, because Luke is genuinely heroic at the climax. But the distribution of cognitive competence between the two leads is not even.

tropeAudit.name: Non-white authority figure as moral voice
tropeAudit.explanation: Arian Moayed's Inspector Abbas is the Interpol officer who initially opposes the protagonists and eventually joins forces with them. His function in the third act is to provide institutional authority that validates the heroes' choices. He also speaks some of the film's more explicit moral dialogue about the danger of pursuing forbidden things. A Middle Eastern authority figure as the institutional moral voice is a casting choice made deliberately. Low severity and centrality because the character works on his own terms and doesn't dominate the film's values argument.

tropeAudit.name: Female antagonist as most physically competent character
tropeAudit.explanation: Eiza Gonzalez's Esme is presented as the most physically dangerous character in the film. She defeats multiple trained adversaries, survives situations that kill others, and outfights or outmaneuvers every male combatant she faces. The film hints at her backstory as a Protector of the Path, which gives her actions a purpose. But the visual presentation of a woman as the apex physical combatant in a film full of male fighters reflects a genre convention that has become so common it reads as reflexive rather than motivated by character.

seoTitle: Is Evil Dead Rise Woke? Lee Cronin Horror Film Review | VirtueVigil
seoDescription: VirtueVigil's full VVWS v1.1 review of Evil Dead Rise (2023). Lily Sullivan, Alyssa Sutherland. Lee Cronin directs. Trope audit, parental guidance. Verdict: TRADITIONAL (+10 margin).
seoKeywords: Evil Dead Rise woke or not

director.name: Lee Cronin
director.ideology: MIXED. Cronin is an Irish filmmaker who made his feature debut with The Hole in the Ground (2019). His politics aren't prominently on display. Evil Dead Rise has a female-led cast and a single-mother household at its center, but neither element functions as agenda-driven messaging. Cronin's apparent interest is in craft: how do you put a family under maximum pressure in a confined space and squeeze 96 minutes of genuine horror out of it? He succeeds at that. His framework for family, for what it means that children need to be protected and that adults step up to protect them, is traditional even if his casting choices reflect contemporary Hollywood norms.
director.profile: Cronin was hired by producer Rob Tapert and executive producers Sam Raimi and Bruce Campbell after the success of The Hole in the Ground established him as someone who could work in the supernatural horror genre with control and craft. The decision to relocate the Evil Dead mythology from the cabin in the woods to a Los Angeles apartment building was his, and it was the right call. It makes the Deadite threat feel inescapable in a new way. Cronin directs gore with precision and creativity. The film has five or six set pieces that are among the most technically accomplished in recent horror.

writers.profile: Cronin wrote his own screenplay, which is a strength. He had a clear vision of what story he wanted to tell inside the Evil Dead mythology, and the discipline of the screenplay reflects that. The decision to make the central protagonist Beth rather than the children, and to give her a pregnancy she's uncertain about, is the screenplay's one concession to contemporary identity politics. It doesn't pay off as a political statement; the film forgets about it once the Deadites arrive. That's not quite a betrayal of the premise. It's more like the screenplay had one foot in a different kind of movie and decided not to go there.

composer.name: Stephen McKeon
composer.profile: McKeon's score is one of the film's underrated elements. Evil Dead scores can go wrong in either direction, too campy or too generic. McKeon splits the difference well. The score creates dread rather than just marking it, and the quieter passages in the apartment are scored with an unease that the visual track can't always sustain alone.

cinematographer.name: Dave Garbett
cinematographer.profile: The apartment building is shot with a claustrophobic intelligence that serves the film's premise. Garbett finds angles and framing that make familiar horror geometry feel threatening in new ways. The late-film sequences where the apartment has been essentially transformed by demonic activity are photographed with a grim beauty. This is confident work.

casting_director.name: Nikki Barrett
casting_director.profile: The casting is the film's second-biggest asset after Cronin's direction. Alyssa Sutherland as Ellie takes the Deadite possession to a different register than the franchise has attempted before. She's a mother being used against her own children, and Sutherland plays the character's fractured maternal identity through the possession with real commitment. Lily Sullivan as Beth is exactly right as the audience's surrogate: competent, scared, doing what has to be done. Nell Fisher as young Kassie is the performance that should have been harder to get right than it is. She's extraordinary in an unshowy way.
