woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Cliffhanger (2026) does not qualify as a woke trap under VVWS v1.1 rules. A woke trap requires an actual woke score (negative margin, WOKE LEAN or worse verdict). This film carries a +18.17 TRAD margin and a PREDICTED: TRADITIONAL LEAN verdict. The female lead replacing the male icon is a scored woke signal, but it does not dominate the film. The premise is a daughter saving her father and sister. That is a family protection narrative, not a feminist reframing. The Stallone original was built on a man saving his friends through mountain mastery. The 2026 reboot is built on a daughter saving her family through the same environment. The throughline is survival and loyalty, not gender ideology. Jaume Collet-Serra has never injected progressive messaging into a survival thriller. The Shallows and Jungle Cruise are both clean. No trap.

director.name: Jaume Collet-Serra
director.ideology: NEUTRAL LEANING TRADITIONAL. Collet-Serra has directed three films that are relevant benchmarks for ideological scoring. The Shallows (2016) is a one-woman survival thriller with zero progressive subtext. Blake Lively is stranded, a shark is trying to kill her, and the film is entirely about survival competence. It scored clean. Jungle Cruise (2021) is a nostalgic adventure built on a classic template, with Dwayne Johnson and Emily Blunt navigating a traditional quest structure with no ideological freight. Black Adam (2022) is a superhero film with a non-white lead, which carries a mild woke signal, but the film's content was not ideologically aggressive. Across three films, Collet-Serra has never used a survival or action framework to deliver a progressive lecture. He is a craftsman who makes movies people want to see in theaters. His reputation is for visceral, efficient genre filmmaking. Cliffhanger fits that profile.
director.profile: Jaume Collet-Serra is a Spanish filmmaker who has built one of the most commercially reliable careers in mid-budget Hollywood genre filmmaking. His thriller output with Liam Neeson (Unknown, Non-Stop, Run All Night, The Commuter) established him as a director who can generate sustained tension from contained, high-stakes premises. The Shallows was a commercial breakthrough that earned $119 million on a $17 million budget by stripping the survival thriller to its absolute minimum: one woman, one shark, one reef. That restraint is the signature of a director who understands that genre mechanics are more powerful when the human stakes are clear and uncluttered. Jungle Cruise gave him a larger canvas with a bigger studio and a more complex production. The result was a commercially solid adventure film that leaned into nostalgia and practical adventure over spectacle. Black Adam was the most complex entry in his filmography from a franchise standpoint, operating inside the DC Extended Universe's crowded mythology. Even there, Collet-Serra's instinct was to stage action clearly and keep the human conflict as the connective tissue. Cliffhanger returns him to the terrain where he is most dangerous: a contained, survival-driven premise with a tight location, high stakes, and a protagonist who must rely on physical competence and courage. The Dolomites are one of the most visually dramatic mountain ranges on earth. If any director working today knows how to use an extreme natural environment as both setting and antagonist, it is Collet-Serra.

writers.profile: Mark Bianculli and Melanie Toast are the credited writers on Cliffhanger. Bianculli is a television writer whose credits include NCIS and other broadcast procedural work. His background is in plot-efficient, character-driven writing for mainstream audiences with no known ideological bias in his output. Melanie Toast is a less publicly documented writer at this stage, with limited credits traceable before this production. The combination of a television proceduralist and a developing writer suggests a script built around mechanics: the kidnapping, the escape, the clock, the rescue. That kind of procedural construction is ideologically neutral by default. Thriller screenwriting that prioritizes cause-and-effect plot logic over character-driven message-delivery tends to produce traditional content by design. The genre demands that the protagonist's competence and courage be the answer to the antagonist's power. There is no room in a well-constructed survival thriller for a lecture.

composer.name: TBD
composer.profile: Composer not publicly confirmed at time of review. For an action-thriller set in the Italian Dolomites, the score will need to serve both the landscape and the suspense. Collet-Serra's previous films have used scores effectively without overwhelming the tension mechanics. The Shallows used a Marco Beltrami score that amplified isolation and dread without musical manipulation. A similarly restrained approach would fit Cliffhanger's survival structure. Scoring analysis will be updated post-release if ideologically relevant musical choices emerge.

cinematographer.name: TBD
cinematographer.profile: Cinematographer not publicly confirmed at time of review. The Italian Dolomites provide one of the most cinematographically rich mountain environments on earth: vertical limestone faces, high-altitude light, and vast scale that dwarfs human figures. A Collet-Serra production will use that landscape aggressively. His visual instinct with The Shallows was to make the ocean feel genuinely threatening by shooting it at its most beautiful. Expect the same approach to the Dolomites: gorgeous and dangerous simultaneously.

casting_director.name: Not publicly disclosed at time of review
casting_director.profile: The casting of Lily James as Naomi Cooper and Pierce Brosnan as Ray Cooper is the production's central creative decision. James is a British actress whose career spans Cinderella (2015), Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again (2018), and Yesterday (2019). She is a technically capable performer with strong screen presence but no track record in action-thriller lead roles of this physical intensity. The Cliffhanger casting is the biggest physical challenge she has taken on. Brosnan brings legacy action credibility from his James Bond tenure and a filmography that includes action, thriller, and adventure material across four decades. His presence as Ray Cooper, the experienced mountaineer father, grounds the film in a generation of action cinema that predates the current era. Nell Tiger Free, known for Game of Thrones and Servant, plays Sydney Cooper, the sister in danger. Her casting is structurally appropriate for a character who functions as the emotional stakes of the rescue mission rather than an active agent. Franz Rogowski as the villain is the most interesting casting choice in the ensemble. Rogowski is a German-Austrian arthouse actor whose work with directors like Christian Petzold and Terrence Malick is a world away from genre villainy. His presence suggests the production is reaching for a villain with psychological depth rather than a two-dimensional antagonist. That ambition is a traditional signal: well-constructed villains make well-constructed heroes necessary.

tropeAudit.name: Family Protection as Primary Narrative Engine
tropeAudit.explanation: The entire plot of Cliffhanger (2026) is structured around one question: will Naomi get to her father and sister before it is too late? The kidnapping of Ray and Sydney Cooper is not a backdrop. It is the story. Every survival decision Naomi makes, every risk she takes in the mountains, is motivated by family loyalty. That is not a surface-level traditional signal. It is the deepest structural form of traditional storytelling: a protagonist who acts not for personal glory but for the people she loves. The original 1993 Stallone film also used family loyalty and friendship as its core motivation. The 2026 version retains that structural engine while shifting the protagonist. The engine itself is unchanged. Family as the reason to survive, to fight, to refuse to quit, is the oldest and most powerful traditional narrative driver in action cinema.

tropeAudit.name: Father-Daughter Bond Under Siege
tropeAudit.explanation: Ray Cooper is not a passive victim waiting to be rescued. He is described as an experienced mountaineer, a man of competence and mastery who built his life in the mountains. The father-daughter dynamic between Ray and Naomi is the film's emotional core. Naomi is staying with her father when the attack occurs. She witnesses him taken. Her entire subsequent arc is defined by that relationship: a daughter who cannot abandon her father because the bond between them is the thing worth risking everything for. The casting of Pierce Brosnan as Ray Cooper deepens this signal. Brosnan carries decades of screen authority as an action figure, which makes him a credible father whose capacity for strength has been temporarily neutralized by captivity, not eliminated. The father-daughter bond in survival thrillers is a traditional archetype that predates cinema itself. This film places it at the center of its premise and builds everything else around it.

tropeAudit.name: Survival Courage and Self-Reliance Under Duress
tropeAudit.explanation: Naomi Cooper does not have a team. She does not have a system. She has the mountains, her wits, and whatever courage she can summon. The survival thriller as a genre is classically traditional precisely because it strips away all institutional support and forces the protagonist to rely entirely on her own resources. There is no government to call. There is no rescue helicopter coming. There is only the mountain and the choice to act or surrender. Collet-Serra's The Shallows established the template: a woman alone against a hostile environment, forced by circumstances to find reserves of courage she did not know she had. Cliffhanger applies the same framework to a mountain setting with added stakes: she is not only surviving herself, she is trying to save two people she loves. Self-reliance under those conditions is one of the most potent traditional values any narrative can dramatize.

tropeAudit.name: Classic Action-Thriller Genre Fidelity
tropeAudit.explanation: Cliffhanger (2026) is a reboot of Renny Harlin's 1993 Stallone film, one of the defining action thrillers of its decade. The original Cliffhanger is a masterclass in contained, physically grounded action filmmaking: a mountain setting, a clear threat, a hero who must use environment and physical competence as his primary weapons. The 2026 version maintains that structural template. It is not a deconstruction of the original. It is not an ironic commentary on what action thrillers used to be. It is an attempt to deliver the same genre satisfactions in a new setting with a new protagonist. That fidelity to genre form is itself a traditional signal. Action-thriller mechanics, when executed without ideological subtext, produce traditional content by default: competence is rewarded, courage is necessary, and the antagonist who uses force to dominate others is defeated by someone who refuses to be dominated.

tropeAudit.name: Mountain Competence and Physical Mastery as Heroic Credential
tropeAudit.explanation: The Dolomites are not a location. They are a crucible. Ray Cooper built his life in them. His expertise is the foundation of the luxury chalet he runs and the identity he has constructed as a mountaineer. Naomi, his daughter, arrives at that environment and is forced to master it under conditions of maximum duress. The film's values around physical competence, knowledge of terrain, and respect for the environment as both tool and threat are classically traditional. Adventure fiction from Jack London to Hemingway to Cormac McCarthy has always treated the natural world as a test of human character rather than a setting to be commented on. The Italian Dolomites in Cliffhanger are not backdrop. They are the proving ground. That framing is traditional in its roots and in its execution.

tropeAudit.name: Female Lead Replacing Male Icon
tropeAudit.explanation: The most visible woke signal in Cliffhanger (2026) is the replacement of Sylvester Stallone, the male lead of the 1993 original, with Lily James in an original female protagonist role. This is a scored woke trope under VVWS v1.1: when a franchise previously anchored by a male lead is rebooted with a female protagonist as the primary action agent, that is a meaningful ideological signal regardless of the quality of the execution. The authenticity is scored Moderate rather than High because the character is new rather than a gender-swapped version of Gabe Walker, and because the film's premise does not frame Naomi's gender as the source of her heroism. She is a daughter protecting her family, not a woman proving she can do what men do. That distinction matters. The score reflects the structural reality of the casting choice, not a verdict on Lily James's performance potential.

tropeAudit.name: Diverse Ensemble Supporting Cast
tropeAudit.explanation: The supporting ensemble includes Shubham Saraf, Assaad Bouab, and Suzy Bemba, whose casting creates a diverse supporting group around the primarily white Cooper family leads. This is a low-severity, low-centrality woke signal: the supporting cast's diversity does not appear to drive the narrative or carry ideological weight in the premise. It is consistent with the international location and production context of a European co-production set in the Italian Dolomites. The authenticity is scored Low because the casting choice is more consistent with practical international production logistics than deliberate ideological messaging. At minimum severity, this is the weakest possible woke score entry available under the scoring system.

summary.headline: A Daughter, a Mountain, a Family Worth Saving. Cliffhanger Knows What It Is.
summary.overview: Cliffhanger (2026) is a StudioCanal action thriller directed by Jaume Collet-Serra, starring Lily James as Naomi Cooper, a woman forced to survive the Italian Dolomites alone after kidnappers take her father and sister. It is a reboot of the 1993 Stallone film. It scores PREDICTED: TRADITIONAL LEAN at +18.17 TRAD with an authIndex of 76.
summary.woke_analysis: The wokeScore of 3.67 rests on two tropes. The primary signal is the female lead replacing a male icon. Stallone's Gabe Walker was the anchor of the 1993 original. The 2026 version replaces that anchor with a woman, which is a scored structural woke input under VVWS v1.1. The secondary signal is the diverse supporting ensemble, scored at minimum severity. What the wokeScore does not contain is more significant than what it does: there is no gender ideology in the premise, no feminist framing of Naomi's heroism as a rebuttal to male inadequacy, and no progressive lecture track visible in any available material. The woke signals here are structural (the casting decision) rather than thematic (the content of the film). Collet-Serra's track record provides the strongest available evidence that the structural signals will not translate into ideological content. The Shallows featured a lone woman surviving a brutal natural environment and contained zero feminist subtext. The survival was the story. Cliffhanger appears to follow the same logic.
summary.trad_analysis: The tradScore of 21.84 is built on five traditional tropes. The two highest-scoring entries, Family Protection as Primary Narrative Engine (6.30) and Father-Daughter Bond Under Siege (6.30), are the structural foundation of the entire film. The plot exists to put Naomi in a position where she must choose between safety and her family, and she chooses her family without hesitation. That is the simplest and most powerful traditional narrative statement available. Survival Courage and Self-Reliance Under Duress (5.04) reinforces the core value: no institution saves Naomi. No system protects her. She has to do it herself, with whatever she can find on a mountain, because the alternative is losing the people she loves. Classic Action-Thriller Genre Fidelity (2.10) and Mountain Competence as Heroic Credential (2.10) round out a tradScore that reflects the film's consistent traditional orientation at every structural level.
summary.verdict_explanation: The margin of +18.17 TRAD places Cliffhanger in the TRADITIONAL LEAN band (10-19 range). The PREDICTED prefix will be removed after full release when post-release scoring can be completed. The gap between TRADITIONAL LEAN and TRADITIONAL is the female-lead replacement signal. If that scoring were removed or if the film's content actively redeems the structural concern by demonstrating that the female lead operates within traditional rather than feminist frameworks, the post-release score could move to TRADITIONAL. Confidence in the prediction is moderate-high. The primary uncertainty is whether the film's execution of Naomi's heroism leans on her gender as a point of emphasis or simply allows it to be incidental to the survival stakes. Collet-Serra's track record strongly suggests the latter.
summary.bottom_line: The question is whether Cliffhanger (2026) is woke. The short answer, based on everything available before release, is no. The slightly longer answer is that it contains one real structural woke signal, the female lead replacing a male icon, and no visible ideological content beyond that choice. The distinction matters.
summary.overall:
There is a version of Cliffhanger (2026) that nobody would want to see. It features a woman who is better than everyone around her because she is a woman, a villain who represents patriarchal power, and a father who needs to be rescued because competent fathers have no place in the contemporary action film. That version exists in the cultural imagination because Hollywood has produced it before, many times, in the past decade.

This does not appear to be that film.

What the available materials suggest is something considerably simpler and considerably more valuable: a survival thriller about a daughter who will not give up on her father and sister. The Dolomites are the setting. The kidnapping is the catalyst. The rest is Naomi Cooper alone on a mountain, trying to find a way to win against people who are better resourced and better organized than she is.

Jaume Collet-Serra directed this film. That matters. His record in the survival thriller genre is one of the clearest in contemporary Hollywood. The Shallows (2016) featured Blake Lively stranded on a reef with a shark actively trying to kill her. The film ran ninety minutes. In those ninety minutes, there was not a single moment of feminist subtext, not one beat where Lively's character paused to consider what her survival meant for women in general. She was trying not to die. The movie was about whether she would succeed. It is one of the most purely traditional survival films of the decade because it never mistook its premise for a thesis statement.

Cliffhanger gives Collet-Serra a bigger canvas and a more complex emotional premise. Lily James is not fighting a shark. She is fighting men who have taken the people she loves most in the world, and she is doing it on a mountain that requires real knowledge and real courage to navigate. Pierce Brosnan as Ray Cooper, her father, is the emotional anchor even in captivity. Brosnan has been playing authoritative men in action contexts for four decades. His presence as the experienced mountaineer who built his life in the Dolomites and now needs his daughter to save it is precisely the kind of casting that signals a production with genuine feeling for its story rather than a production assembling demographic checkboxes.

Franz Rogowski as the villain is worth noting. Rogowski is one of the most interesting performers in European cinema, an arthouse actor with deep reserves of strangeness and presence who has worked with directors like Christian Petzold and Terrence Malick. Casting him as the antagonist suggests the production wants a villain who is genuinely frightening rather than generically menacing. That ambition is a traditional signal in the most basic sense: a well-constructed villain makes the hero's courage necessary rather than decorative.

The scored woke signal in this film is the female lead replacing the male icon. Stallone's Gabe Walker was the 1993 original's center of gravity. Lily James's Naomi Cooper is a new character, but the structural reality is the same: a franchise previously anchored by a man is now anchored by a woman. That is a scored input under VVWS v1.1, and it deserves the wokeScore it receives.

What it does not deserve is to define the film. The premise is a daughter saving her family. That is not a feminist premise. That is a human premise. The original Cliffhanger was about a man whose survival mattered because of the people depending on him. If the 2026 version simply replaces the gender of the protagonist while maintaining that same structure of obligation, courage, and family loyalty, then the film's traditional content will have absorbed the structural woke signal rather than been defined by it.

Collet-Serra's track record says that is exactly what will happen.

For VirtueVigil readers who want the bottom line: Cliffhanger (2026) scores PREDICTED: TRADITIONAL LEAN at +18.17 TRAD. It is a survival thriller about a family under siege in one of the most dramatic mountain environments on earth. The director does not make message films. The premise is built on family loyalty. The casting is credible. Go in knowing what the woke signal is, watch for whether the film's execution neutralizes it, and update accordingly after April 3.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults who enjoy the classic action-thriller format from the 1980s and 1990s have a specific question about Cliffhanger: does the female lead choice mean the film is going to spend its runtime proving a point about women in action movies, or does it simply use a female protagonist to tell a survival story about family? That question is the right one to ask. Collet-Serra's history with The Shallows suggests the answer is the latter. A director who made Blake Lively's survival the entire story without pausing to comment on what it means for female action heroes is a director who will likely make Lily James's survival the entire story for the same reasons. If the post-release score confirms that prediction, TRADITIONAL LEAN will likely upgrade to TRADITIONAL. Either way, the film is not a lecture. It is a thriller. Adults who want a thriller can reasonably attend.

title: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy does not qualify as a woke trap. The film scores TRADITIONAL with a +14.98 margin. A woke trap can only be flagged for films that score woke (negative margin). This film's progressive elements, primarily the toyboy subplot, are present from early in the runtime and are not concealed. The film's dominant register is grief, motherhood, and earned romance. No bait-and-switch is present.

tropeAudit.name: Widowed Mother Raising Young Children
tropeAudit.explanation: Bridget Jones has been a widow for four years when the film opens. Her two young children, Billy and Mabel, are not narrative decoration; they are the gravitational center of her life. Every romantic decision Bridget makes is filtered through the question of what is best for them. She attends school pickups, navigates their grief over their father, and ultimately chooses the man who understands and respects her role as a mother. This is the film's thesis-level traditional signal: a woman whose identity is inseparable from her children. Authenticity is high because the trope is organic to Fielding's source novel and to the character's two-decade arc.

tropeAudit.name: Mark Darcy as Idealized Deceased Husband and Virtuous Male Anchor
tropeAudit.explanation: Mark Darcy, played by Hugh Grant in brief flashback and referenced throughout, functions as the film's moral and emotional standard. He was a human rights barrister who died in Sudan doing selfless work. Bridget measures every new man against him, not obsessively but honestly. The film treats his memory with reverence: he was a good husband, a devoted father, and a man of principle. This idealized male anchor is a strongly traditional signal. It frames marriage as something worth grieving, not escaping. Authenticity is high; this characterization follows directly from the source novel and prior films.

tropeAudit.name: Mr. Wallaker as Responsible Single Father
tropeAudit.explanation: Mr. Wallaker, the composed and quietly decent single father from Bridget's children's school, is the film's traditional male ideal in the present tense. He is not glamorous or manipulative. He is patient, emotionally available, and actively involved in his own child's life. The film presents his responsible fatherhood as attractive and admirable, not as a curiosity or a compromise. His arc converges with Bridget's precisely because they are both parents first. This is a strong traditional signal: a man whose worth is measured by his character and his commitment to family.

tropeAudit.name: Marriage and Family as Ultimate Aspiration
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's emotional destination is not sexual liberation or self-actualization in isolation; it is belonging, partnership, and a reconstituted family. Bridget's journey through grief and tentative romance is framed as a path back to the kind of lasting love she had with Mark. The toyboy detour is presented as a stage in healing, not as the destination. The ending confirms that domestic partnership with a good man is what Bridget, and by extension the film, values most. Authenticity is high; the rom-com genre and Fielding's novels have always pointed in this direction.

tropeAudit.name: Age-Appropriate Relationship Chosen Over Fling
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's structural choice is explicit: Bridget ultimately leaves the toyboy subplot behind and gravitates toward Mr. Wallaker, a peer-appropriate partner who shares her values and her season of life. The Roxster arc is not condemned, but it is clearly marked as transitional. The film rewards maturity, depth, and compatibility over novelty and physical excitement. This arc sends a clear traditional signal: youthful passion is fun but wisdom means choosing the right person, not the exciting one.

tropeAudit.name: Motherhood as Core Identity Driver
tropeAudit.explanation: Bridget's identity in this film is not defined by her career, her appearance, or her romantic status. It is defined by her children. Billy and Mabel are not subplot; they are her primary relationship, the one that shapes every other decision. The film treats this with warmth and specificity: Bridget is a good mother who is also a flawed human being navigating grief, and the film honors both truths simultaneously. This is a meaningfully traditional signal in a cultural landscape where female protagonists are increasingly defined by professional achievement or romantic conquest.

tropeAudit.name: Friends and Community as Support Network
tropeAudit.explanation: Bridget's longtime friends and her therapist, played by Emma Thompson, form a genuine community around her as she navigates widowhood. The film presents these relationships as essential infrastructure, not as comic relief. The message is that belonging to a community of people who know and love you is how human beings survive loss. This is a quietly traditional signal: community, not radical individualism, is the answer to grief.

tropeAudit.name: Age-Gap Toyboy Plotline Treated Positively
tropeAudit.explanation: The Roxster subplot occupies a significant portion of the film's runtime. A 51-year-old widow pursuing a physically driven relationship with a 30-year-old man is presented without shame or serious moral scrutiny. The film treats this as liberating and even comedically celebratory. While the narrative ultimately redirects Bridget toward a more age-appropriate partner, the Roxster arc is not presented as a mistake. It is presented as a valid and enjoyable phase. This normalizes an age-gap arrangement in a way that registers as a woke signal: the framing implies no traditional constraints should apply to a woman's sexual choices at any age or in any configuration. Authenticity is Moderate; the trope appears in Fielding's novel but is amplified in the film adaptation.

tropeAudit.name: 51-Year-Old Female Protagonist as Unapologetic Sex Object
tropeAudit.explanation: The film makes a deliberate point of presenting Bridget, at 51, as a sexually desirable and sexually active woman. This is not incidental to the plot; it is a stated theme. The audience is invited to celebrate this. In isolation, positive aging is a traditional value. But the framing here leans into a particular strand of feminist messaging: that women should feel no different about their sexuality at 51 than they did at 25. This mild ideological coating registers as a woke signal, though it does not dominate the film.

tropeAudit.name: Mild Feminist Self-Reinvention Messaging
tropeAudit.explanation: Scattered through the film are brief beats asserting that Bridget's journey is about reclaiming herself as an individual beyond wifehood and motherhood. Dr. Rawlings and occasional dialogue nudge this reading. The messaging is mild and never polemic, but it is present. It does not drive the film and is outweighed by the traditional signals, but it contributes a small woke score.

summary.headline: Grief, Growth, and Getting It Right the Second Time
summary.overview: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy arrives fourteen years after Bridget Jones's Baby and over two decades after the original made Renee Zellweger's hapless diarist a global icon. It is, by any honest measure, the most emotionally ambitious entry in the franchise. Bridget is 51, a widow four years into life without Mark Darcy, and she is doing her imperfect, recognizable best. The film opens not on a joke but on grief: a stone dropped into still water, the kids asking questions she cannot fully answer, the particular ache of mornings when the other side of the bed is permanently empty. Director Michael Morris, known for his television work on Better Call Saul and Succession, brings a restraint the franchise has not always had. The comedy is still here, but it earns its laughs against a backdrop of something real.
summary.woke_analysis: The film carries real woke weight in one specific area: the Roxster subplot. A substantial portion of the runtime is given to Bridget's relationship with a 30-year-old named Roxster, played with breezy charm by Leo Woodall. The affair is played for laughs and warmth in roughly equal measure, and the film makes no apology for it. For audiences attuned to these signals, the framing does normalize an age-gap arrangement in a way that goes beyond merely depicting human behavior. The film is not saying this is a mistake Bridget regrets; it is saying this is a thing a 51-year-old woman gets to do and enjoy. There is also a thread of gentle feminist messaging, mostly channeled through Emma Thompson's therapist, that positions Bridget's romantic journey as self-reclamation rather than purely family-formation. These signals register and they score. But they do not dominate.
summary.trad_analysis: Where the film earns its TRADITIONAL verdict is in its bones. Bridget's children are not accessories. Billy and Mabel are present, specific, and demanding in the way actual children are, and Bridget's primary identity in this film is mother. Every romantic calculation she makes runs through them first. The ghost of Mark Darcy is handled with genuine reverence: he was a good man, a devoted father, a person worth mourning. The film does not rehabilitate him as a villain to justify her moving on. It simply acknowledges that he was real and good and gone. Mr. Wallaker, the single father from school played by Chiwetel Ejiofor with precise emotional intelligence, is the film's true traditional ideal: a man whose appeal is his character, his patience, and his willingness to show up. The film's climax is not a sex scene; it is a moment of emotional honesty between two people who have both lost something and are ready to try again. The destination is partnership, family, belonging. That is the traditional register, and the film commits to it.
summary.verdict_explanation: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy scores TRADITIONAL at +14.98 because its central architecture, widowed motherhood, idealized marriage, responsible fatherhood, and the choice of a lasting partner over a temporary thrill, outweighs the Roxster subplot and its mild feminist framing. The woke signals are real but they are transitional; the traditional signals are where the film ends up and where its emotional weight lives.
summary.bottom_line: This is the best Bridget Jones film since the original, and it is a genuinely good film by any standard. The grief is real, the comedy is earned, and the ending is satisfying in the way that only a film that has actually cost its protagonist something can be. Zellweger is extraordinary. Ejiofor is perfect. The franchise grew up.
summary.overall:
Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy arrives fourteen years after Bridget Jones's Baby and over two decades after the original made Renee Zellweger's hapless diarist a global icon. It is, by any honest measure, the most emotionally ambitious entry in the franchise. Bridget is 51, a widow four years into life without Mark Darcy, and she is doing her imperfect, recognizable best.

Director Michael Morris, known for his television work on Better Call Saul and Succession, brings a restraint the franchise has not always had. The comedy is still here, but it earns its laughs against a backdrop of something real: a stone dropped into still water, kids asking questions their mother cannot fully answer, the particular ache of mornings when the other side of the bed is permanently empty.

The film carries real woke weight in one specific area: the Roxster subplot. A substantial portion of the runtime is given to Bridget's relationship with a 30-year-old named Roxster, played with breezy charm by Leo Woodall. The affair is played for laughs and warmth in roughly equal measure, and the film makes no apology for it. For audiences attuned to these signals, the framing does normalize an age-gap arrangement in a way that goes beyond merely depicting human behavior. The film is not saying this is a mistake Bridget regrets; it is saying this is a thing a 51-year-old woman gets to do and enjoy. There is also a thread of gentle feminist messaging, mostly channeled through Emma Thompson's therapist, that positions Bridget's romantic journey as self-reclamation rather than purely family-formation. These signals register and they score.

But they do not dominate. Where the film earns its TRADITIONAL verdict is in its bones. Bridget's children are not accessories. Billy and Mabel are present, specific, and demanding in the way actual children are, and Bridget's primary identity in this film is mother. Every romantic calculation she makes runs through them first. The ghost of Mark Darcy is handled with genuine reverence: he was a good man, a devoted father, a person worth mourning. The film does not rehabilitate him as a villain to justify her moving on. It simply acknowledges that he was real and good and gone.

Mr. Wallaker, the single father from school played by Chiwetel Ejiofor with precise emotional intelligence, is the film's true traditional ideal: a man whose appeal is his character, his patience, and his willingness to show up. The film's climax is not a sex scene; it is a moment of emotional honesty between two people who have both lost something and are ready to try again. The destination is partnership, family, belonging.

The structural choice the film makes is explicit: Bridget leaves Roxster and gravitates toward a peer-appropriate partner who shares her values and her season of life. The Roxster arc is not condemned, but it is clearly marked as transitional. The film rewards maturity, depth, and compatibility over novelty and physical excitement. That is a traditional arc regardless of what is in the middle.

Renee Zellweger delivers the best performance of her Bridget Jones career. This version of Bridget is tired and funny and brave and occasionally undignified in exactly the right ways. Ejiofor is restrained to perfection. Emma Thompson, as the therapist Dr. Rawlings, anchors the film's emotional logic with the kind of precision that makes everything around her look effortless. Hugh Grant appears briefly and his presence lands with the weight the film needs it to carry.

This is the best Bridget Jones film since the original, and it is a genuinely good film by any standard. The grief is real, the comedy is earned, and the ending is satisfying in the way that only a film that has actually cost its protagonist something can be. Audiences agree: 94% on Rotten Tomatoes. The critics agree: 87%. VirtueVigil agrees too, just for different reasons.
summary.adultInsight: A rare mainstream rom-com that takes grief seriously without becoming a grief film. The emotional maturity here will hit differently for anyone who has had to start over after loss.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R. Contains sexual content and some language. The Roxster subplot includes implied and referenced sexual activity between a 51-year-old woman and a 30-year-old man, treated without moral judgment. Not appropriate for younger viewers. Fine for mature teens with parental awareness of the age-gap framing.

director.name: Michael Morris
director.profile: Michael Morris is a British-American television director whose credits include Better Call Saul, Succession, and Fleabag. His work is characterized by tonal precision: the ability to move between comedy and genuine emotional weight without rupturing either register. He has no strong ideological track record. His Bridget Jones direction is notable for its restraint; he does not oversell the comedy or the grief. The result is the most tonally assured film in the Bridget Jones franchise. Ideologically, Morris appears interested in human beings more than in arguments.

writers.profile: Helen Fielding's 2013 source novel Mad About the Boy was controversial among Bridget Jones fans for killing Mark Darcy. The film adaptation softens nothing about his death but does everything it can to honor his memory. Abi Morgan, the British screenwriter behind Suffragette and Iron Lady, co-wrote the adaptation. Morgan's track record includes strong female characters and some progressive messaging in historical contexts. In this film, her contributions appear to be the feminist framing around Bridget's self-reclamation; this is mild and does not overwhelm the traditional architecture Fielding built.

Morris's television background shows: the framing is clean, the coverage is efficient, and the camera serves the performances rather than announcing itself. This is the correct choice for a character-driven romantic comedy.

title: Wednesday: Season 2
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
director: Multiple (Tim Burton, Gandja Monteiro, Victor Gaudioso, Paco Cabezas)
studio: Millar Gough Ink / Tim Burton Productions
productionCompany: Millar Gough Ink / Tim Burton Productions / Toluca Pictures / MGM Television

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Wednesday: Season 2 does not qualify as a woke trap despite its WOKE LEAN verdict (-6 WOKE). A woke trap requires ideological content that remains hidden until past 50% of the runtime, using a traditional-seeming exterior to lure in conservative audiences before revealing its agenda. Season 2's ideological content - the conversion camp LGBTQ allegory, the diversity casting, the outcasts-as-oppressed-minority framework - is present from the first episode and visible in pre-release materials, interviews, and trailers. The show does not pretend to be something it is not. Furthermore, the source IP (The Addams Family) has always been a satirical commentary on normal society's treatment of eccentrics. Wednesday's status as an outsider who is persecuted by conformity is inherent to the character. None of this was hidden. Audiences who watched Season 1 know exactly what kind of show they are returning to. A woke trap requires deceptive packaging. Season 2's progressive content is part of the brand, not concealed beneath it.

externalScores.globalBoxOffice: Netflix streaming (exact view counts not disclosed at time of review)

director.name: Tim Burton (EP/Director), Alfred Gough & Miles Millar (Showrunners)
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT with progressive elements. Tim Burton's output is consistently eccentric but not politically programmatic - his best films (Edward Scissorhands, Big Eyes, Ed Wood) are about outsiders who refuse to conform to social pressure, which is a conservative-adjacent theme when examined carefully. He does not lecture. His influence on Wednesday operates primarily through aesthetic and tone. The showrunners Alfred Gough and Miles Millar are more ideologically directive: Season 2 under their full control introduces the conversion camp allegory (previously only implicit) as an explicit storyline, expanding the show's social commentary into territory that goes beyond mere Addams Family eccentricity.
director.profile: Tim Burton serves as executive producer and directed four of the eight Season 2 episodes. His creative influence maintains the show's visual identity: the Gothic architecture of Nevermore, the practical creature effects, the washed-out color palette interrupted by flashes of Wednesday's black palette. Burton has described his relationship to the Wednesday character as personal - he identifies with the outsider who refuses to conform. His four episodes are the season's most visually distinctive. Gough and Millar as showrunners have taken the franchise in a more explicitly allegorical direction in the second season, using the world of outcasts versus normies as a more pointed commentary on real-world social divisions. The conversion camp storyline, in which werewolves are sent to a camp designed to suppress their transformations, is the season's most discussed creative choice and its most politically obvious one.

writers.names: Alfred Gough, Miles Millar, Meredith Averill
writers.profile: Alfred Gough and Miles Millar created the show and have been the primary creative voice throughout. Their credits include Smallville (2001-2011), Into the Badlands (2015-2019), and Shanghai Knights (2003). Their approach to Wednesday has always been built on the source material's fundamental tension: Wednesday Addams is defined by her refusal to conform, and Nevermore Academy is a school for the children of monsters who are themselves refused by normie society. This tension between outcasts and normals is the show's engine. Season 2 escalates the allegory to include direct parallels to real-world discrimination against LGBTQ+ individuals, specifically through the conversion camp subplot. Meredith Averill joins as a writer/EP for Season 2 and is credited with sharpening the season's political edge.

lead_producer.name: Gail Berman / Jonathan Glickman
lead_producer.company: Millar Gough Ink / MGM Television / Netflix
lead_producer.profile: Wednesday is a co-production between multiple entities with Netflix as the distribution partner and primary creative driver. The show's renewal for a third season (July 2025) before the second season finished its run confirms Netflix's confidence in the property. The platform's investment in Wednesday - it was the second-most watched English-language Netflix series ever after its debut - guarantees creative latitude. Netflix's willingness to let Gough and Millar expand the show's allegorical ambitions in Season 2, including the conversion camp storyline that generated controversy, reflects its confidence that the fanbase will follow the show wherever it goes.

composer.name: Danny Elfman / Chris Bacon
composer.profile: Danny Elfman, Tim Burton's longtime creative partner and one of the most distinctive film and TV composers working, scored the original theme and continues to provide sonic identity to Season 2. Chris Bacon handles the episode-by-episode scoring, working within the framework Elfman established. The Wednesday theme - a harpsichord-driven, cello-punctuated motif that evokes Gothic horror while maintaining a sardonic edge - is one of the most immediately recognizable original TV themes of the 2020s. The Season 2 score expands this palette for new creatures and settings while maintaining the established character themes.

cinematographer.name: David Lanzenberg / Stephan Pehrsson
cinematographer.profile: The season employs multiple directors of photography consistent with its multi-director structure. The visual language established in Season 1 - desaturated greens and grays punctuated by Wednesday's blacks, practical lighting that makes Nevermore feel inhabited rather than designed, wide-angle compositions that give the architecture imposing scale - is maintained across Season 2. The Season 2 camping sequences mark a visual departure toward natural light and forest aesthetics, which creates a productive contrast with the Gothic academy setting.

casting_director.name: Netflix/MGM Television casting
casting_director.profile: The returning ensemble is largely intact. Steve Buscemi joins as new Principal Barry Dort, replacing Larissa Weems, and brings a specific energy: he is not merely eccentric but actively suspicious, a normie-adjacent administrator whose motives gradually complicate. His casting is the season's best creative decision - Buscemi has a physical specificity that makes Dort feel like a genuine institutional antagonist rather than a villain-waiting-to-be-revealed. The departure of certain Season 1 cast members and the addition of new characters including Billie Piper in a recurring role maintains the show's casting diversity while adding new dramatic possibilities. Pugsley's enrollment at Nevermore is a crowd-pleasing addition for Addams Family fans, and Isaac Ordonez handles the role with genuine comic timing.

parentalGuidance.guidance: Wednesday: Season 2 carries a TV-14 rating appropriate for its content. Parents evaluating it for younger teenagers should be aware that the conversion camp storyline is not subtle: the show draws explicit parallels between the camp's suppression of werewolf transformations and real-world conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ individuals. This is not background allegory - it is a featured storyline that the show intends audiences to map onto current cultural debates. The show does not present both sides of this debate. Parents who would not want their 13-year-old watching a show that frames conversion therapy as unambiguous evil should note that this content is present and central to Season 2, not peripheral. For parents comfortable with the show's LGBTQ-allegorical content: Wednesday remains one of the more craft-committed pieces of Gothic YA entertainment on any streaming platform. The production values, Jenna Ortega's performance, and Tim Burton's visual influence make it genuinely excellent television within its genre. The TV-14 rating is accurate. The ideological content is more pointed than Season 1. Parents who were comfortable with Season 1 should know the allegory has been escalated.

tropeAudit.name: Conversion Camp as LGBTQ Allegory: Werewolf Suppression as Conversion Therapy Parallel
tropeAudit.explanation: Season 2's most discussed creative choice is Camp Jericho's program of suppressing werewolf transformations using methods that the show explicitly parallels to conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ individuals. The camp counselors enforce rules against transformation, tell the werewolves their nature is something to be controlled or eliminated, and use psychological pressure and shame as tools. The show's framing is unambiguous: the camp is wrong, the counselors are villains (or at minimum, agents of harm), and the suppression of a person's nature is presented as abuse. This is not a veiled or subtle allegory. Critics from Polygon and other outlets criticized the show for using the conversion therapy parallel in a hamfisted way ("the grace of a butterfingered buffoon"), and the LGBTQ community criticized the show from the opposite direction for using their real trauma as a fantasy metaphor. Both criticisms have merit. The content is nonetheless there, it is unambiguous in its ideological positioning, and it is high-centrality. Severity 4: drives a major Season 2 subplot. Moderate authenticity: the outcasts-versus-normies framework has always been in the show, but this specific conversion camp escalation is a new injection. High centrality. Score: 4 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 7.20.

tropeAudit.name: Outcast Identity as Identity Politics: Supernatural Beings as Marginalized Group
tropeAudit.explanation: The first season's outcast/normie tension was already allegorical - Nevermore Academy functions as a space where marginalized supernatural beings find community and safety from mainstream society's hostility. Season 2 escalates this into explicit identity politics: the outcasts are described in terms that mirror real-world marginalized group language, Barry Dort's administration of Nevermore involves normie-driven institutional pressure to assimilate and suppress outcast identity, and Wednesday's arc centers on defending Nevermore's right to exist as a separate community. The show presents this as a binary: outcasts are who they are (authentic, marginalized, worth defending) and normie pressure to change or assimilate is institutional oppression. This maps directly onto contemporary progressive frameworks for identity, authenticity, and institutional discrimination. Severity 4: central to the season's macro conflict. Moderate authenticity (inherent to the source material but elevated in Season 2). High centrality. Score: 4 x 1.0 x 1.8 = 7.20.

tropeAudit.name: Artificially Inflated Diversity in Rural Vermont Setting
tropeAudit.explanation: Jericho, Vermont - a small rural town - is depicted with a level of racial and ethnic diversity that critics, including value-based review outlets, have noted as comically and artificially inflated relative to the real demographic composition of rural New England. This is diversity casting not justified by the setting's internal logic. The school and the town are both depicted with diversity levels that reflect a progressive casting philosophy rather than a plausible population. Worth It or Woke noted that 'the diversity is comically and artificially inflated, though not just at the school, but also in the small rural town that neighbors it.' Severity 3: visible and pervasive. Low authenticity: clearly injected rather than organic to the setting. Moderate centrality: background rather than plot-driving, but constant. Score: 3 x 1.4 x 1.0 = 4.20.

tropeAudit.name: Institutional Authority as Default Antagonist
tropeAudit.explanation: Season 2 introduces Barry Dort as the new principal, whose administrative agenda centers on bringing Nevermore closer to normie norms. He is the show's primary institutional antagonist: an authority figure using his position to impose conformity on those who do not share his values. The show does not offer a sympathetic rendering of his perspective - his role is to represent oppressive institutional power that the main characters must resist. This is structurally progressive: authority exercising institutional power is presumptively suspect, and resistance to authority is valorized without significant qualification. Severity 2. Moderate authenticity (fits the source material's satirical tradition but applied with contemporary political framing). Moderate centrality. Score: 2 x 1.0 x 1.0 = 2.00.

tropeAudit.name: Queerbaiting Criticism Alongside Implicit LGBTQ Coding
tropeAudit.explanation: Wednesday and Enid's relationship carries significant fan-interpreted queer subtext that the show neither confirms nor resolves, generating criticism from both conservative audiences (who object to the coding) and LGBTQ audiences (who are frustrated the show uses their community's emotional investment without committing to explicit representation). The Reddit thread from the SapphoAndHerFriend subreddit cited by critics called it 'queerbaiting final boss.' The actual show content - Wednesday and Enid are not depicted in a romantic relationship - contains only implicit coding. This is scored at low severity for what the show actually depicts rather than what fans project onto it. Severity 1. Moderate authenticity. Low centrality. Score: 1 x 1.0 x 0.5 = 0.50.

tropeAudit.name: Wednesday's Authentic Self-Determination: Individual Against the Crowd
tropeAudit.explanation: Wednesday Addams is, at her core, an individual who refuses to accommodate social pressure. She will not perform emotions she does not feel. She will not pretend to enjoy things she finds tedious. She will not change herself to make others comfortable. This is the character's defining trait across every iteration from Charles Addams's cartoons through Christina Ricci's films and Jenna Ortega's series. It is entirely organic to the IP and entirely non-ideological in the contemporary sense. The instinct to celebrate an individual who refuses to conform to the crowd's expectations is a conservative value as often as a progressive one. Wednesday is not a victim of social systems - she is a fierce individual who regards pity as beneath her. The show's treatment of her self-determination is its most traditionally resonant quality. Severity 5: defines the character and drives every major choice. High authenticity: core to the source material across 80 years of Addams Family iterations. High centrality. Score: 5 x 0.7 x 1.8 = 6.30.

tropeAudit.name: Gomez and Morticia as Model of Devoted Long-Term Marriage
tropeAudit.explanation: The Addams Family has always featured one of the most genuinely loving marriages in popular culture. Gomez and Morticia Addams are devoted, affectionate, and explicitly committed to each other across decades of the IP. Season 2 maintains this - their scenes together convey genuine warmth and the physical affection that made their relationship memorable in the 1991 film. Luis Guzman and Catherine Zeta-Jones have the chemistry to sell it. In a season that uses the outcast/normie framework to make progressive arguments, the Addams parents' marriage remains the most consistently traditional element: a man who adores his wife, a woman who adores her husband, and a household built on mutual commitment. This has been the franchise's best-kept secret for 80 years - a deeply conservative depiction of marriage hiding inside a Halloween aesthetic. Severity 4. High authenticity. Moderate centrality (they have less screen time in Season 2 than Season 1). Score: 4 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 2.80.

tropeAudit.name: Mystery and Detection as the Show's Core Genre Commitment
tropeAudit.explanation: Wednesday's primary mode of engagement with her world is investigation and deduction. The show is a Gothic detective story as much as a supernatural horror or coming-of-age narrative. Wednesday solves problems through observation, logical inference, and methodical investigation - not through social capital, emotional intelligence, or community solidarity. The detective genre is a traditionally conservative one: it assumes that truth is discoverable, that evidence is real, and that there is a correct answer worth finding. Wednesday's approach to detection is analytical to the point of social dysfunction, which the show treats as a feature rather than a flaw. Severity 3. High authenticity. Moderate centrality. Score: 3 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 2.10.

tropeAudit.name: Genuine Sibling Affection: Wednesday and Pugsley
tropeAudit.explanation: Pugsley's enrollment at Nevermore in Season 2 gives the show the sibling dynamic that the source material always centered. Wednesday and Pugsley's relationship - outwardly hostile, genuinely protective - is one of the most enduring dynamics in the IP. Season 2 expands it: Pugsley's presence at Nevermore creates new problems and new comedic situations, and Wednesday's care for him, expressed in the Addams way through creative violence and competitive contempt, is played with genuine affection. Isaac Ordonez delivers the performance with the right energy. Severity 3. High authenticity. Moderate centrality. Score: 3 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 2.10.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences for Villains Who Abuse Institutional Authority
tropeAudit.explanation: Barry Dort's ambitions for Nevermore, including bringing the school closer to normie norms and undermining its outcast-affirming mission, are revealed to be motivated by self-interested scheming rather than genuine educational concern. He receives consequences. This structural commitment - that those who abuse institutional authority for personal gain or ideological imposition should face accountability - is a traditional value regardless of whether the authority figure is coded as conservative or progressive. Severity 2. High authenticity. Moderate centrality. Score: 2 x 0.7 x 1.0 = 1.40.

tropeAudit.name: Loyalty to Friends as Non-Negotiable Moral Commitment
tropeAudit.explanation: Wednesday's relationship with Enid operates through her code of loyalty. Wednesday does not make friends easily and does not extend loyalty lightly, but once extended, it is not withdrawn without cause. When Enid faces the conversion camp threat, Wednesday's response is to fight the institution. This loyalty is not sentimentalized - it is treated as a commitment with personal cost. The show's understanding of friendship as a covenant with obligations rather than a feeling is a traditionally conservative view of social bonds. Severity 2. High authenticity. Low centrality. Score: 2 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.70.

summary.overall:
The first season of Wednesday was a cultural phenomenon by Netflix's own metrics, becoming the second-most watched English-language Netflix series ever. It succeeded because it understood its core asset: Jenna Ortega playing Wednesday Addams as a genuinely alien intelligence navigating a world she finds stupid, and finding that the world has things in it worth protecting despite herself.

Season 2 has that same asset. Ortega is still the reason to watch. She is one of the most controlled performers working in television - her ability to play an emotionally contained character across eight episodes without ever making Wednesday feel cold or inaccessible is technically remarkable. You never doubt that she cares about the people she cares about. You also never doubt that she would rather not show it.

So: what changed?

The show's allegorical ambitions escalated. Season 1's outcast-versus-normie framework was satirical and light-footed - a Gothic comedy about a school for monsters navigating small-town Vermont hostility. Season 2 tightens that allegory into something more pointed. The conversion camp storyline for werewolves is not veiled. The show intends the audience to map it directly onto conversion therapy for LGBTQ+ individuals, and it says so with all the subtlety of a Nevermore cafeteria tray to the face.

This is where Season 2 diverges from its predecessor. The show that Season 1 was - a stylish, eccentric Gothic mystery that happened to center an outcast community - was ideologically diffuse enough to be enjoyed across a wide audience. The show that Season 2 is has chosen sides in a specific cultural debate, and it has not chosen neutrality.

Whether this makes it unwatchable depends on your tolerance for the allegory. Critics who found it graceless in its execution have a point - Polygon's review that the show handles the conversion camp parallel 'with the grace of a butterfingered buffoon wielding a sledgehammer' is accurate as a craft criticism. The show is not subtle. It was never going to be subtle. It is a show where the entire aesthetic is maximalist Gothic excess.

What the show does not do is hide its agenda. This is not a trap. Wednesday Season 2 is not pretending to be a traditional values show while secretly advancing a progressive one. It is exactly what it presents itself as: a Gothic teen mystery with genuine craft, a legendary character, and a progressive allegorical framework that has been present since Season 1 and escalated in Season 2.

For VirtueVigil's traditional values audience: the scorecard is mixed but tips WOKE LEAN. The conversion camp storyline is the primary reason, alongside the identity-politics framing of the outcast community. These are not concealed - they are featured.

The things the show does that are worth defending: Jenna Ortega's performance, the Addams family marriage (Gomez and Morticia remain one of the most genuinely romantic couples in any mainstream franchise), the Gothic craft, the mystery plotting, and Tim Burton's visual contributions. These are real.

The things worth noting for traditional audiences: the conversion camp LGBTQ allegory is explicit and central, the outcast-as-marginalized-group framework maps directly onto contemporary identity politics, and the rural Vermont diversity casting is visibly artificial. These are also real.

The show is excellent television that happens to have a progressive social argument embedded in its second season. Adults can engage with it critically. Families with teenagers should be aware that the allegorical content is present and pointed.

title: The Mummy
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
studio: New Line Cinema / Atomic Monster / Blumhouse Productions

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: The Mummy (2026) does not qualify as a woke trap under VVWS v1.1 rules. A film can only be flagged as a woke trap if it actually scores woke (negative margin, WOKE LEAN or worse verdict). This film carries a +22.08 TRAD margin and a STRONGLY TRADITIONAL predicted verdict. There is no bait-and-switch. Lee Cronin's creative profile from Evil Dead Rise shows zero ideological injection into horror frameworks. The film's family-in-crisis premise is traditional from the premise line. No trap. No sleight of hand. What you see in the marketing is what you get in the theater.

director.name: Lee Cronin
director.ideology: TRADITIONAL. Lee Cronin is an Irish horror director whose debut feature The Hole in the Ground (2019) centered on a mother protecting her son from supernatural corruption. Evil Dead Rise (2023) doubled down on exactly that framework: a mother fighting ancient evil to protect her children. Both films are structurally and ideologically traditional. Cronin has never used his platform for progressive messaging. His stated creative philosophy centers on visceral, craft-first horror storytelling. The Mummy continues his pattern: family in danger, parent as protector, supernatural evil as the antagonist that tests the bonds holding a family together.
director.profile: Lee Cronin is one of the most exciting working directors in mainstream horror. Born in Cork, Ireland, he broke through with The Hole in the Ground (2019), a slow-burn supernatural thriller about a mother convinced her son has been replaced by something malevolent. The film premiered at Sundance, earned strong critical reviews, and established Cronin's signature: domestic horror that uses the family as both the setting and the stakes. Evil Dead Rise (2023) took that instinct and applied it to one of horror's most beloved franchises. The result was a film that grossed $147 million worldwide on a fraction of blockbuster budgets, scored 83% on Rotten Tomatoes, and left audiences physically shaken. Critics and fans praised Evil Dead Rise for delivering exactly what it promised: relentless, well-crafted horror with a mother-protecting-children core that gave the carnage genuine emotional weight. Cronin brought back his core crew for The Mummy: cinematographer Dave Garbett, composer Stephen McKeon, and editor Bryan Shaw. That continuity signals a filmmaker who knows what he is doing and trusts the people he is doing it with. His stated ambition for The Mummy, 'unlike any Mummy movie you ever laid eyeballs on before,' reads as a craft challenge rather than an ideological one. He is digging into the earth, not into Twitter discourse.

writers.profile: Cronin wrote The Mummy solo, which is consistent with his pattern: he wrote The Hole in the Ground and Evil Dead Rise as well. This is a director who controls his scripts, which matters for scoring purposes. There is no co-writer pulling in a different ideological direction. The family-in-crisis premise, the eight-year gap between disappearance and return, the corruption of the returned child, these are all decisions that belong entirely to Cronin. His track record as a solo writer is one of disciplined, character-grounded horror with no political subtext. The screenplay reportedly takes the mummification concept in directions distinct from both the Universal horror tradition and the 1999 adventure franchise. Cronin has said the film goes back to something older and more frightening than either. Based on the trailer line, 'Don't worry grandma, it's fun to be dead,' the tone is both genuinely creepy and willing to let horror have dark ironic edges.

composer.name: Stephen McKeon
composer.profile: Stephen McKeon is a longtime Cronin collaborator who scored both The Hole in the Ground and Evil Dead Rise. His work on Evil Dead Rise received strong praise for a score that escalated alongside the film's violence without ever telegraphing the scares before they hit. McKeon brings an understanding of how Cronin builds dread through environment and atmosphere rather than conventional horror score manipulation. For The Mummy, his score is expected to serve a film with a slower, more psychological first act (the eight-year gap, the family's grief, the return) before the horror fully surfaces. That structural challenge plays to McKeon's strengths: he is a composer who can sustain unease across quiet scenes, not just punctuate the loud ones.

cinematographer.name: Dave Garbett
cinematographer.profile: Dave Garbett shot Evil Dead Rise and worked with Cronin on Ash vs. Evil Dead. His visual approach to Evil Dead Rise was widely praised for the way it found horror in the confined domestic space of an apartment building. For The Mummy, the visual palette expands: the film was shot in Ireland and Spain, which gives Garbett desert landscapes, ancient architecture, and Irish countryside to work with. That geographic range, from open desert to enclosed domestic space, mirrors the film's narrative arc: a disappearance in vast emptiness, a return to the claustrophobic pressure of family.

casting_director.name: Not publicly disclosed at time of review
casting_director.profile: The casting of Jack Reynor as Charlie Cannon is the production's key creative bet. Reynor is an Irish actor best known for his roles in Midsommar (2019) and Free Fire (2016), both genre films that required physical and emotional range. As the journalist father whose family is shattered by his daughter's disappearance, Reynor's casting suggests the film is serious about the human stakes, not just the horror spectacle. Laia Costa as Larissa Cannon brings a Spanish-language career that includes Victoria (2015), one of the most technically ambitious films of the past decade, shot in a single continuous take. Casting Costa opposite Reynor creates a genuinely international family unit, which fits the film's shooting locations and gives the couple's dynamic cross-cultural texture. Natalie Grace carries the film's central mystery as Katie Cannon, the daughter who returns transformed. Her work on Yellowjackets (2021) demonstrates she can handle material that requires her to project both innocence and something deeply wrong.
