parentalGuidance.guidance: The Watchers earns its PG-13 rating and sits comfortably within it. The horror is atmospheric rather than visceral. Parents should note that the sustained tension and dread may be too intense for sensitive children under 12. The film's mythology draws on Irish folklore rather than demonic or satanic themes, which some faith-based parents may appreciate. There is no sexual content and no strong profanity. The film's core emotional theme, the weight of abandoning someone you love and carrying that guilt forward, is age-appropriate for teens. The Irish forest setting and fae mythology make it a good entry point for teens interested in European folklore and supernatural horror that is not cheap slasher product.

summary.overall:
Ishana Night Shyamalan's directorial debut is a better film than its 27% Rotten Tomatoes score suggests and a less complete film than its atmospheric first act promises. The gap between critical reception and audience response (27% critics vs. 68% audience) tells you something: this is a film that delivers genuine mood and competent craft but does not satisfy the critics who wanted something more formally ambitious.

The setup is legitimately strong. Mina (Dakota Fanning) is a young American pet-store employee in Galway who has been drifting for years, punishing herself for an act of abandonment she can never undo. She's asked to transport a rare golden conure parrot to Belfast. Her car dies in the middle of an ancient, trackless Irish forest. Darkness falls. A woman emerges from the tree line and says: run.

The Coop is a mirrored shelter in a clearing. One-way glass faces outward toward the forest. Every night, the four occupants stand in front of that glass and present themselves to the creatures outside. They call them the Watchers. The rules are simple: never go into the Burrows, never be outside after dark, always stand at the glass. Break the rules and you die.

This is good horror geography. The Coop creates immediate spatial economy. There are four people trapped together, unable to leave, watched every night by things that need to see them. The power dynamic, the Watchers as audience, the humans as compelled performers, has genuine menace. The film's first act uses this pressure beautifully. Madeline (Olwen Fouere) is the survivor who has been there longest, who has mastered the rules and become their keeper. Ciara (Georgina Campbell) is the emotional center, the person most desperate to escape. Daniel (Oliver Finnegan) is young, impulsive, and bad at following rules. Mina is the newcomer who arrives already broken.

The ensemble chemistry works. Fouere is the film's best performance, giving Madeline layers of controlled resignation that pay off when her backstory is revealed. The mystery of why Madeline has been there so long, what she knows that the others do not, drives the second act effectively. When the reveal arrives, it reframes everything you thought you understood about the character's motivations, and it lands.

Where the film loses traction is in the third act, when it must explain the Watchers and deliver a resolution. The mythology is actually richer than expected, drawing on genuine Irish fae folklore: the creatures are ancient shapeshifters who have always observed humans, who envy human form, who study humanity from a position of obsessive need. The backstory of a young woman who loved one of them and chose to stay is genuinely sad. But Ishana's father's influence shows most clearly in the final act's ambition to flip the script with a revelation, and the revelation here, while not bad, does not have the earned weight it needs.

For VirtueVigil purposes: The Watchers is a clean film operating in the supernatural horror tradition. Its values are conservative in the literary sense. Mina's arc is about confronting guilt, accepting responsibility for past failures, and choosing to reconnect with living people rather than hiding in self-imposed isolation. The Watchers' society is hierarchical and rule-bound. The community of survivors inside the Coop depends on adherence to rules for survival. The film does not contain progressive ideology. It does not lecture. A young female director adapting an Irish novel about Celtic mythology is not by itself a woke product. This is a sincere genre effort with real craft in its first two acts and a slightly underpowered landing.
summary.verdict_explanation: TRADITIONAL (+10 TRAD). The Watchers is built around a female protagonist whose arc is fundamentally about accepting personal guilt for abandonment, reconnecting with human community, and finding the courage to confront something genuinely terrifying. Its mythology draws on ancient, pre-modern, pre-progressive worldviews. Its primary woke deduction is a capable all-female protagonist quartet in a survival situation with a male character cast as the liability. The traditional score, anchored by a deep guilt-and-redemption arc and a mythological worldview grounded in pre-modern tradition, carries this into TRADITIONAL territory.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults with an interest in atmospheric horror and European folklore will find this more rewarding than the critical consensus suggests. The first act is genuinely well-constructed. The Coop geography is efficient. Fouere's performance is worth the ticket alone. The film's weakness is the third act, where the explanation of the Watchers' nature feels simultaneously over-elaborated and under-developed. It is a promising debut that does not fully stick its landing. Compare it to early Shyamalan rather than late Shyamalan: the craft is present, the ending doesn't quite pay off everything the setup earns.
summary.oneLiner: A young artist stranded in a trackless Irish forest must survive nightly observation by ancient fae creatures who punish anyone who refuses to be watched. A genuinely atmospheric debut with one great performance and a third act that can't match the setup.
summary.woke_trap_assessment: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The Watchers is exactly what it advertises. The mythology is drawn from Celtic tradition. The female ensemble is organic to a survival story about four people who happened to be in the forest. Nothing is concealed or revealed late to ambush conservative viewers.
summary.parentalGuidance: PG-13. Recommended for 13+. Violence, terror, and some thematic elements. Sustained atmospheric dread throughout. The film is not a jump-scare machine but maintains genuine tension. The Watchers are shown briefly and effectively. Their physical design is unsettling without being explicitly gory. A character is dragged underground and killed in the opening sequence. A character has their throat slit off-camera with sounds audible. A character dies from a fall. The film contains a brief scene of a character looking through a one-way mirror at creatures in a voyeuristic, zoo-like arrangement that some viewers may find psychologically disturbing. Brief depiction of suicide backstory (character abandoning a parent, not self-harm). No sexual content. No nudity. No profanity beyond mild language. The Watchers earns its PG-13 rating and sits comfortably within it. The horror is atmospheric rather than visceral. Parents should note that the sustained tension and dread may be too intense for sensitive children under 12. The film's mythology draws on Irish folklore rather than demonic or satanic themes, which some faith-based parents may appreciate. There is no sexual content and no strong profanity. The film's core emotional theme, the weight of abandoning someone you love and carrying that guilt forward, is age-appropriate for teens. The Irish forest setting and fae mythology make it a good entry point for teens interested in European folklore and supernatural horror that is not cheap slasher product.

tropeAudit.name: Guilt, Accountability, and Redemption
tropeAudit.explanation: Mina's entire arc is built on accepting responsibility for abandoning her mother when she needed her most. She left. Her mother died alone. Mina has spent years punishing herself by refusing to form attachments. The Watchers' forest is literalized guilt: a place she cannot leave, where she is trapped with her choices. The film does not excuse her. It requires her to confront what she did, accept the consequences, and choose to reconnect with people rather than remain in self-imposed exile. This is a traditional moral framework: guilt is real, it has weight, and the only escape is honest reckoning, not self-pity.

tropeAudit.name: Ancient Myth and Pre-Modern Worldview
tropeAudit.explanation: The Watchers are drawn from genuine Irish fae mythology, creatures as old as the land that predate modern categories of good and evil. They operate by ancient rules and ancient hungers. The film treats this mythology with seriousness rather than irony. It does not explain the creatures through science or rationalize them through psychology. They are simply what they are: ancient, powerful, and bound by the rules of their own kind. This is a traditional horror sensibility: some things exist outside human understanding and will not be talked down to.

tropeAudit.name: Community Through Shared Rules
tropeAudit.explanation: The Coop survivors stay alive by following Madeline's rules. Daniel's impulsiveness almost gets everyone killed multiple times. Mina's first act of integration is accepting the rules she was given rather than questioning their legitimacy. The film presents rule-following not as submission but as the practical foundation of a community under threat. When Daniel breaks the rules, bad things happen. The traditional message is clear: civilization, even tiny improvised civilization, requires that individuals subordinate impulse to shared code.

tropeAudit.name: Sacrifice as Love
tropeAudit.explanation: Madeline's secret backstory involves a profound act of sacrifice rooted in love, the most ancient and traditional motivation for self-abnegation. Without spoiling the reveal: the reason Madeline has been in the forest so long is not cowardice or selfishness. It is love expressed through decades of self-imposed suffering. The film honors this. It does not present her sacrifice as pathological. It presents it as the natural and tragic consequence of caring deeply about someone.

tropeAudit.name: Return to Roots
tropeAudit.explanation: Mina's journey ends with her return to the life she abandoned rather than the construction of some progressive new identity. She goes home. She reconnects with her twin sister. She chooses people over isolation. The film's resolution is conservative in the classical sense: the prodigal returning, not the wanderer finding liberation. It says that the connections you abandoned are worth returning to, that the people who needed you still matter even when you failed them.

tropeAudit.name: All-Female Survivor Ensemble
tropeAudit.explanation: Three of the four Coop survivors are women. The one male survivor, Daniel, is young, impulsive, and repeatedly makes things worse. This ensemble configuration reflects contemporary female-led horror conventions. It is not weaponized against traditional values but does reflect a genre trend toward female-dominated survival casts. The authentic score is moderate: an Irish forest in an isolated survival scenario plausibly produces mixed groups, but the 3:1 ratio with the male as the liability character is a recognizable pattern.

tropeAudit.name: Female Director Debut Signaling
tropeAudit.explanation: The promotional apparatus around The Watchers leaned heavily on Ishana's status as a young female director making her feature debut, with her father M. Night Shyamalan as producer. This framing is Hollywood's standard mode for credentialing female directors in genre film. The content of the film is not ideologically woke, but the meta-narrative packaging carries the usual progressive industry signaling.

tropeAudit.name: Toxic Jealousy of Male Creatures
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's backstory hints that male Watchers' obsession with human women carries a possessive, jealous dimension. This is not a central theme but a supporting texture that aligns with a contemporary horror tendency to code supernatural male aggression as a metaphor for patriarchal control. In The Watchers it is atmospheric rather than polemical, but it is present and worth noting.

comparison_films.title: Hereditary (2018)
comparison_films.note: Both films feature a female protagonist processing guilt and grief through supernatural horror. Hereditary is more formally accomplished and more ideologically neutral. The Watchers is less transgressive but also less savage in its treatment of family.

comparison_films.title: The Village (2004)
comparison_films.note: M. Night Shyamalan's closest comparison to his daughter's debut: isolated community, external creatures requiring rules for survival, a mystery about the true nature of the threat. The Village executes the formula more successfully. Both films reward viewers who engage with the mythology rather than demanding action-oriented payoffs.

comparison_films.title: Midsommar (2019)
comparison_films.note: Both films involve Americans stranded in old-world settings with folklore-based supernatural communities. Midsommar weaponizes its mythology as feminist vengeance fantasy. The Watchers does no such thing. They are very different films wearing similar genre clothes.

title: The Phoenician Scheme
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team
cast: Benicio del Toro as Zsa-zsa Korda

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The Phoenician Scheme is marketed and delivered as a Wes Anderson film: symmetrical compositions, deadpan delivery, pastel color palettes, and an ensemble of eccentric characters pursuing overlapping agendas in a stylized mid-century setting. The film's content is exactly what the trailer advertises. No ideological ambush occurs past the halfway mark. Wes Anderson's work has always operated in a politically ambiguous register that frustrates simple categorization. This film continues that pattern: its treatment of a father-daughter reconciliation, corporate betrayal, and institutional corruption contains no discoverable progressive agenda items. Conservative viewers who enjoy Anderson's aesthetic will find nothing ideologically hostile here.

director.name: Wes Anderson
director.ideology: POLITICALLY AMBIGUOUS. Wes Anderson is the most aesthetically distinctive working American director and the least ideologically transparent one. He has no documented political history. He is not a progressive activist. He does not make films with overt ideological agendas. His films are set in stylized alternate pasts that comment obliquely on human institutions, family dysfunction, and the gap between ambition and reality. The Phoenician Scheme fits this pattern exactly. Anderson lives and works largely in Europe, contributing to the European art-house sensibility of his later work. VirtueVigil has consistently found his films in the TRADITIONAL LEAN to MIXED range because his aesthetic conservatism, respect for craft, formal discipline, and interest in family bonds, offsets his political ambiguity.
director.profile: Wes Anderson is the director of Bottle Rocket, Rushmore, The Royal Tenenbaums, The Life Aquatic, The Darjeeling Limited, Fantastic Mr. Fox, Moonrise Kingdom, The Grand Budapest Hotel, Isle of Dogs, The French Dispatch, Asteroid City, and now The Phoenician Scheme. He has been nominated for multiple Academy Awards. The Grand Budapest Hotel is widely considered his finest work: a film that is formally perfect, emotionally moving, and politically conservative in its lamentation for a lost civilization of grace and refinement. The Phoenician Scheme is less formally perfect than The Grand Budapest Hotel but operates in the same register: a ruthless man of the mid-century business world, a daughter who chose vocation over family, and the machinery of institutional betrayal grinding against both of them.

writer.name: Wes Anderson (story with Roman Coppola)
writer.profile: Anderson and Roman Coppola have collaborated on story since The Darjeeling Limited (2007). The Phoenician Scheme follows their established pattern: an original story concept developed between them, with Anderson handling the final screenplay alone. The film's plot, a tycoon who survives multiple assassination attempts and appoints his estranged nun daughter as heir while pursuing a massive infrastructure project in Phoenicia, has the structured absurdism characteristic of Anderson's best work. The script is sharper than Asteroid City (2023), which many critics found impenetrable, and more character-driven than The French Dispatch (2021), which prioritized formal experimentation over emotional access.

lead_producer.name: Wes Anderson, Steven Rales, Jeremy Dawson, John Peet

composer.name: Alexandre Desplat
composer.profile: Desplat returns for his seventh collaboration with Anderson, following The Grand Budapest Hotel, Isle of Dogs, The French Dispatch, and others. He is one of the most skilled film composers working today: his scores for The Imitation Game, The Shape of Water, and Phyllis Schlafly biopic Mrs. America demonstrate extraordinary range. For The Phoenician Scheme he works in a Mediterranean-inflected orchestral register appropriate for the Phoenicia setting, combining his typical chamber orchestra density with wind instruments that evoke ancient trade routes and modern corporate boardrooms in the same musical gesture.

top_performers.name: Benicio del Toro
top_performers.note: Del Toro is Anderson's best leading man since Bill Murray's Aquatic character. Zsa-zsa Korda is ruthless, self-made, nearly indestructible across a series of escalating assassination attempts, and genuinely desperate for his daughter's regard. Del Toro plays the film's emotional core with the kind of deadpan vulnerability that only very skilled actors can achieve: the grief is visible under the comedy without ever breaking the formal surface. It may be his best performance in a decade.

top_performers.name: Mia Threapleton
top_performers.note: Kate Winslet's daughter makes her major film debut as Sister Liesl and holds the screen against an enormous ensemble without apparent effort. Her performance is the still center of a chaotic comedy: a woman who chose God and discipline over the chaos of her father's world, now required to re-engage with that world as its nominal heir. Threapleton's restraint is precisely calibrated.

top_performers.name: Michael Cera
top_performers.note: As Bjorn, Korda's hapless associate, Cera is doing what Cera does best: comic vulnerability with an undercurrent of genuine pathos. He has the film's funniest sequences and handles them with the control of someone who has learned to make awkwardness look effortless. His physical comedy in the assassination-attempt scenes is particularly precise.

fidelity_casting.summary: The Phoenician Scheme is an original screenplay. No source material to evaluate fidelity against. The film's international setting and Anderson's European production base (filmed at Babelsberg Studio in Germany) reflect the practical and aesthetic demands of the story rather than any casting agenda. The ensemble is diverse in the way that global co-productions naturally are.

There is no gore, no extended graphic violence, and no sexual content. The film's mature themes, corporate betrayal, the inheritance of guilt, the difficulty of reconciling with an absent parent, are handled with Anderson's characteristic emotional restraint. The film's fast-moving dialogue and dense ensemble may be more challenging for younger viewers than any content concern. Families with teenagers who enjoy Anderson's work should have no concerns.

summary.overall:
Wes Anderson's thirteenth feature is his most purely entertaining film since The Grand Budapest Hotel and his most emotionally direct film since Moonrise Kingdom. After the formal experiments of The French Dispatch and Asteroid City left audiences divided, The Phoenician Scheme returns to the pleasure of story: a man surviving the world's attempts to kill him and trying, badly, to reconcile with his daughter before one of those attempts succeeds.

Zsa-zsa Korda (Benicio del Toro) is a Levantine business magnate who has survived seven assassination attempts in the opening sequence. He is building an infrastructure project of staggering ambition in the historical region of Phoenicia, a project that has made him powerful enough to attract enemies across multiple intelligence services, corporate boards, and rival states. He has a daughter, Sister Liesl (Mia Threapleton), whom he has not seen in years. She became a nun. He appoints her his sole heir.

What follows is a spy-espionage-comedy-thriller that is formally the most Anderson-esque of all Anderson films: an intricate machine of competing agendas, deadpan delivery, and meticulously designed production geometry that somehow contains a genuine emotional story about a father who chose empire over family and is now trying to buy back what he gave away.

Anderson's formal signature, the bilateral symmetry, the overhead shots, the rapid panning cuts, the period-accurate costuming in colors that do not exist in nature, is operating at full power. The Babelsberg Studio production design is extraordinary. The Phoenicia of Anderson's film is a fictional mid-20th century state that combines Ottoman and Mediterranean influences with the tailored aesthetic of The Grand Budapest Hotel's mountain republic. It is the best-designed world in any film this year.

Del Toro is doing something Anderson has not quite had before: a leading man with physical menace who can hold the Anderson deadpan register. Korda is the kind of man who orders executions and arranges them with the same calm precision he uses to manage construction permits. Del Toro makes this specific combination of power and controlled desperation genuinely affecting.

Mia Threapleton's Sister Liesl is the film's moral center. She is not a progressive icon. She is a woman who chose a vocation over a broken family and is now being asked to re-engage with that family from a position of relative powerlessness. Her arc, from dutiful religious to reluctant heir to active participant in her father's survival, is handled with more subtlety than the plot requires. The Anderson aesthetic usually smooths character development into production design. Sister Liesl's development resists smoothing.

The ensemble, Tom Hanks, Bryan Cranston, Riz Ahmed, Scarlett Johansson, Michael Cera, Benedict Cumberbatch, Bill Murray, Willem Dafoe, and more, serves the film efficiently. This is not the ensemble showpiece of The French Dispatch, where characters were episodically separated. Everyone here serves the central plot. The villains, Cumberbatch's Radestock and Cranston's Kasernenraum, are given exactly as much screen time as the plot requires and not a frame more.

For VirtueVigil purposes: The Phoenician Scheme is a Wes Anderson film, which means it is operating in a register that is neither progressive nor traditionally conservative but is aesthetically conservative in the deepest sense: it believes in craft, form, and the moral seriousness of storytelling. Its emotional center is a father-daughter reconciliation. Its villain is corporate greed wearing the mask of geopolitical necessity. Its heroine is a nun. None of this is ideologically loaded. It is simply the story Wes Anderson wanted to tell, told with the technical mastery he has spent twenty-five years developing.
summary.verdict_explanation: TRADITIONAL LEAN (+6 TRAD). The Phoenician Scheme is built around a father-daughter reconciliation that the film treats with genuine emotional seriousness. Its formal aesthetics are deeply conservative: discipline, craft, and respect for narrative structure over message. The woke deductions are minor: a diverse ensemble in an Anderson film reflects his European production base and global story sensibility rather than ideological mandate, and the villain being corporate rather than governmental is genre texture in an espionage film. The traditional score outweighs these deductions comfortably.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults who appreciate craft and formalism will find The Phoenician Scheme the most accessible Anderson film in a decade. The emotional story is clear and genuinely affecting. Del Toro is extraordinary. The production design is the finest of Anderson's career. The film's weakness is the mid-section, where the espionage plot mechanics are somewhat more labyrinthine than the emotional payoff requires, but Anderson has always been willing to let his plots run dense. The ending earns its emotional weight. It is one of the year's better films.
summary.oneLiner: A Levantine tycoon survives a seventh assassination attempt, appoints his estranged nun daughter as sole heir, and drags her into the murderous geopolitics of his infrastructure empire. Wes Anderson at his most emotionally direct, with Benicio del Toro giving one of the year's best performances.

The film's values are formal rather than political: discipline, craft, emotional honesty. Conservative viewers who enjoy Anderson's aesthetic can engage freely.

tropeAudit.name: Father-Daughter Reconciliation as Emotional Core
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's entire emotional architecture rests on Zsa-zsa Korda's desperate, clumsy attempt to reconnect with a daughter he drove away by choosing his empire over his family. This is a traditional family-reconciliation story dressed in espionage comedy clothes. Korda's guilt about his failure as a father is the wound the film is probing. Sister Liesl's guarded response to his overture is neither feminist lecturing nor simple forgiveness: it is the response of a real person who needed something from a parent and did not receive it, and who now has to decide whether to accept imperfect reconciliation or hold to a principled distance. The film believes in the possibility of reconciliation and earns it.

tropeAudit.name: Religious Vocation Treated with Respect
tropeAudit.explanation: Sister Liesl's choice to become a nun is presented as a genuine vocation rather than as a flight from reality, an act of psychological dysfunction, or an ideology to be dismantled by the film's events. Anderson takes her religious life seriously. The convent is shown as a community of genuine purpose. Her values, duty, restraint, refusal to be swept up in her father's chaos, are presented as strengths rather than limitations requiring liberation. For a contemporary film to treat a nun's vocation with this level of seriousness and respect is genuinely unusual.

tropeAudit.name: Formal and Aesthetic Conservatism
tropeAudit.explanation: Wes Anderson's filmmaking represents aesthetic conservatism in the deepest sense: a belief in craft, discipline, formal mastery, and the moral seriousness of storytelling. In an era of content-over-form filmmaking, Anderson insists that how a story is told is as morally important as what story is told. This is a conservative artistic philosophy rooted in the classical tradition. The Phoenician Scheme demonstrates this commitment at full power.

tropeAudit.name: Villain is Corporate-Geopolitical Rather Than Traditional
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's antagonists are rival tycoons and state intelligence services pursuing their own institutional interests against Korda. The villains are not the result of Korda's traditional values failing. They are the result of his business success attracting powerful enemies. This framing does not attribute institutional corruption to traditional values. It attributes it to ambition and power-seeking, which is ideologically neutral.

tropeAudit.name: Global Ensemble Diversity Casting
tropeAudit.explanation: Anderson's ensemble reflects his European production base and the film's international setting rather than a diversity mandate, but the casting result aligns with contemporary Hollywood inclusive casting. Riz Ahmed, Jeffrey Wright, and other actors of diverse background appear in significant roles without any cultural or political comment attached. The authenticity score is moderate: a Levantine business empire genuinely would involve diverse stakeholders.

tropeAudit.name: Institutional Authority as Corrupt
tropeAudit.explanation: The film presents intelligence agencies, corporate boards, and rival state actors as motivated entirely by self-interest and willing to commit murder for institutional advantage. This is the standard espionage film critique of institutional authority: power corrupts, institutions lie, the official story is never the real story. Anderson does not render this as a political lecture, but it contributes a mild anti-institutional undercurrent throughout the film. The critique is aesthetically deployed rather than ideologically argued, but it is present.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Colonial Infrastructure Critique
tropeAudit.explanation: Korda's infrastructure project in historical Phoenicia carries an implicit critique of Western capital operating in the Global South: powerful outside interests funding large projects in smaller nations for their own benefit, drawing opposition from parties who view the project as exploitation. The film does not develop this critique into a thesis, but it is present as background texture, and several antagonist factions are framed as protecting local interests against Korda's imperial ambitions.

comparison_films.title: The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014)
comparison_films.note: Anderson's finest film and the most direct comparison for The Phoenician Scheme: a ruthless but charming man of an earlier era, a young protege, institutional betrayal, and a deep lament for a civilization of grace that is being destroyed by forces beyond anyone's control. The Grand Budapest Hotel achieves more. The Phoenician Scheme is more emotionally accessible.

comparison_films.title: Asteroid City (2023)
comparison_films.note: Anderson's immediately preceding film was his most formally experimental and least emotionally accessible. The Phoenician Scheme is a correction in the direction of story and feeling. Viewers who bounced off Asteroid City should give The Phoenician Scheme a chance.

comparison_films.title: The French Dispatch (2021)
comparison_films.note: The Phoenician Scheme is more cohesive and less politically freighted than The French Dispatch, which contained explicit left-wing political commentary in its student-revolution segment. The Phoenician Scheme lacks that kind of direct political content.

title: Reminders of Him
author: Debra Ducane

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. Reminders of Him is a straightforward Colleen Hoover romance adaptation. The progressive elements -- an ex-convict heroine, a neighbor with Down syndrome, drug use backstory -- are present from the premise onward and were discussed in the book's widespread readership before production. There is no ideological bait-and-switch. The film is exactly what it advertises: a tearjerker romance about forgiveness, motherhood, and second chances.

director.name: Vanessa Caswill
director.ideology: APOLITICAL / COMMERCIAL. British director Vanessa Caswill is primarily a television director known for Misfits, Waterloo Road, and First Kill. Reminders of Him is her theatrical feature debut. Her direction prioritizes emotional authenticity over political statement. Critics have noted she executes Hoover's melodramatic peaks competently without imposing a distinct visual or ideological signature.
director.profile: Vanessa Caswill comes to Reminders of Him with a strong television drama background. Her comfort with intense emotional scenes and her ability to draw grounded performances from a cast dealing with grief, guilt, and longing are evident in the film's strongest moments. The Plugged In review notes the film 'leans into smoldering sensuality,' which is consistent with Caswill's ability to create atmospheric romantic tension without tipping into vulgarity.

writers.profile: Colleen Hoover is the literary phenomenon behind CoHo, the BookTok movement that turned romance publishing upside down. Reminders of Him was her bestselling novel of 2022. Her co-screenwriter Lauren Levine is also her producing partner, suggesting the adaptation was tightly controlled by the source material's author. Hoover's fiction traffics in heavy-duty trauma -- grief, addiction, incarceration, parenthood -- deployed in service of intensely romantic love stories. The progressive elements (ex-convict heroine, drug use, incarcerated father characters) come from the source material rather than Hollywood injection.

composer.name: Tom Howe
composer.profile: Tom Howe is a British composer known for Downton Abbey: A New Era and several Netflix romantic dramas. His score for Reminders of Him reportedly emphasizes strings and piano for the grief sequences, shifting to something warmer when Kenna and Ledger's relationship develops. Functional romantic scoring with no notable ideological dimension.

top_cast.name: Maika Monroe
top_cast.notes: Monroe is best known for horror (It Follows, Watcher) and brings an unusual quality of raw, slightly feral vulnerability to this role. Critics note she is more effective in the damaged, isolated sequences than in the sunny romantic ones, which gives the film an unexpectedly dark texture.

top_cast.name: Tyriq Withers
top_cast.notes: Rising actor from Winning Time. Withers plays Ledger as a man torn between loyalty to his dead best friend and genuine feeling for the woman who -- however accidentally -- caused that friend's death. His performance is understated and effective.

top_cast.name: Lauren Graham
top_cast.notes: Graham is perfectly cast as the grieving mother who has displaced her pain into maternal custody of Diem. Her transformation from antagonist to ally is the film's most emotionally satisfying arc.

top_cast.name: Lainey Wilson
top_cast.notes: Country singer Lainey Wilson makes her film debut here as Kenna's co-worker. Her naturalness and warmth are praised by critics as a highlight of the supporting cast.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: Reminders of Him by Colleen Hoover (2022)
fidelityCasting.assessment: The casting is faithful to the novel's characters. Kenna Rowan, the lead, is white in the source material; Maika Monroe is white. Ledger Ward is not specifically racialized in the text; Tyriq Withers, a Black actor, was cast in this role. This is the only notable racial casting choice, and it is an original script decision rather than a corrective swap of a previously-established character. The interracial romance is not flagged or politicized within the film's narrative -- it is simply a love story. No casting concerns rise to the level of ideological injection.

summary.overall:
This is a tearjerker built around one of the most traditional premises in modern romance fiction: a mother fighting to know her child. It is not a politically complicated film. It is not interested in being provocative. It is a Colleen Hoover adaptation, which means it is interested in exactly one thing -- making you feel the full weight of love when it has been separated from itself by tragedy.

That is not a criticism. For VirtueVigil readers, the scores tell the story: Woke 5.6, Trad 16.38, margin +10.78 TRADITIONAL. This film leans the way most Hoover readers already suspected it would. The central values are maternal love, forgiveness, and family restoration. The woke elements are real but minor, and they land in the background rather than in the film's moral center.

Kenna Rowan (Maika Monroe) spent five years in prison for vehicular manslaughter. She and her boyfriend Scotty were high when the car went off the road. He died. She gave birth to their daughter Diem in prison and never held her. When she gets out on parole, she comes back to the small town where Scotty's parents -- Grace (Lauren Graham) and Patrick (Bradley Whitford) -- are raising Diem. They have every reason to hate her. She has every reason to be afraid of them. The film's architecture is a countdown: how long before the truth, the grief, and the love all collapse into each other?

Director Vanessa Caswill, making her theatrical feature debut after years of British television drama (Misfits, First Kill), does not try to intellectualize this setup. She leans into the emotional machinery and lets it run. The result is a film that cries at you often and earns those tears more often than critics have been willing to admit.

For the CoHo fanbase -- and it is enormous, the film crossed $41M domestic by week three -- the central question is always whether a Hoover adaptation respects the source. With Hoover herself co-writing the screenplay alongside producer Lauren Levine, this is the most author-controlled Hoover adaptation yet. The bones of the novel are intact: the bar, the notebooks, the slow burn of Kenna and Ledger finding each other across a landscape of shared grief. Readers who wept through the book will find their tears honored here.

The romance between Kenna and Ledger Ward (Tyriq Withers, rising and worth watching) is the film's secondary engine. Withers plays Ledger as a man genuinely trapped between loyalty to a dead friend and something new and real growing inside him. He is understated where the film is otherwise prone to maximum volume. Critics at Rotten Tomatoes landed at 67% (divided), while audiences scored it 89% (enthusiastic). The gap is familiar with Hoover: critics want craft and restraint, audiences want catharsis and connection. The audience is getting the better deal here.

What earns this film its +10.78 TRAD margin? Three things, and they are all load-bearing.

First: motherhood as an irreplaceable, sacred bond. Kenna's entire existence after prison is organized around one goal -- knowing Diem. Not co-parenting rights, not systemic advocacy, not personal fulfillment. Her daughter. The film treats this as the most serious possible human motivation and never condescends to it. The reunion scene, when Diem falls asleep on Kenna, is the emotional climax of the film and the most traditionally structured moment of parental love you will see in a 2026 theatrical release.

Second: forgiveness as the moral resolution. Grace and Patrick Landry read Kenna's notebooks and choose to forgive. Not because the justice system demanded it or because a therapist told them to. Because Scotty would have wanted it, and because their love for their son demands they honor what he would have chosen. This is a profoundly traditional moral framework -- forgiveness as an act of courage, not accommodation.

Third: the romance is a man and a woman, complicated by loyalty and grief and eventually resolved by commitment. No ambiguity, no deconstruction. A heterosexual romance treated as worth building a future around.

The woke scoring is not zero for a reason. Kenna's incarceration is framed with heavy sympathy that occasionally tips toward the system-failed-her territory, though the film never makes that argument explicitly. She did plead guilty. She did serve her time. The drug-use backstory that caused the accident is treated more as tragedy than moral failure -- the film acknowledges her culpability without making her pay for it emotionally beyond what she has already paid.

Country singer Lainey Wilson, making her film debut as Kenna's co-worker Amy, is warm and funny in ways that provide necessary relief from the film's relentless grief. Her naturalness is a pleasant surprise. A supporting character named Lady Diana, a neighbor with Down syndrome, is handled with warmth and dignity rather than as an ideology delivery mechanism.

Bring tissues. Maika Monroe's performance is better than critics have given her credit for -- she makes Kenna's desperate, damaged love feel viscerally real even in the film's weaker scenes. Lauren Graham's transformation from cold antagonist to anguished ally is the film's best acting moment, the kind of thing she can do in her sleep but chooses to do for real here.

The values at the center of this film are real and they are traditional. Mothers fighting for their children. Families choosing forgiveness. Love surviving loss. That is worth two hours of anyone's time.
summary.oneLiner: A Colleen Hoover adaptation with genuine emotional power -- maternal love, forgiveness, and family restoration at its core, with only minor woke elements in the incarceration framing.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults who enjoy Hallmark-adjacent tearjerkers with genuine emotional stakes will find plenty to appreciate here. The film's commitment to motherhood as an irreplaceable bond, its treatment of forgiveness as a moral act rather than a political one, and its uncomplicated heterosexual romance are all assets. The PG-13 rating earns its keep -- the drug-use backstory and sensual scenes require parental awareness for teen viewers, but this is not a film with progressive ideology as its agenda. It is a film about whether love can survive loss. For most of its runtime, it makes a convincing case.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13. Appropriate for ages 15 and up with parental awareness. The primary content concerns are: the drug-use backstory that caused the inciting accident (discussed explicitly), sensual romantic content between the leads (not graphic), and heavy themes of grief and parental separation. The film presents an ex-convict as a sympathetic heroine, which parents should be prepared to discuss in terms of consequences, forgiveness, and the difference between understanding and excusing. No LGBTQ content. No strong violence. The emotional intensity is the film's most significant challenge for younger viewers.

title: Project Hail Mary (2026)
author: Debra Ducane

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. Project Hail Mary cannot be a woke trap because it does not score woke. The margin is strongly positive (+19.88 TRAD). The film's traditional values are present from the opening frame: a man wakes alone on a spacecraft, remembers his duty, and gets to work. There is no bait, no pivot, no ideological ambush. What you see in the trailer is what you get in the theater. This is one of the cleanest mainstream blockbusters of the decade.

director.name: Phil Lord & Christopher Miller
director.ideology: CENTER. Lord and Miller operate as humanists rather than ideologues. Their filmography, The LEGO Movie, 21 Jump Street, Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, consistently prioritizes character, wit, and emotional honesty over political messaging. Lord has described his filmmaking philosophy as trusting the audience. Miller has spoken publicly about letting story drive every decision. Neither has a history of injecting progressive messaging into source material that does not call for it.
director.profile: Phil Lord and Christopher Miller are one of the most commercially reliable and critically respected directing duos working today. They turned a LEGO toy commercial into a stealth masterpiece about creativity and parental control (The LEGO Movie, 2014). They turned a forgotten TV cop show into a sharp comedy meta-commentary (21 Jump Street, 2012). They produced the Oscar-winning Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018), which redefined what an animated superhero film could look like without abandoning story fundamentals. Their track record on adaptations is specifically strong: they tend to identify the core emotional truth of source material and protect it, rather than retrofitting contemporary ideology onto established stories. For Project Hail Mary, they were handed perhaps the most adaptation-friendly sci-fi novel of the decade: a book that is already cinematic, already humane, already apolitical. They did not blow it.

writer.name: Phil Lord & Christopher Miller (screenplay); Andy Weir (novel)
writer.profile: Lord and Miller wrote the screenplay themselves, which is the single most important structural decision in this production. Bringing in outside screenwriters with different sensibilities is where adaptations most often go wrong. By keeping the script in-house, they maintained direct fidelity to what makes Weir's novel work: the voice of Ryland Grace, the methodical problem-solving sequences, and the slow reveal of Rocky's existence and the pair's developing friendship. Weir served as an executive producer, which suggests the production treated his material with institutional respect rather than treating him as a name to license. The result is a screenplay that feels like a translation rather than a reinvention.

lead_producer.name: Amy Pascal, Aditya Sood, Rachel O'Connor

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: Project Hail Mary by Andy Weir (2021)
fidelityCasting.assessment: STRONG FIDELITY. Ryland Grace is deliberately racially ambiguous in Weir's novel. Weir has confirmed in multiple interviews that he intentionally left Grace's physical appearance unspecified, allowing readers to project themselves onto the character. Ryan Gosling was cast for his qualities as a performer, specifically his ability to project warmth, accessibility, and intellectual engagement while working largely alone on screen, rather than for any demographic consideration. This is not diversity casting and it is not whitewashing. It is a production team making a smart creative call about screen presence for a character defined entirely by personality and competence. The ensemble cast (Ken Leung, Milana Vayntrub, Sandra Huller) reflects genuine creative variety rather than a DEI checkbox exercise. The supporting roles are minor relative to Grace's dominance of the narrative, and the casting does not reshape or redefine the story's moral architecture.
fidelityCasting.castingNotes: No character race-swaps from established canon. Original IP with ambiguous protagonist. Ensemble diversity is incidental to the story's setting and natural in context.

summary.overall:
Project Hail Mary opens with a man waking up alone on a spacecraft with no memory of who he is or why he is there. It ends with him choosing to stay, alone, in a distant solar system, because someone else needs him more than Earth does. Everything between those two moments is one of the most satisfying, morally coherent, and genuinely optimistic science fiction films produced by a major studio in the last fifteen years.

Ryan Gosling plays Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who was recruited against his will for a last-chance mission to save Earth. The sun is dying, slowly, because a mysterious organism called Astrophage is feeding on it. Grace woke up as the sole survivor of a three-person crew. He has no memory. He is alone. He has to figure out everything from scratch: where he is, why he is there, what he is supposed to do.

This is the premise Phil Lord and Christopher Miller inherited from Andy Weir's 2021 novel, and they execute it with a fidelity that should be studied in film schools. They trusted the book. The book is good. The result is a film that is also good.

What makes Project Hail Mary work is its moral universe. Grace does not save Earth because he is the chosen one. He is not a hero who wanted the job. He is a man who understood what was at stake and did what needed to be done, including erasing his own memory to force himself onto a mission he had already refused. That is not a superhero. That is an adult. The film treats its audience the same way.

The friendship between Grace and Rocky, an alien from another star system pursuing the same problem from the opposite side, is the film's emotional core. Rocky communicates through musical tones rather than language. The early sequences where the two work out how to talk to each other are genuinely funny and genuinely moving, sometimes simultaneously. Their collaboration is built on competence, mutual respect, and shared stakes. It is not a diversity partnership. It is a scientific one.

Lord and Miller bring their signature lightness to the film without undercutting its weight. Grace is funny, specifically the low-key funny of a person who copes with terror through dry observation. Gosling has rarely been better. The film earns every emotional beat it collects.

At $164.3 million domestic through two weeks and currently sitting at number one, Project Hail Mary is delivering the box office numbers that remind studios that audiences will show up for original, well-crafted stories. This film does not exist in a franchise. There is no cinematic universe waiting to absorb it. It stands alone, as Ryland Grace stands alone, and it is more than enough.
summary.oneLiner: A faithful, optimistic, morally serious sci-fi film about a man who saves the world by being good at his job and willing to pay the cost. Gosling is exceptional. Lord and Miller trusted the book. The audience is rewarding them for it.
summary.verdict: Project Hail Mary is the rare blockbuster that believes in something. It believes science is a tool for human survival. It believes sacrifice is real and meaningful. It believes friendship is possible across any difference, even interstellar ones. These are not radical propositions. They are classical ones. The film makes them feel urgent again.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults should buy tickets and bring their kids. Project Hail Mary is one of the cleanest major releases of 2026 by content standards and one of the most intellectually nourishing by any standard. The film's values are classical: competence over credential, sacrifice over self-preservation, collaboration over ideology. Ryland Grace is not a government program. He is not the output of a diversity initiative. He is a middle school science teacher who knew enough chemistry and biology and physics to do what no one else could, and who was willing to die alone to do it. That is a hero worth watching. The film is also, frankly, a corrective to years of sci-fi films that used space as a backdrop for Earth's culture wars. In Project Hail Mary, the universe does not care about our politics. The problem is the problem. The solution is the solution. This is what science fiction is supposed to do.
summary.parentalGuidance:
MPAA Rating: PG-13

Recommended Age: 10 and up

Content Details: Mild language (no strong profanity). Peril and tension throughout, including sequences dealing with death of crew members (handled off-screen and through memory flashbacks, not graphic). Some depictions of physical danger in space. Rocky's appearance may startle very young children initially but is handled with warmth throughout the film. No sexual content. No gratuitous violence.

Positive Indicators: Strong science education content woven into the narrative. Multiple sequences model systematic problem-solving, hypothesis testing, and intellectual humility. Excellent conversation starter for families interested in space, biology, chemistry, and the nature of courage.

Bottom Line: One of the most family-appropriate wide releases of 2026. Adults will not be bored. Kids who love science will be electrified. A rare genuine cross-generational experience.

tropeAudit.name: Identity Politics / Forced DEI Casting
tropeAudit.explanation: Ryan Gosling is cast as Ryland Grace, a character who is racially ambiguous in Weir's novel. This is not race-swapping from established canon. However, a major Hollywood production casting a white A-list star in a role written as racially ambiguous does reflect the industry's default casting hierarchy. Gosling was chosen for performer qualities suited to the role. The supporting ensemble (Leung, Vayntrub, Huller) reflects genuine creative variety. Authenticity is Moderate because the creative justification is real but the industry default assumption also applies. Centrality is Moderate because casting choices are always present throughout the film.

tropeAudit.name: Nihilism / Civilization Critique
tropeAudit.explanation: Near-absent. The film's entire premise is that human civilization is worth saving and the protagonist dedicates his life to that proposition. There is no critique of civilization embedded in the narrative. The slight score reflects the unavoidable framing of human extinction as a scenario: the premise acknowledges that humanity faces an external threat, but frames this as a problem to solve rather than a punishment deserved.

tropeAudit.name: Progressive Agenda Imposed on Source Material
tropeAudit.explanation: The production team maintained strong fidelity to the source novel, with Andy Weir serving as executive producer. No reported insertions of progressive messaging absent from Weir's text. However, the film's institutional framing (international scientific cooperation, government mission authorization) carries a mild progressive undertone that is organic to the story but present. Lord and Miller did not inject this; it comes from Weir's source. Authenticity is Moderate because the framing is from the novel but exists in a modern context where institutional science carries political connotations. Score reflects the trace-level presence of institutional framing without explicit progressive agenda injection.

tropeAudit.name: Scientific Consensus as Progressive Signaling
tropeAudit.explanation: The film depicts real-world scientific institutions and international cooperation as positive forces. In the current environment this can read as progressive signaling. However, the film's scientific enthusiasm is apolitical in presentation: it celebrates the scientific method and individual problem-solving rather than institutional authority or government programs. Authenticity is High because this framing is organic to Weir's pro-science source material, not a political injection.

tropeAudit.name: Self-Sacrifice / Service to Humanity
tropeAudit.explanation: The defining moral act of the film. Ryland Grace erased his own memory to force himself onto a suicide mission. At the film's climax, he sacrifices his return to Earth to save Rocky and, through Rocky, Rocky's home world. This is not performed heroism or reluctant duty. It is deliberate, informed, costly sacrifice made by a character who understands exactly what he is giving up. The film's thesis is that some things are worth more than your own survival, and it earns that thesis by showing the full weight of the cost.

tropeAudit.name: Scientific Ingenuity / Human Problem-Solving
tropeAudit.explanation: The spine of the entire film. Every plot advancement is driven by a character identifying a problem, forming a hypothesis, testing it, and adapting based on results. Grace does not have superpowers. He has a biology background, a physics background, and enough chemistry to improvise. The film depicts scientific thinking as the most powerful tool humans possess for survival. This is not a lecture. It is a demonstration, and it is thrilling.

tropeAudit.name: Friendship Across Difference (Non-Ideological)
tropeAudit.explanation: Grace and Rocky are not allies because of shared politics or shared identity. They are allies because they share a problem and a method. Their friendship develops through competence, honesty, and mutual vulnerability. It is the most non-ideological example of cross-cultural friendship in a major 2026 release. The film does not pat itself on the back for depicting this friendship. It simply depicts it, which is how you know it is real.

tropeAudit.name: Optimism / Hope for Human Survival
tropeAudit.explanation: The film is constitutionally opposed to nihilism. Its entire narrative structure is a refusal of despair. Grace wakes up in the worst possible situation and immediately begins trying to fix it. The film never questions whether humans deserve to survive. The answer is yes, obviously, now solve the problem. This is increasingly rare in mainstream science fiction, which has spent a decade telling audiences that civilization is the problem rather than the solution.

tropeAudit.name: Duty / Heroism Without Ego
tropeAudit.explanation: Grace does not want credit. He does not want recognition. He originally refused the mission and had to be manipulated into accepting it. His heroism is not driven by ambition or ideology. It is driven by the simple recognition that he is the only person who can do what needs to be done. This is the classical heroic template: the reluctant servant who rises to the occasion not for glory but because there is no one else.

tropeAudit.name: Fidelity to Source Material (No Agenda Injection)
tropeAudit.explanation: Lord and Miller wrote the screenplay themselves with Andy Weir serving as executive producer. The result is an adaptation that protects the moral architecture of the source novel rather than retrofitting it with contemporary ideology. The book is apolitical and pro-human. The film is apolitical and pro-human. This is not an accident. It reflects a deliberate production choice to honor what made the source material beloved rather than use it as a delivery vehicle for unrelated messages.

The trailer, A24's own synopsis, and all promotional materials are transparent about the film's psychosexual female-female affair at the story's center. The queer identity of Hunter Schafer's character Hilda is not hidden. The absence of male characters from the core dynamic is visible from the first promotional images. Audiences know exactly what they are getting before they buy a ticket.

director.name: David Lowery
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT to LEFT. Lowery consistently gravitates toward art cinema that foregrounds interiority, queerness, and non-linear narrative. A Ghost Story, The Green Knight, and Peter Pan and Wendy all demonstrate a filmmaker interested in psychological and spiritual liminality. His choice of material here is unambiguous: a psychosexual thriller about two women whose estrangement is as erotic as it is emotional. Lowery is a thoughtful filmmaker who does not make ideological propaganda, but his sympathies are clear and they run left of center.
director.profile: David Lowery is an Austin-based filmmaker who established his reputation with Ain't Them Bodies Saints (2013) and cemented it with A Ghost Story (2017). He directed Pete's Dragon for Disney in 2016 and later returned to independent work with The Old Man and the Gun (2018) and The Green Knight (2021). His films are united by a preoccupation with time, grief, myth, and the afterlife of relationships. Mother Mary is his most commercially ambitious original screenplay. The film was shot in Germany starting May 2023, with music composed by Daniel Hart and original songs by Jack Antonoff, Charli XCX, and FKA Twigs. Lowery secured a SAG-AFTRA strike waiver to continue production. The project took over a year in post-production. Whatever it is, it is clearly a serious artistic vision.

writers.profile: Lowery wrote the original screenplay himself. It is described as a 'pop music epic' and a 'psychosexual affair' story. The premise follows pop star Mother Mary and fashion designer Sam Anselm, whose reunion on the eve of a comeback tour resurrects buried wounds. Lowery's scripts tend to be atmospheric, image-driven, and resistant to conventional three-act structure. Expect the narrative to work more like a dream than a plot.

lead_producer.name: Toby Halbrooks, James M. Johnston, David Lowery, Jonas Katzenstein

composer.name: Daniel Hart
composer.profile: Daniel Hart has scored every David Lowery film since A Ghost Story (2017) and won the Sundance Special Jury Prize for his work on that film. His scores are textural and ambient, built around longing and dread in equal measure. The original songs for Mother Mary were contributed by Jack Antonoff, Charli XCX, and FKA Twigs. Anne Hathaway performs all songs on the soundtrack album Mother Mary: Greatest Hits, released April 17, 2026 via A24 Music. The lead single 'Burial' was released in March 2026.

top_cast.name: Michaela Coel
top_cast.role: Sam Anselm (fashion designer, estranged best friend)

fidelityCasting.assessment: Mother Mary is an original screenplay by David Lowery. There is no source text, prior adaptation, or historical figure to evaluate fidelity against. The casting reflects Lowery's artistic choices for original characters. The all-female principal ensemble is intentional and organic to the story being told, not a recasting of established characters. No fidelity concerns apply.

parentalGuidance.guidance: This is a hard pass for families. Mother Mary is an A24 psychological thriller centered on a psychosexual female-female affair, directed by a filmmaker who specializes in psychological dread and spiritual ambiguity. The BBFC rated it 15. American audiences should expect an R rating. There is no family-friendly version of this story. Conservative adults who can handle dark psychological material and are willing to engage with a film whose worldview they may find challenging will find craft worth respecting. Anyone looking for entertainment that affirms traditional values will find precious little of it here.

summary.overall:
Let's be honest about what Mother Mary is before we pretend it's a mystery.

A24 has made a David Lowery psychological thriller about two women who used to be everything to each other, the long silence that followed, and what happens when the pop star calls the costume designer back into her orbit before a comeback show that might define or destroy her. Anne Hathaway plays Mary. Michaela Coel plays Sam. Their reunion is not warm. It is a reckoning. And the word 'psychosexual' in every press release is doing a lot of work.

I want to start with what is genuinely good here, because there is real craft. Lowery makes films that feel like memories you're not sure you had. A Ghost Story is one of the best films of the last decade. The Green Knight took Arthurian legend and turned it into something genuinely strange and philosophically serious. He does not make propaganda. He makes atmosphere. Mother Mary has two extraordinary lead performances. Hathaway sings her own songs on the soundtrack (composed with Jack Antonoff and Charli XCX, with original contributions from FKA Twigs), and if 'Burial' is any indication of the album's emotional temperature, the music is genuinely haunting. Cinematography by Andrew Droz Palermo and Rina Yang. Sound design and score by Daniel Hart. This is a technically accomplished film by people who know exactly what they're doing.

It's also a film where the entire principal cast is women, the central dynamic is a psychosexual affair between two of them, Hunter Schafer plays a queer artist whose identity is woven into the story, and there isn't a meaningful male presence anywhere in the narrative. That's not an accident. It's the movie.

Michaela Coel is extraordinary on screen. Her work in I May Destroy You showed what she can do with material about trauma and desire. She's the kind of performer who makes silence mean something. Hathaway is playing a character type she has circled for years now: the famous woman whose public persona is armor. She's good at it. The two of them together are the reason to see this film if you're going to see it at all.

Sian Clifford (Fleabag) appears as Jade. Jessica Brown Findlay as Tessa. Alba Baptista, Kaia Gerber, FKA Twigs in undisclosed roles that the production has been deliberately vague about. The casting is entirely female and deeply intentional. Lowery built a world that excludes men at the structural level. The story doesn't need them. That's a creative choice, not an oversight.

For conservative viewers: this film scores woke, and it scores woke honestly. The psychosexual affair, the queer characterization, the all-female world, the normalization of non-traditional relationships as the film's primary emotional terrain. These are not hidden. The marketing is transparent. A24 knows exactly who they made this for. The audiences who find Lowery's work compelling will go. The audiences who don't, won't. No one is being deceived.

There is a sliver of traditional content here. The friendship between Mary and Sam, whatever it has become, carries the weight of a genuine bond. Long buried wounds is not a progressive concept. Estrangement and the impossibility of going back is a theme that cuts across ideology. The film does not lack emotional truth. It lacks ideological alignment with traditional values, which is a different thing.

At 112 minutes with Lowery's deliberate pacing and A24's theatrical rollout (limited April 17, wide April 24), this will be a critical darling. Critics who love slow, psychologically dense filmmaking about women in extremis will adore it. Conservative audiences have no reason to seek it out unless they're interested in the craft.

Bottom line: it scores what it scores. Respect the craft if you can. Skip it if you can't.
summary.oneLiner: David Lowery's psychosexual pop thriller is gorgeous, deliberately queer, and emotionally uncompromising. It's also exactly what the marketing promises: not for traditional audiences.
summary.verdict: A well-made film whose woke content is upfront and unapologetic. The psychosexual female-female affair, queer characters, and male-free narrative are the movie's conscious design. Scores WOKE. No trap.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults who track A24's output should know this film is coming. Lowery is too good a filmmaker to dismiss, but Mother Mary is not a film that will reward viewers looking for traditional values. The craft is real. The ideology is also real. If you're interested in what prestige art cinema looks like in 2026, this is a data point. If you want entertainment that affirms your worldview, look elsewhere. The performance by Michaela Coel alone may be worth the price of admission for cinephiles who can separate craft from politics.
summary.parentalGuidance: Not rated (BBFC 15). Inappropriate for minors. Psychosexual content, psychological intensity, LGBTQ themes, strong language. Conservative families should skip entirely.

tropeAudit.name: Psychosexual Female-Female Affair as Central Narrative
tropeAudit.explanation: The entire film's plot engine is the psychosexual affair between pop star Mary (Anne Hathaway) and fashion designer Sam (Michaela Coel). A24's official synopsis describes their reunion as surfacing 'long-buried wounds.' IndieWire's coverage explicitly labels it a 'psychosexual affair.' This is not a subplot or a background element. It is the story. The relationship's romantic and sexual dimensions between two women are presented as the primary dramatic event of the film.

tropeAudit.name: Queer Character Central to Story (Hunter Schafer as Hilda)
tropeAudit.explanation: Hunter Schafer, a trans actress known for her role in Euphoria, plays Hilda, described as a queer artist. Schafer's real-world identity and the character's queer framing are clearly intentional casting. The character is not a background figure. Schafer received prominent billing in all publicity. Authenticity is scored High because Lowery made an active choice to write this character; her presence is organic to the film's thematic concerns about identity and desire, not an extraneous insertion.

tropeAudit.name: Male-Free Narrative / All-Female World
tropeAudit.explanation: The entire principal cast is female. There are no named male characters in any publicly available casting information. The story of Mary and Sam operates entirely within a world built by women, around women, for women. Authenticity is High because this is Lowery's deliberate creative vision, not a retrofit. He wrote an original screenplay and cast it accordingly.

tropeAudit.name: Pop Stardom as Female Self-Actualization / Comeback as Empowerment Arc
tropeAudit.explanation: The comeback narrative frames Mary's musical career as an expression of personal identity and female power. The comeback performance functions as a site of emotional reckoning, not just professional achievement. This is a familiar progressive pop culture trope: the famous woman who must reclaim her voice, her stage, and herself. It's present but not aggressive.

tropeAudit.name: Non-Traditional Relationship Structures Normalized
tropeAudit.explanation: The film normalizes a complex psychosexual dynamic between two women as the default emotional framework for the story. The relationship does not exist in opposition to a heterosexual norm; it simply is the norm within the film's world. There is no traditional romantic counterpart. The film treats this arrangement as emotionally complete and narratively sufficient.

tropeAudit.name: Female Friendship and Loyalty as Core Theme
tropeAudit.explanation: At the center of the film's emotional life, beneath the psychosexual intensity, is the history of a genuine friendship. Mary and Sam were estranged best friends before the plot begins. The film is, among other things, about what happens to a deep bond when ambition, desire, and time corrupt it. Female friendship as a site of grief and loyalty is a traditional value that predates and transcends progressive politics.

tropeAudit.name: Consequences of Ambition and Lost Relationships
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's central wound is an estrangement: Mary chose her career, and Sam was left behind. The comeback setting means Mary is now confronting what success cost her. This is a conservative-adjacent narrative: ambition has consequences, and those consequences are relational. The film does not celebrate Mary's choices; it examines their cost.

tropeAudit.name: Redemption Through Reconnection with the Past
tropeAudit.explanation: Mary's arc involves returning to an estranged relationship she abandoned. The premise requires her to confront what she buried. This is a traditional narrative structure: the past must be reckoned with, not discarded. Lowery's films consistently treat the past as something that haunts and demands acknowledgment, which is a fundamentally conservative view of time and moral consequence.

comparison_films.title: A Ghost Story (2017)
comparison_films.relationship: Same director. Lowery's signature slow, atmospheric grief-porn style. If you liked Ghost Story, you know what you're getting here.

comparison_films.title: Tar (2022)
comparison_films.relationship: Another prestige film about a powerful woman in the arts whose personal life collapses. Scored WOKE on VirtueVigil. Mother Mary has similar DNA.

comparison_films.title: May December (2023)
comparison_films.relationship: Todd Haynes' psychosexual drama about two women circling each other's damage. Same genre territory. Also scored WOKE.

title: Hoppers
author: Debra Ducane

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. Hoppers wears its environmental activism and anti-development messaging on its sleeve from the opening frames. Trailers showed Mabel as a self-described feral animal-rights activist battling a corrupt male mayor over her beloved glade. Critics discussed the eco-messaging in their first reviews. There is no deceptive packaging. The film is openly ideological and audiences knew what they were buying before they sat down.

director.name: Brian Fee
director.ideology: CENTER-LEFT. Fee is a Pixar veteran and co-writer of Cars 3. His environmental themes in Hoppers are genuine and organically expressed rather than bluntly didactic, but the progressive scaffolding is unmistakable: a female eco-activist heroine vs. a corrupt conservative-coded male politician using development as the villain's tool.
director.profile: Brian Fee joined Pixar in 2005 as a storyboard artist and worked on Cars, Ratatouille, WALL-E, and Up before stepping up to direct Cars 3 (2017). Hoppers is his second feature and his first original Pixar property. Fee has described the film as a deeply personal story about 'the places we love and the people who love us back,' drawn from childhood memories of a small creek behind his house that was paved over for a strip mall. The film's anti-development animus is autobiographical, not ideological on the surface, though the political framing (corrupt male politician vs. passionate young female activist) reflects contemporary progressive aesthetics.

writers.profile: Stephany Folsom is a screenwriter known for Thor: Ragnarok (story credit) and 1917 (uncredited polish). Her involvement brings some commercial sharpness to Fee's personal vision. The script is praised for balancing slapstick comedy with genuine emotional stakes, though critics note the villain is cartoonishly corrupt in ways that strain credulity.

composer.name: Bryce Dessner
composer.profile: Bryce Dessner is a guitarist and composer for The National who has scored several indie films. His score for Hoppers reportedly blends folk instruments with orchestral sweeps, giving the glade sequences an earthy, grounded warmth distinct from standard Pixar bombast.

top_cast.name: Piper Curda
top_cast.notes: Young actress known from I Didn't Do It (Disney Channel). Her voice performance is widely praised as carrying genuine warmth and wit beneath the activist-teen framing.

top_cast.name: Jon Hamm
top_cast.notes: Hamm clearly relishes playing the smarmy, self-serving mayor. The role is broadly written as a cartoon villain of development politics, but Hamm gives it enough comic texture to avoid pure caricature.

top_cast.name: Tom Hanks
top_cast.notes: Hanks as the warm, wise grandfather is the film's emotional anchor. His relationship with Mabel is the traditional core that elevates the film above pure eco-lecture.

fidelityCasting.assessment: Hoppers is an original Pixar property with no prior source material, so traditional fidelity casting analysis does not apply. The animated cast is a mix of established comedic voices. Diversity casting in the supporting cast (Wanda Sykes, Awkwafina) is appropriate for a modern Pixar ensemble and does not distort any pre-existing character. No casting concerns for VirtueVigil readers.
