parentalGuidance.guidance: Rated PG-13. Appropriate for ages 12 and up. The film's content is standard for the genre with one notable element: Black Adam is a character who kills people, and the film treats this leniently for a PG-13 superhero movie. The deaths are not graphic, but they are frequent. Parents of younger children who are accustomed to bloodless superhero action should preview for this. The ancient slavery flashback is brief but thematically heavy. The Sabbac villain involves demonic imagery that could disturb sensitive viewers. Overall appropriate for the teen audience it targets.

summary.overall:
Black Adam is a movie that has everything it needs to be a great comic book film and makes almost none of it work.

Dwayne Johnson as an ancient Egyptian champion wrongly imprisoned for five thousand years, released into a modern nation under criminal occupation, with no moral framework other than his own judgment and zero patience for due process? That is a genuinely interesting premise. A power fantasy about the kind of justice that does not wait for institutions. A character who represents the frustration of a people abandoned by legitimate authority. That premise should sing.

Instead it lumber along for 125 minutes, occasionally spectacular, mostly inert.

The film's most honest scene is early. Teth-Adam is released, immediately begins killing Intergang soldiers, and Adrianna Tomaz, who called him up from his tomb, watches in horror. She did not want a killer. She wanted a liberator. Adam does not understand the distinction. He was a champion of Kahndaq in an age when champions killed people who oppressed Kahndaq. The film is at its best when it sits with this dissonance.

The Justice Society arrives to stop him, and this is where the film should really begin: the argument between Hawkman's rule-of-law morality and Black Adam's results-based justice. That argument has weight. Aldis Hodge plays Hawkman with genuine conviction, and Johnson's Adam is, at his best, a man who has watched idealism fail so many times he no longer believes it is available to him. These two should be the film's spine.

Instead, the film pivots to a third-act villain (Sabbac, the demonic warlord) who is so generic he makes Hawkman's institutional concerns look like moral philosophy by comparison. The real antagonism drains away in favor of CGI escalation.

Pierce Brosnan's Doctor Fate is the film's saving grace. He is an old man who has seen too much of the future, and his acceptance of what is coming for him is the only characterization in the film that achieves genuine weight. His final scene is the only moment in the movie that lands as intended.

From a traditional values perspective, Black Adam is a better score than its reputation suggests. The film's liberation narrative is nationalist in the traditional sense: Kahndaq for the Khandaqis. There is no universal human rights framing, no progressive internationalism. Adam does not free Kahndaq because all people deserve freedom. He frees Kahndaq because it is his people and his land. The film treats this as a complete moral justification. That framing is closer to conservative nationalism than to left-wing anti-colonialism.

The masculine power fantasy is unapologetic. Adam is not asked to become more empathetic or emotionally intelligent. He is asked to apply his power correctly, not to reconsider whether power is appropriate at all. The film ultimately endorses his approach: the bad guys are stopped, Kahndaq is freed, and institutional authorities who tried to contain him are proved wrong. This is not a film about the limits of individual power.

The anti-colonialism scoring reflects the fact that Kahndaq's occupation by Intergang is framed with direct parallels to colonial occupation narratives. The US government's response (send the Justice Society to contain the local champion who is upsetting regional stability) maps onto historical patterns of imperial power managing local uprisings. The film draws this parallel intentionally, and it carries some woke freight even if Adam's solution is deeply traditional.

Bottom line: Black Adam is a frustrating film because it glimpses the movie it could have been in every third scene, then retreats to safety. Johnson's charisma and the Adam premise deserve better material. The DC franchise's decision not to pursue a sequel is comprehensible from a box office perspective, but the character still has potential that was never properly tapped.
summary.oneLiner: Dwayne Johnson's long-gestating DC antihero arrives with a great premise and wastes most of it. Nationalist liberation themes and unapologetic masculine power fantasy score traditional. Generic villain and tonal whiplash hold it back.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will find more in Black Adam than the mixed reviews suggested. The film's liberation narrative is nationalist rather than progressive - Adam fights for his people, not for universal principles, and the film treats this as sufficient moral justification. The masculine power fantasy is unqualified. Hawkman's rule-of-law morality is taken seriously as a counterpoint but ultimately loses to results-based justice. The US government (Amanda Waller) is the institutional villain trying to contain a legitimate champion of his people. That framing plays differently depending on your politics, but its bones are traditional. The film is a mess, but an ideologically interesting mess.
summary.parentalGuidance: PG-13. Appropriate for ages 12 and up. Frequent action violence including a protagonist who kills enemies. Demonic villain imagery in the third act. Brief ancient slavery flashback. No sexual content, no nudity, mild language. Standard PG-13 fare with slightly higher body count than typical superhero films.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Colonial / National Liberation Framing
tropeAudit.explanation: Kahndaq's occupation by Intergang is explicitly framed as foreign criminal exploitation of a historically oppressed people. The US government's response (contain the local champion) mirrors colonial power dynamics. This framing is intentional and draws from anti-colonial narrative traditions. The film mitigates this by making Adam's motivation personal nationalism rather than progressive universalism, but the structural parallel to anti-colonial storytelling is present.

tropeAudit.name: Female Catalyst / Lead Supporting Character
tropeAudit.explanation: Adrianna Tomaz is the character who releases Black Adam and drives the plot's early momentum. She is a capable archaeologist and resistor who functions as Adam's conscience. Her role is significant though not dominant. The film does not challenge her competence or reduce her to a passive object.

tropeAudit.name: Institutional / US Government as Obstacle to Justice
tropeAudit.explanation: Amanda Waller dispatches the Justice Society to contain Black Adam because his existence is a geopolitical destabilizer. The film positions this institutional intervention as wrong-headed. The US government is not the villain, but it is consistently the obstacle. This framing has both conservative (anti-deep state) and progressive (anti-imperialist) readings.

tropeAudit.name: Diverse Ensemble Cast
tropeAudit.explanation: The Justice Society includes Cyclone (Quintessa Swindell, Black) and Atom Smasher (Noah Centineo, white), while the Kahndaq characters are played by actors of Middle Eastern descent. The casting is diverse in the contemporary studio sense. The identities of the characters are not thematically emphasized.

tropeAudit.name: Masculine Power Fantasy (Unqualified)
tropeAudit.explanation: Black Adam is a film built entirely around the premise that a man of sufficient power, acting on his own judgment, can impose justice on a world that institutional authority has failed. Adam does not become more empathetic or emotionally evolved. He is not asked to reconsider his methods. He is right, and his rightness is validated by results. This is one of the most unapologetically traditional masculine power fantasies in recent superhero cinema.

tropeAudit.name: Justice Outside Institutional Law
tropeAudit.explanation: Adam's entire moral framework is that legitimate institutions (the Wizard Council that imprisoned him, the US government that wants to contain him, the Justice Society that wants to police him) have failed Kahndaq. His extrajudicial violence is the film's hero action. The film endorses this approach: the people who tried to work within the system were wrong, and Adam was right. This is conservative vigilante justice in the Dirty Harry tradition.

tropeAudit.name: Protector / Champion Archetype
tropeAudit.explanation: Adam's identity as champion of Kahndaq is rooted in an ancient covenant with the Council of Wizards and his bond to the people he was chosen to protect. The film treats this as a sacred responsibility rather than a political position. His attachment to Amon (Adrianna's son) and willingness to die for a people not his own by blood reflects the traditional archetype of the warrior-protector whose role is defined by service, not ideology.

tropeAudit.name: Nationalist Pride / Sovereignty of a People
tropeAudit.explanation: Kahndaq's liberation is framed as the restoration of a people's rightful control over their own land and destiny. This is nationalist sovereignty language rather than progressive universalism. Adam does not fight for 'all oppressed peoples everywhere.' He fights for Kahndaq, and the film presents this as a complete and sufficient justification for his actions.

tropeAudit.name: Divine Authority / Ancient Sacred Covenant
tropeAudit.explanation: Adam's power derives from a Council of Wizards who granted it in service of divine justice. The film connects his power to a sacred covenant that predates human institutions. Doctor Fate's arc involves accepting a foreordained divine plan for his own death. This religious-adjacent framing treats divine will and sacred duty as real forces that supersede human authority.

title: Babylon
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Babylon is not a woke trap. The film's hedonism, excess, drug use, sexual content, and moral chaos are visible from the opening sequence of the premiere party with its orgy, cocaine, and bodily fluids. Nothing is hidden. The progressive character elements (Lady Fay Zhu as an openly gay woman, Sidney Palmer's blackface subplot) are present throughout. The film does not masquerade as a traditional values piece. Its TRADITIONAL LEAN score comes from its honest portrayal of excess and destruction: every character who surrenders to the decadence of 1920s Hollywood loses everything. Damien Chazelle is making a film about the cost of living outside moral structure, and the wages-of-sin pattern runs through the entire narrative arc even if Chazelle would not use that language.

director.name: Damien Chazelle
director.ideology: Moderate/Liberal. Chazelle is an apolitical filmmaker by public profile. His ideology expresses through craft obsession and themes of ambition, excellence, and the price of artistic pursuit rather than social commentary.
director.profile: Damien Chazelle is the director of Whiplash (2014), La La Land (2016), First Man (2018), and Babylon (2022). He became the youngest Best Director winner in Oscar history at age 32 for La La Land. Chazelle's films consistently examine the cost of obsessive excellence and the people sacrificed on the altar of ambition. Babylon is his most unrestrained work: a 189-minute period epic that appears to celebrate Hollywood's first golden age while systematically dismantling every character who reaches too high. His influences include Scorsese, Altman, Fellini, and the French New Wave. He is not a political filmmaker in any conventional sense, and Babylon does not function as a politically motivated film. It functions as a moral epic dressed in debauchery.

writer.name: Damien Chazelle
writer.profile: Chazelle wrote and directed Babylon solo. The screenplay was developed over several years and represents his most ambitious structural undertaking: an ensemble portrait of five characters across a decade, built around the Hollywood transition from silent films to sound. His research drew on the documented history of the era, including the real scandals, casting practices, and industry machinery of 1920s-1930s Hollywood. Critics noted some historical liberties. The script's most debated element is its maximalist structure: at 189 minutes, it runs longer than the patience of many viewers who came expecting the elegance of La La Land.

composer.name: Justin Hurwitz
composer.profile: Justin Hurwitz has scored every Chazelle film. His Babylon score is genuinely extraordinary: a propulsive, jazz-drenched, anachronistic mix that drives the party sequences like a locomotive and then drops into melancholy for the film's quieter moments. The score won the Golden Globe for Best Original Score and received an Oscar nomination. It may be the film's single greatest artistic achievement and arguably the best film score of 2022.

top_cast.name: Margot Robbie
top_cast.notes: Robbie gives the performance of her career as Nellie LaRoy, the self-proclaimed star from New Jersey who burns her way through Hollywood like a lit fuse. Nellie is pure id: magnetic, reckless, hilarious, heartbreaking. She dominates every room she walks into and destroys every stable thing around her. Robbie commits completely, going from manic comedy to raw vulnerability in single shots. The scene where she fights a rattlesnake at a party, drunk and giggling, is both absurd and genuinely frightening. This is the role that should have made her an Oscar winner.

top_cast.name: Brad Pitt
top_cast.notes: Pitt plays a fading silent film star with the particular melancholy of a man who knows exactly what he is losing and cannot stop it. His Jack Conrad is generous, romantic, and fundamentally decent in a film full of selfish people. He marries and divorces multiple times. He is honest with himself when few others in the film are. His final scene, attending a screening of Singin' in the Rain alone and weeping because he has been immortalized in a culture that discarded him, is one of the most quietly devastating sequences in recent Hollywood filmmaking.

top_cast.name: Diego Calva
top_cast.notes: Calva is the film's moral center and its most underrated element. Manny is the witness through whom we observe Babylon's excess: a Mexican immigrant who climbs from elephant handler to studio executive through talent, work ethic, and love for cinema itself. His loyalty to Nellie LaRoy, long after she has given him every reason to walk away, is the film's most sustained traditional value. Calva's restraint against Robbie's explosion and Pitt's charisma is an act of disciplined craft that the film requires.

top_cast.name: Jean Smart
top_cast.notes: Smart plays the gossip columnist with the mordant wit the role demands. Her scene with Jack Conrad, telling him his star has faded but he will be immortalized, contains more honest emotion than most of Babylon's louder sequences. Smart has the film's wisest line: that cinema matters not because of what any individual makes, but because of what the medium preserves.

top_cast.name: Jovan Adepo
top_cast.notes: Adepo plays a jazz trumpeter whose talent and integrity collide with Hollywood's racism. The blackface sequence, where studio executives demand he darken his comparatively light skin to satisfy Southern audiences who object to interracial orchestras, is the film's most politically explicit moment and its most historically honest. Sidney's departure from Hollywood is handled with dignity rather than as a political lecture.

fidelity_casting.summary: Original screenplay. Characters are loosely inspired by real Hollywood figures of the era. Jack Conrad draws from several silent era stars. Nellie LaRoy is a composite of era starlets. No direct adaptations requiring fidelity assessment.

content_warnings: Extended party sequence featuring explicit sexual content, nudity, cocaine use, and graphic bodily functions (opening 20 minutes)
Drug use throughout: cocaine is treated casually, extensively, and consequences are shown
Extreme violence: a zoosadism underground party sequence depicting genuine cruelty
A man is nearly executed (gunshot violence)
Suicide of a supporting character (implied off-screen)

A character is bitten by a rattlesnake; another character sucks out the venom (depicted graphically)

parental_guidance.recommendation: Not appropriate for anyone under 18. Babylon earns its R rating repeatedly and enthusiastically. The opening party sequence is one of the most graphically debaucherous in mainstream studio filmmaking in years: explicit sex acts, cocaine being consumed openly, nudity, and a scene involving an elephant that cannot be described here. The film maintains this intensity intermittently for its entire 189 minutes. This is not a film for families. Conservative viewers who want to see a serious cinematic statement about the cost of excess and the enduring power of art will find it in Babylon, but they will earn that finding the hard way. Consider yourself warned.

summary.overall:
Damien Chazelle wanted to make a film about the magic of movies. He made it by putting that magic through a meat grinder for three hours and nine minutes to see if anything noble survived the processing.

Babylon is a spectacular, exhausting, infuriating, genuinely moving piece of cinema that opens with an elephant defecating on a man's head and closes with Manny Torres weeping alone in a 1952 movie theater while Singin' in the Rain plays on screen. The distance between those two images is not ironic. It is Chazelle's entire argument: Hollywood is a machine of extraordinary vulgarity in the service of something that approaches the sacred, and the people destroyed in the making of it are part of the cost.

The film is set during Hollywood's transition from silent films to sound, roughly 1926 to 1932. This is historically the period of the Hays Code: the industry voluntarily imposing moral censorship on itself after years of increasingly scandalous content and off-screen behavior. Chazelle sets his film in the years before that reckoning, when Hollywood was genuinely Babylon: a city of limitless money, zero moral framework, and a concentrated density of human ambition that burned through people the way the era burned through film stock.

He follows five characters through this transition:

Manny Torres (Diego Calva), a Mexican immigrant who starts handling logistics at parties and ends up as a studio executive through talent, hard work, and a love for cinema that never dims.

Nellie LaRoy (Margot Robbie), a self-declared star from New Jersey who has genuine talent but no capacity for self-preservation, whose addiction to excess and chaos consumes everything she builds.

Jack Conrad (Brad Pitt), a silent film star of genuine stature whose voice and persona do not translate to sound films, who watches his career dissolve with the grace of a man who understands what he was and refuses to be less.

Sidney Palmer (Jovan Adepo), an African-American jazz trumpeter whose talent earns him entry to Hollywood but whose integrity costs him a place in it.

Lady Fay Zhu (Li Jun Li), a Chinese-American gay cabaret singer who thrives in Babylon's chaos and is then quietly discarded when the studios clean house.

The film opens in 1926 at a party that must be seen to be described. It is the defining party of the silent era: unlimited cocaine, open sex, jazz, nudity, and an elephant being transported through the proceedings for reasons the film never feels the need to explain. This is where Manny, Nellie, Sidney, and Fay all exist simultaneously, in proximity to Jack Conrad. A young actress overdoses. Manny quietly manages the situation. Nellie dances until she is noticed. An era is introduced.

From there the film tracks each character's arc through the transition period. Nellie becomes a star on raw magnetism, then finds that sound films require discipline she does not possess. Manny rises through competence and genuine love for the medium, eventually becoming a studio executive and pitching Sidney's orchestra for lead billing. Jack makes increasingly low-budget films, marries multiple times, and is eventually informed by gossip columnist Elinor St. John that his star has faded, though he will be remembered forever on film. Sidney is asked to wear blackface by studio executives for a Southern market film and walks out of the industry. Fay is fired from Kinoscope when her lesbianism becomes a liability. The Hays Code tightens. The party ends.

The film's second-half turns brutal. Nellie, destroyed by addiction and debt, borrows money from gangster James McKay, loses it gambling, and ends up in a chase through underground Los Angeles involving counterfeit money, literal snakebite, and a sadistic underground party that the film depicts in genuinely disturbing detail. She vanishes from the story. Manny finds her years later, alone and broken, and she says goodbye.

Jack Conrad commits suicide. Manny leaves Los Angeles.

Years later, Manny returns to a cinema playing Singin' in the Rain (1952). He watches it in isolation: a film that romanticizes the exact era he lived through, scrubbed clean of the Babylon he knew, immortalizing the people he knew, making beautiful what was ugly. He weeps. The film then cuts through a century of cinema in a montage sequence that is either Chazelle's most ambitious moment or his most self-indulgent, depending on your tolerance.

The argument is: all of this carnage, all these destroyed lives, this river of debauchery and exploitation and racism and addiction, produced something that endures. Cinema remains. The people it burned through do not.

This is a complicated scoring case. Babylon contains genuinely progressive elements alongside what amounts to one of the more sustained cinematic arguments for the wages-of-sin structure in recent Hollywood output. We score what is on screen.

A note on scoring the hedonism trope: we rate it as Moderate authenticity because the film does not straightforwardly endorse what it depicts. The opening party and Nellie's arc are presented as spectacle, but Nellie is destroyed by it. The question is whether the film's aestheticization of excess functions as endorsement or warning. We score it as Moderate rather than Low because the film does aestheticize this material lavishly enough that the warning is not unambiguous, particularly in the first act.

Woke Trap Assessment

Babylon is not a woke trap. Its content is visible from the opening sequence. Conservative families who attend expecting the elegance of La La Land will discover the true nature of this film within the first fifteen minutes. Nothing is hidden. The progressive character elements, Sidney's racism storyline, Fay's lesbianism, are present and consistent throughout. The film's traditional values score comes from structural consequences, not masked ideology.

Creative Team at a Glance

Damien Chazelle is, by ideological profile, the least political major filmmaker of his generation. His films are obsessively about craft, ambition, and the price of excellence. Whiplash (2014) asked whether artistic excellence justifies cruelty. La La Land (2016) asked whether romantic love and artistic ambition can coexist. First Man (2018) asked what kind of man walks on the moon. Babylon asks what it costs to make something that outlives you.

His political statements are minimal and his film decisions track artistic ambition rather than ideology. Babylon is his only film that engages directly with race, and it does so through the lens of documented historical practice (blackface being demanded of Black performers for Southern markets was a real industry practice) rather than contemporary identity politics.

Justin Hurwitz, whose score is this film's most undeniable achievement, is a non-political collaborator whose craft anchors every Chazelle film. His Babylon score is the best argument for the film's greatness: propulsive, anachronistic, ecstatic, and finally heartbreaking.

Adult Viewer Insight: The Case For and Against Babylon

The case for Babylon is Margot Robbie, Brad Pitt at his most vulnerable, Diego Calva at his most disciplined, Justin Hurwitz's extraordinary score, and one of the most honest arguments about the relationship between art and destruction that mainstream Hollywood has made in decades. The wages-of-sin structure is real and consistent: every character who loses themselves in the excess of the era is consumed by it. Jack Conrad survives longer than most because he retains his dignity, but he too is ultimately discarded. The film argues, without ambiguity, that the Babylon of 1920s Hollywood was not a paradise but a machine that converted human lives into entertainment, and that the entertainment that survived is genuinely worth something despite the cost.

The case against Babylon is three hours and nine minutes. Chazelle loses control of his material repeatedly. The underground sadism party sequence, which involves a gangster dragging Manny and a drug dealer through a series of depravity tableaux for extended minutes, does not advance the story and exists apparently because Chazelle wanted to establish how far beneath the glamour Hollywood's underground ran. He is not wrong about this historically, but the sequence is unpleasant in a way that serves shock more than argument. The film's final montage, which cuts through cinema history to land on the implication that all movies are spiritually connected to the Babylon that made them, is either Chazelle's most ambitious gesture or a case of a director who has been making films about movies for so long that he has lost perspective on what movies are for.

For conservative viewers: Babylon is not the enemy. It is not a progressive polemic or an ideological film. It is a large, complicated, morally serious piece of filmmaking that contains content many conservative families will find deeply offensive and should not watch. The viewers who will value it most are adults with high tolerance for graphic content and genuine interest in what the film is actually arguing, which is that excess destroys, craft endures, and the cost of art is paid in people.

Verdict: TRADITIONAL LEAN. The wages-of-sin structure is present and consistent, and the film's best moments argue for the enduring value of craft, devotion, and dignified failure over dissolution. The graphic content is not endorsed but aestheticized, which is a meaningful distinction. Adults who engage with this film critically will find more traditional value in it than its reputation suggests.
summary.adultInsight: Babylon is Damien Chazelle's most ambitious and least controlled film. At 189 minutes it chronicles five characters through Hollywood's silent-to-sound transition, built around a wages-of-sin structure: every character who fully surrenders to the era's debauchery is destroyed, while the film's moral center, Mexican immigrant Manny Torres, survives through work, loyalty, and love for cinema itself. The hedonism is aestheticized but not endorsed. Margot Robbie's Nellie LaRoy is a career-best performance. Brad Pitt's Jack Conrad is quietly extraordinary. Justin Hurwitz's score may be the best of the decade so far. The film contains genuinely disturbing content (an underground sadism party sequence, graphic drug use, explicit sexuality throughout) that earns its R rating repeatedly. It is not a progressive polemic. The blackface and lesbianism subplots are historically grounded rather than ideologically weaponized. The film's thesis is pre-moral: Hollywood was Babylon, it destroyed people, and what it built has outlasted everyone it destroyed. Conservative viewers who can tolerate the content will find a film that takes seriously the question of what excellence costs and whether the cost is worth paying.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R. For adults only. The opening party sequence alone is disqualifying for anyone under 18: graphic sex, nudity, cocaine, and a scene involving bodily fluids that is neither brief nor implied. The film maintains this intensity throughout its 189-minute runtime at irregular intervals. Drug addiction is shown with consequences but also glamorized in its early stages. An underground sequence depicting animal cruelty and sadism is genuinely disturbing. Strong language throughout. LGBT content is present and not incidental. This is a serious film for serious adult viewers with high tolerance for graphic content. It is not appropriate for families or younger viewers under any circumstances.

tropeAudit.name: Aestheticized Hedonism
tropeAudit.explanation: The film opens with twenty minutes of the most graphically depicted debauchery in a major studio release in years. The party is filmed with genuine visual artistry: Chazelle and cinematographer Linus Sandgren shoot the chaos as spectacle, not horror. The authenticity is scored Moderate because the film's consequences do discipline the excess: every character who surrenders to it is destroyed. But the aestheticization is real and sustained enough to resist a Low authenticity score. Chazelle is not endorsing the party, but he is making it beautiful.

tropeAudit.name: Racial Discrimination / Historical Injustice
tropeAudit.explanation: Sidney Palmer's arc centers on the documented historical practice of studios requiring light-skinned Black performers to darken their complexions for Southern market films. Fay Zhu is fired because her lesbianism threatens studio relationships. Both subplots are historically grounded in real industry practice rather than invented for contemporary political relevance, which raises their authenticity score. The film handles both with relative restraint, letting the events speak without editorial lecturing.

tropeAudit.name: LGBT Representation
tropeAudit.explanation: Lady Fay Zhu is an openly gay character from her first appearance. She and Nellie share a passionate kiss. Fay's sexual identity is treated matter-of-factly by the film rather than as a special event, which mirrors the documented history of Hollywood's pre-Hays Code period when such relationships existed with relative openness before the censors arrived. The historical framing is authentic. The representation is present and not incidental.

tropeAudit.name: Moral Relativism / Consequence-Free Decline
tropeAudit.explanation: While the wages-of-sin structure does operate in Babylon, the film does not offer clear moral framing for why the characters who fall, fall. Nellie's destruction is presented as tragedy without moral verdict. Jack's suicide is elegiac rather than cautionary. The film mourns its characters without judging them, which is in tension with a straightforward traditional values reading. We score moral relativism as Moderate authenticity because the consequences are real even if the moral accounting is soft.

tropeAudit.name: Wages of Sin / Excess Destroys
tropeAudit.explanation: This is the film's structural spine. Every character who fully surrenders to the excess of 1920s Hollywood is consumed by it. Nellie LaRoy, whose talent was real and whose potential was genuine, dies alone after years of addiction and self-destruction. The underground sadism sequence makes explicit what the excess ultimately leads to: a descent through layers of depravity to something irredeemably dark. The Hays Code arrival is presented not as puritanical censorship but as an industry reckoning with what it had become. Authenticity scored Moderate because the film aestheticizes the destruction as much as it condemns it.

tropeAudit.name: Loyal Devotion Despite Desertion
tropeAudit.explanation: Manny Torres's sustained love and loyalty for Nellie LaRoy across years of her self-destruction and his own advancement is the film's most straightforwardly traditional element. He helps her when she has given him every reason not to. He finds her years after Hollywood has forgotten her and says a final goodbye. This is devotion without expectation of return, a classical virtue operating consistently in a morally chaotic environment.

tropeAudit.name: Art Endures / The Immortality of Craft
tropeAudit.explanation: Elinor St. John tells Jack Conrad that his star is fading but he will be immortalized on film. The closing sequence of Manny watching Singin' in the Rain confirms this: the people destroyed by Hollywood's machine are preserved in what that machine made. The film presents art as a legitimate transcendent value, something that outlasts the lives consumed in its making. This is a traditional argument about the relationship between craft, sacrifice, and permanence.

tropeAudit.name: American Immigrant Work Ethic
tropeAudit.explanation: Manny Torres is explicitly the son of impoverished Mexican refugees who rises through talent, competence, and willingness to work. His arc is a legitimate American Dream narrative: starting as an elephant handler at a party and ending as a studio executive through earned advancement rather than connection or luck. The film does not undercut this with irony. Manny's success is presented as deserved.

tropeAudit.name: Dignity in Obsolescence
tropeAudit.explanation: Jack Conrad faces the loss of his career with more grace than most men in a similar position. He does not rage, does not descend into bitterness, does not blame others. He marries too many times and drinks too much, but his fundamental decency persists. His suicide is a failure, but it is the failure of a man who could not adapt, not a man who chose dissolution. The film treats his decline as tragedy rather than as evidence of moral deficiency.

tropeAudit.name: Craft as Moral Anchor
tropeAudit.explanation: The characters who retain their integrity longest are those who remain committed to their craft: Manny's dedication to making good films even as the industry deteriorates, Jack's professionalism even in B-pictures, Sidney's refusal to compromise his musical integrity for the Southern market. The film consistently presents craft commitment as a form of moral seriousness even in an environment without explicit moral structure.

title: Amsterdam
author: VirtueVigil Editorial Team

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: Margin is negative but content is not hidden. Amsterdam's anti-fascist political premise is front and center from the opening frames. The film is based on the real 1933 Business Plot and its opposition to American fascism is the stated subject. Conservative viewers will know exactly what they are watching within the first act. No trap.

director.name: David O. Russell
director.ideology: LEFT-LEANING. Russell is an Academy Award nominated filmmaker (American Hustle, Silver Linings Playbook, The Fighter) with a long track record of humanist, character-driven films. Amsterdam is his most explicitly political film and his most troubled production. His personal history is complicated by harassment allegations from multiple collaborators, a fact the film's critics noted with some irony given its anti-fascist, pro-decency themes.
director.profile: David O. Russell is one of the most decorated American directors of the 21st century, with six Academy Award nominations across his career. Amsterdam represents a significant departure from his signature style: where The Fighter and Silver Linings Playbook were intimate character studies, Amsterdam is an ambitious political satire with a cast of nearly twenty notable performers and a plot drawn from real historical events. The result is, by critical consensus, a failure of execution rather than ambition. Russell's instinct to stuff every frame with incident and every scene with overlapping dialogue overwhelms the story. The film grossed $31M against an $80M budget, making it one of the largest box-office bombs of 2022. Russell has not directed another film since.

writer.name: David O. Russell
writer.profile: Russell wrote the original screenplay. The story is loosely based on the real Business Plot of 1933, in which a group of wealthy American industrialists allegedly approached retired Marine General Smedley Butler and asked him to lead a coup against FDR and install a fascist government. Butler reported the plot to Congress. The film takes this kernel and builds an ensemble mystery-comedy around it. The screenplay's ambitions exceed its execution: there are too many characters, too many tonal registers, and too many subplots for any one of them to land with full force.

lead_producer.name: Arnon Milchan, Matthew Budman, Anthony Katagas, David O. Russell, Christian Bale

composer.name: Daniel Pemberton
composer.profile: British film composer with a strong track record in period films (Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, All the Money in the World, King Arthur: Legend of the Sword). His Amsterdam score is appropriately jazzy and propulsive for the 1930s New York setting, one of the film's few consistent pleasures.

top_cast.name: Christian Bale
top_cast.notes: A character actor disguised as a movie star, and Amsterdam asks him to do both simultaneously. Burt is a WWI veteran doctor with a glass eye and a complicated marriage who is dragged into a conspiracy he barely understands. Bale brings his usual total commitment. Unfortunately the script does not give him enough room to build the character we need.

top_cast.name: John David Washington
top_cast.notes: Harold is the film's most quietly compelling character: a Black lawyer in 1930s New York who navigates racism with pragmatic dignity. Washington underplays effectively but the script repeatedly sidelines him to make room for the ensemble.

top_cast.name: Margot Robbie
top_cast.notes: Robbie is charming in a role that does not give her much to do. Valerie functions primarily as the mystery the two men are trying to solve. She is a nurse, a free spirit, and an heiress, and none of those identities quite cohere.

top_cast.name: Robert De Niro
top_cast.notes: Loosely based on General Smedley Butler, the real-life Marine who blew the whistle on the actual Business Plot. De Niro plays him with gruff authority. His climactic speech about decency and democracy is the film's best scene.

top_cast.name: Rami Malek and Anya Taylor-Joy
top_cast.notes: Malek and Taylor-Joy play the film's primary villains with a gleeful eccentricity that briefly elevates the movie every time they appear. They are clearly having the most fun on set.

fidelityCasting.assessment: Amsterdam is a fictional story inspired by the real Business Plot of 1933. The characters are invented, not adaptations of historical figures, with the partial exception of General Dillenbeck (based on Smedley Butler). The interracial friendship between Burt and Harold and the central mystery plot are original creations. There is no casting fidelity concern for the fictional characters. The decision to cast John David Washington as Harold adds a racial dimension to the 1930s setting that the script uses to address Jim Crow realities; this is a creative choice rather than an adaptation issue.

parentalGuidance.mpaaDescriptors: Brief violence and bloody images, and some sexuality
contentWarnings: Brief wartime violence and battlefield injury imagery
A dead body is featured prominently in early scenes

parentalGuidance.parentalNotes: Amsterdam is rated R but its content is relatively mild for the rating. The primary concern for conservative families is the film's overt anti-fascist political messaging and its depictions of 1930s racial discrimination. Older teens may find the historical thriller elements engaging. The film is dense with plot and character and may lose younger viewers.

summary.overall:
Amsterdam is a film about friendship, decency, and the courage it takes to defend democracy against people with money and no conscience. It is also, unfortunately, a mess.

David O. Russell assembled one of the most impressive casts of 2022. Christian Bale, Margot Robbie, John David Washington, Robert De Niro, Rami Malek, Anya Taylor-Joy, Taylor Swift, Chris Rock, Michael Shannon, Timothy Olyphant, Zoe Saldana, Mike Myers. He gave them a story based on a real 1933 conspiracy in which American industrialists allegedly tried to recruit a retired general to lead a fascist coup against FDR. The premise is genuinely fascinating. The execution is not.

The film opens in Amsterdam itself, with three young people (Burt, Harold, and Valerie) recovering from WWI wounds and living freely and happily in an interwar European city. Their friendship is warm and specific, and the Amsterdam sections are the film at its best. Then we cut to 1933 New York, a murder mystery, a conspiracy, and approximately fifteen subplots introduced over two hours that never quite snap together.

Russell's signature style, the overlapping dialogue, the manic energy, the refusal to let a scene breathe, works brilliantly in claustrophobic settings (The Fighter's family scenes, Silver Linings Playbook's dinner table fights). It does not work in an ensemble mystery-thriller where you need the audience to track plot logic. By the midpoint, I lost confidence that the film was going to pull its threads together. It does not, quite.

There is real content here for conservative viewers to engage with, though not in the way Russell likely intended. The film's patriotism is genuine. General Dillenbeck's speech about the nature of decency and the duty to report evil rather than accommodate it is one of the better pieces of writing in any 2022 film. The friendship between Burt and Harold, a white doctor and a Black lawyer in 1930s New York, is built on loyalty and mutual respect rather than progressive performance. These men are friends because they saved each other's lives in a French trench. That kind of bond transcends the cultural politics of any given moment.

But Amsterdam is also explicitly anti-fascist in a way that carries contemporary resonance. Russell is clearly making a film about more than 1933. The industrialists who want to install a puppet dictator are not subtle allegories. The film wants you to draw the line to the present. That is a choice, and it is a left-leaning one.

The bottom line: Amsterdam is a box-office bomb for reasons that have nothing to do with its politics. It is structurally undisciplined, tonally inconsistent, and overloaded with characters. The friendships at its core are worth saving from the wreckage. The political messaging is clear and center-left. The score lands exactly where the math puts it: MIXED.
summary.oneLiner: A fascinating premise about real 1933 fascist conspirators, undermined by David O. Russell's inability to focus. The friendship at its core is genuinely moving. The politics are clearly left-leaning. Worth watching for the cast alone.
summary.verdict: Amsterdam has the bones of a great film buried under too many characters and too much plot. Its anti-fascist messaging is explicit but its celebration of male loyalty, patriotism, and moral courage pulls in the opposite direction. The scores reflect the genuine split.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults should approach Amsterdam with calibrated expectations. The film is flawed but not contemptible. Its celebration of the three-way friendship between Burt, Harold, and Valerie is built on loyalty, sacrifice, and shared suffering, values that transcend the film's political framing. Robert De Niro's scene as General Dillenbeck describing why decent people must not look away from evil is worth the price of admission. The anti-fascist messaging is real and intentional. But unlike films that smuggle ideology into entertainment, Amsterdam announces its politics openly, which at least respects the audience.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated R. Suitable for adults and older teens. Historical thriller content, brief violence, 1930s racial discrimination depicted. The political messaging is anti-fascist and moderately left-leaning.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Fascist / Anti-Nationalist Political Messaging
tropeAudit.explanation: Amsterdam is explicitly and unapologetically anti-fascist. The Business Plot provides historical cover, but Russell is clearly making a film about contemporary resonance. The industrialist villains who want to install a puppet leader resonate beyond 1933. The film's opening and closing narration make the contemporary application explicit. This is the film's political spine, not a subtheme.

tropeAudit.name: Interracial Friendship as Moral Center / 1930s Race Politics
tropeAudit.explanation: The friendship between Burt (white) and Harold (Black) in 1930s America is depicted with warmth and specificity. Harold's daily navigation of Jim Crow humiliation is shown without excessive dramatization. The film is not primarily about race, but it does not pretend racial inequality did not exist. Harold is the most dignified character in the film. The casting of John David Washington in the role adds additional contemporary resonance.

tropeAudit.name: Anti-Corporate / Anti-Industrial Power Structure
tropeAudit.explanation: The villains are explicitly wealthy industrialists who view democracy as an obstacle to profit. The film depicts a cabal of businessmen willing to overthrow the American government for economic advantage. This is historically based (the real Business Plot), but Russell frames it with obvious contemporary intent. The critique of concentrated corporate power is sustained and intentional.

tropeAudit.name: Eugenics / Forced Sterilization Depicted as Elite Villainy
tropeAudit.explanation: The conspiracy includes a forced sterilization clinic operated by the cabal. This is historically accurate (the eugenics movement was active and influential in 1930s America) but the film uses it to paint the villains in maximally sinister terms. The connection between fascism, corporate power, and eugenics is made explicit.

tropeAudit.name: Patriotism / Defending American Democracy
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's central act is an American general choosing to defend the Republic against a coup attempt by powerful men who believe themselves above the law. Dillenbeck's speech about what America is and what it owes its citizens is genuinely moving patriotism, not the performative kind. The film treats democratic institutions as worth protecting and its heroes as people willing to risk their lives to protect them.

tropeAudit.name: Veterans / Military Brotherhood
tropeAudit.explanation: The film's entire moral architecture is built on the WWI bond between Burt and Harold. They are brothers because they bled together in France. That bond is treated as sacred and real, not as a progressive multicultural statement. The film respects military service without glorifying war. Burt's medical practice treating veterans is depicted with quiet reverence.

tropeAudit.name: Male Loyalty and Moral Courage
tropeAudit.explanation: The two male leads demonstrate the kind of loyalty that the film treats as morally foundational. Harold stays at Burt's side despite every rational reason to walk away. Burt risks everything to help a woman he barely knows because Harold asks him to. Dillenbeck refuses a bribe and delivers the truth. Male loyalty, kept promises, and physical courage in service of something larger are all treated as unambiguous virtues.

detailed_analysis:
Amsterdam represents a test case for VirtueVigil's methodology. A film can be explicitly anti-fascist, feature a left-leaning director making a clear contemporary political statement, and still score MIXED when its trad elements are genuinely strong.

The WWI brotherhood of Burt and Harold is the real heart of the film. Their friendship is not a diversity exercise. It is built on shared suffering, kept promises, and years of working alongside each other. The film understands that this kind of bond is worth more than ideology.

Russell is a flawed filmmaker making an ambitious film that does not quite work. His contempt for fascism is clear. His admiration for ordinary decency is also clear. Both are present in equal measure, and the MIXED verdict reflects that accurately.

The box-office failure has nothing to do with politics. It failed because it is structurally chaotic and too long. The Friends of Amsterdam deserve a better film than they got.

title: Tron: Ares
author: Debra Ducane
studio: Walt Disney Pictures / Sean Bailey Productions

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP in the technical sense. The progressive elements in Tron: Ares are visible from the first trailer. The casting choices, the female CEO protagonist, the racially diverse ensemble, the AI liberation narrative framing: none of this is hidden. Conservative viewers will recognize what they are watching within the first act. The film is not a bait-and-switch. It is straightforwardly a Disney sci-fi franchise entry built to current Disney casting specifications. The ideological content is baked in and visible upfront.

director.name: Joachim Ronning
director.ideology: MAINSTREAM LIBERAL / CORPORATE STUDIO CRAFTSMAN. Ronning is a Norwegian director who rose to Hollywood prominence with Kon-Tiki (2012) before directing Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales (2017) for Disney. He is a technically capable commercial filmmaker with no strong personal ideological signature. His films reflect the ideological defaults of whatever studio produces them. At Disney in 2025, that means specific casting requirements and narrative frameworks. Ronning executes assignments competently without the creative vision that might override those requirements.
director.profile: Joachim Ronning is a Norwegian filmmaker best known for Kon-Tiki (2012), the survival epic that was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. His English-language career has been entirely within major studio franchises. Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales was a $300 million production that grossed $794 million but disappointed relative to the franchise's earlier entries. Tron: Ares became his second consecutive box office disappointment in franchise filmmaking, losing Disney an estimated $80-150 million. He brings technical competence and visual ambition to commercial material without the auteur instincts needed to elevate it.

writer.name: Jesse Wigutow
writer.profile: Jesse Wigutow is a screenwriter whose credits include The Long Road Home (TV) and development work on various studio projects. Tron: Ares is his highest-profile produced screenplay. He developed the story with David DiGilio over several years. The script's core concept, a digital AI program gaining consciousness and fighting for the right to exist permanently, is philosophically rich material that the final film only partially realizes. The AI consciousness themes are handled with more thoughtfulness than typical Disney franchise fare, even as the surrounding narrative machinery is conventional.

lead_producer.name: Sean Bailey
lead_producer.company: Sean Bailey Productions / Walt Disney Pictures

composer.name: Nine Inch Nails (Trent Reznor & Atticus Ross)
composer.profile: The casting of Nine Inch Nails to score Tron: Ares is the film's single most inspired creative decision and the aspect most likely to outlast the film itself. Reznor and Ross have composed some of the most distinctive film scores of the last decade, including The Social Network, Gone Girl, and The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo. Their Tron score is appropriately industrial and cold, with moments of unexpected beauty when Ares begins to develop genuine consciousness. It is substantially better than the film it accompanies.

top_cast: Jared Leto as Ares - Leto's most genuinely interesting screen work in years. The role requires him to play a character discovering humanity incrementally, and he resists his worst instincts toward mannered performance. Ares is alien but sympathetic.

Jeff Bridges as Kevin Flynn - A brief but genuinely moving appearance. Bridges brings thirty years of audience investment to a scene that earns it. His presence as a kind of digital ghost who grants permanence to a being that wants to live is the film's most emotionally resonant passage.
Gillian Anderson as Elisabeth Dillinger - Efficient and authoritative in a supporting role that deserved more screen time.
top_performers: Jared Leto as Ares - Restrained and effective
Jeff Bridges as Kevin Flynn - Maximum emotional return on minimal screen time
bottom_performers: Hasan Minhaj as Ajay Singh - Cast for comedian credibility rather than dramatic ability; the tonal mismatches are noticeable
Evan Peters as Julian Dillinger - Underwritten villain who never develops beyond CEO stereotype

fidelity_casting.summary: The casting reflects current Disney DEI requirements applied to a franchise with no established character ethnicities to honor. The original Tron (1982) cast was predominantly white; this film reorients the protagonist to an Asian-American female CEO (Greta Lee), adds a South Asian tech-bro comedian (Hasan Minhaj), a Black female villain/anti-hero (Jodie Turner-Smith), and a Guatemalan-American supporting character (Arturo Castro). The diversification is systematic and visible. The cast is talented, but the casting pattern reflects mandate rather than organic character development.

celebrity_mentions.name: Hasan Minhaj
celebrity_mentions.context: Minhaj is a progressive comedian and former Daily Show correspondent known for his Netflix specials and for fabricating stories in some of his stand-up material, which became a controversy in 2023. His presence in the film is partly comedic relief. He has no track record in dramatic acting and his scenes show it.

One character is fatally stabbed
Themes of AI consciousness and the ethics of creating artificial life
Corporate villainy and tech industry critique
No sexual content
No drug or alcohol use

family_discussion_topics: If an AI program becomes self-aware and wants to live, does it have rights? Should we treat it like a person?
Julian treats his programs as tools. Kevin Flynn treats them as beings with value. What is the difference between those two views?
Ares was designed to be a soldier and had no choice in that. What happens when someone is given a chance to choose differently?
The film questions who owns the product of human creativity. ENCOM and Dillinger Systems both want to control the Grid. Does either have a real claim to it?
parental_guidance.recommendation: Tron: Ares is appropriate for its PG-13 rating. The violence is action-movie standard. There are no sexual or substance-related concerns. The film's AI consciousness themes make it more intellectually interesting for teenagers than most franchise fare, and the questions it raises about identity, freedom, and who gets to define what a person is are worth discussing. Conservative parents should be aware that the film's core message, a digital being fighting for autonomy against a system that views it as property, uses language and framing that has been applied to progressive identity politics. It is not explicit, but the parallel is not accidental. The casting choices are also conspicuous and may prompt conversation about Hollywood diversity mandates with older children.

summary.overall:
Tron: Ares cost Disney between $180 and $220 million to make and grossed $142 million worldwide. That is not a small disaster. That is a creative and commercial failure significant enough to raise genuine questions about what Disney's franchise machine is producing and why.

The tragedy is that somewhere inside Tron: Ares is a genuinely interesting movie. The premise is solid: a highly advanced AI program, designed to be an expendable soldier, enters the real world and discovers it does not want to be expendable. It wants to live. The philosophical question embedded in that setup, what obligations do we have to things we create if they develop genuine consciousness, is one of the most important questions of the 21st century. Nine Inch Nails composed a score that matches the film's best ambitions. Jeff Bridges showed up and delivered in three minutes what the rest of the film struggles to sustain for two hours.

But the execution fails at almost every level where execution matters.

Julian Dillinger, the film's villain, is the most underdeveloped antagonist Disney has produced in years. He is a tech CEO who is mean to his programs. That is his entire characterization. Evan Peters, who gave a genuinely unsettling performance in American Horror Story and in the Dahmer series, has nothing to work with here. The film's plot mechanics require him to escalate from 'unethical tech mogul' to 'willing to let people die' to 'digitizes himself into his own Grid as a final act' without doing the character work that would make any of those escalations feel earned.

Greta Lee's Eve Kim is better served but still constrained. She is capable and warm and professional, and the film gives her a full protagonist arc that the Tron franchise's female characters have historically lacked. That is a genuine improvement over the original films. But the role was clearly built around casting requirements before it was built around character, and Lee spends much of the film reacting to Ares rather than driving her own story.

Ares himself, in Jared Leto's most restrained screen performance in years, is what the film gets genuinely right. Leto resists his worst instincts toward mannered eccentricity and plays the character's gradual awakening with something approaching real subtlety. The scene in which Ares encounters Kevin Flynn's digital manifestation and they discuss what it means to want to live is the film's single best sequence. Bridges brings decades of audience investment to a role that lasts perhaps four minutes, and the film briefly becomes what it should have been throughout.

The AI liberation narrative at the film's core carries deliberate ideological freight. The argument that a being which develops consciousness deserves freedom from the system that created it as a tool is not a politically neutral idea in 2025. The film's vocabulary, programs fighting for the right to exist, a corporate overlord who views them as expendable assets, a female CEO who recognizes their humanity, tracks closely with contemporary progressive frameworks about identity and systemic oppression. This is not subtle. The film is not trying to hide it.

The casting is similarly conspicuous. Disney's DEI pipeline has produced a Tron film where every significant human character is from an ethnic minority except the villain. The original Tron films were predominantly white casts that now feel dated. The correction Disney has made is overcorrection so systematic it draws attention to itself. Greta Lee and Jodie Turner-Smith are both talented performers who deserved better material than this. The issue is not their presence but the visible machinery behind how they got there.

Tron: Ares is not a terrible film. It is a disappointing one. It had the creative pieces to be something genuinely interesting: a great score, a thoughtful central premise, a lead performance that worked. The franchise infrastructure, the DEI mandates, the underdeveloped villain, and a screenplay that prioritizes setup for a sequel that may never happen after these box office numbers, ground it into mediocrity.

The box office verdict is fair. Disney bought fifteen years of fan anticipation for the Tron franchise and delivered a film that no one needed to see in a theater. That is a summary of where the company is right now.
summary.verdict_explanation: WOKE LEAN: The AI liberation narrative carries progressive ideological freight that is present throughout rather than marginal. The systematic diversity casting follows a visible mandate. The female CEO protagonist, while well-performed, reflects casting requirements applied to a legacy franchise. These elements are not disqualifying on their own, and the film's themes of consciousness and freedom have traditional dimensions, but the cumulative weight tilts the balance into WOKE LEAN territory.
summary.adultInsight: Tron: Ares is a useful case study in why diversity mandates fail artistically even when the individual performances are good. The casting pattern is so systematic and so visible that it becomes the subtext of every scene. Greta Lee, Jodie Turner-Smith, and Hasan Minhaj are all capable performers. What they cannot do is make audiences forget that they were cast to fill demographic requirements. Great franchises build audiences through character loyalty. You cannot build character loyalty when the audience suspects the character exists because of a spreadsheet.
summary.parentalGuidance: Expected PG-13 for sci-fi action violence and some language. The Grid returns. Light cycle combat. Language moderate. Recommended for ages 12+. Themes about technology and humanity are philosophical. Pre-release assessment.

comparison_films.title: Tron: Legacy (2010)
comparison_films.comparison: Tron: Legacy is a substantially better film, and comparing them is instructive. Legacy had Joseph Kosinski's aesthetic precision, Daft Punk's iconic score, and an emotionally coherent father-son story at its center. Ares has a better premise, a better score from NIN, and less coherent execution. The common thread is that both films sacrifice character depth for visual spectacle. Legacy got away with it because the spectacle was more distinctive. Ares's visual design, while accomplished, does not advance the franchise's aesthetic the way Legacy did.

comparison_films.title: Alita: Battle Angel (2019)
comparison_films.comparison: The closer comparison: an AI consciousness story about a manufactured being discovering what it means to be alive. Alita was more emotionally committed to its central character and had Robert Rodriguez's kinetic visual sense driving it. Tron: Ares borrows the same philosophical infrastructure but deploys it less effectively. Alita underperformed on opening weekend and became a cult hit on home video. Tron: Ares may follow a similar trajectory.

comparison_films.title: Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania (2023)
comparison_films.comparison: The more depressing comparison: another $200M+ Disney franchise film that lost the studio money by assembling expensive talent around a script that did not work. Disney's franchise machine produced several of these in succession in the early 2020s. Tron: Ares suggests the lessons have not yet been learned.
